short_description: ABL1 (ABL proto-oncogene 1, non-receptor tyrosine kinase) (eg, acquired imatinib tyrosine kinase inhibitor resistance), gene analysis, variants in the kinase domain
lay_term: The lab analyst performs the technical lab test to analyze variants in the kinase domain of the ABL1 gene, also called BCR/ABL or ABL proto–oncogene 1 nonreceptor tyrosine kinase. Explanation The lab analyst performs all technical steps, from extracting the nucleic acids by methods such as cell lysis (using an agent or substance to break down cells into their components), to increasing and stabilizing the quantity of nucleic acid for analysis by amplification (making more copies of the gene), to detecting the target genes by methods such as nucleic acid probes. Code 81170 involves analyzing specific mutations (alterations in DNA that may lead to pathologic changes) in the kinase domain of the ABL1 gene that may be involved in acquired resistance to tyrosine kinase inhibitor medications such as Imatinib. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians may order this test for patients with chronic myeloid leukemia to help evaluate treatment options or treatment failure, specifically using tyrosine kinase inhibitor medications such as Imatinib. Terminology Amplification: Making more copies of desired gene for study by processes such as polymerase chain reaction, called PCR, or transcription of DNA to RNA and reverse transcription from RNA to make an additional copy of the DNA. Gene: Specific nucleic acid sequence associated with a unique function in the body such as production of a specific protein. Nucleic acid: A sequence of specific biological chemicals, called nucleotides, which carry genetic information; known as deoxyribonucleic acid, or DNA, or ribonucleic acid, or RNA. Proto–oncogene: A normal gene involved in cell growth and differentiation that can change into an active oncogene, a gene that can cause normal cells to change or mutate into abnormal or cancerous cells. Translocation: The process or genetic abnormality that occurs when disparate portions of one or more chromosomes become attached and create a hybrid segment, called a fusion gene, inserted in one or both of the broken chromosomes. Variant: Gene that differs from the usual nucleic acid sequence due to events such as nucleotide deletions/insertions or substitutions; may cause conditions such as genetic disorders or cancer. Tips You may separately report prep work that precedes cell lysis, when documented. If the ordering clinician separately requests physician interpretation of the 81170 test and the pathologist renders an interpretation and writes a report, you can additionally report G0452, Molecular pathology procedure; physician interpretation and report, with modifier 26 to Medicare and perhaps other payers. An M.D. or D.O. physician must perform the interpretation, not a PhD laboratory scientist, according to CMS. Read Less
guidelines: Lab & Path Guidelines Section Specific Guideline Molecular pathology procedures are medical laboratory procedures involving the analyses of nucleic acid (ie, DNA, RNA) to detect variants in genes that may be indicative of germline (eg, constitutional disorders) or somatic (eg, neoplasia) conditions, or to test for histocompatibility antigens (eg, HLA). Code selection is typically based on the specific gene(s) that is being analyzed. Genes are described using Human Genome Organization (HUGO) approved gene names and are italicized in the code descriptors. Gene names were taken from tables of the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee (HGNC) at the time the CPT® codes were developed. For the most part, Human Genome Variation Society (HGVS) recommendations were followed for the names of specific molecular variants. The familiar name is used for some variants because defined criteria were not in place when the variant was first described or because HGVS recommendations were changed over time (eg, intronic variants, processed proteins). When the gene name is represented by an abbreviation, the abbreviation is listed first, followed by the full gene name italicized in parentheses (eg, "F5 [coagulation Factor V]"), except for the HLA series of codes. Proteins or diseases commonly associated with the genes are listed as examples in the code descriptors. The examples do not represent all conditions in which testing of the gene may be indicated. Codes that describe tests to assess for the presence of gene variants (see definitions) use common gene variant names. Typically, all of the listed variants would be tested. However, these lists are not exclusive. If other variants are also tested in the analysis, they would be included in the procedure and not reported separately. Full gene sequencing should not be reported using codes that assess for the presence of gene variants unless specifically stated in the code descriptor. The molecular pathology codes include all analytical services performed in the test (eg, cell lysis, nucleic acid stabilization, extraction, digestion, amplification, and detection). Any procedures required prior to cell lysis (eg, microdissection, codes 88380 and 88381) should be reported separately. The results of the procedure may require interpretation by a physician or other qualified health care professional. When only the interpretation and report are performed, modifier 26 may be appended to the specific molecular pathology code. All analyses are qualitative unless otherwise noted. For microbial identification, see 87149-87153 and 87471-87801, and 87900-87904. For in situ hybridization analyses, see 88271-88275 and 88365-88368. Molecular pathology procedures that are not specified in 81161, 81200-81383 should be reported using either the appropriate Tier 2 code (81400-81408) or the unlisted molecular pathology procedure code, 81479. Definitions For purposes of CPT® reporting, the following definitions apply: Abnormal allele: an alternative form of a gene that contains a disease-related variation from the normal sequence. Breakpoint: the region at which a chromosome breaks during a translocation (defined elsewhere). These regions are often consistent for a given translocation. Codon: a discrete unit of three nucleotides of a DNA or mRNA sequence that encodes a specific amino acid within, or signals the termination of, a polypeptide. Common variants: variants (as defined elsewhere) that are associated with compromised gene function and are interrogated in a single round of laboratory testing (in a single, typically multiplex, assay format or using more than one assay to encompass all variants to be tested). These variants typically fit the definition of a "mutation," and are usually the predominant ones causing disease. Testing for additional uncommon variants may provide additional limited value in assessment of a patient. Often there are professional society recommendations or guidelines for which variants are most appropriate to test (eg, American College of Medical Genetics/American College of Obstetrics and Gynecology guidelines for variants used in population screening for cystic fibrosis). Constitutional: synonymous with germline, often used in reference to the genetic code that is present at birth. Copy number variants (CNVs): structural changes in the genome composed of large deletions or duplications. CNVs can be found in the germline, but can also occur in somatic cells. See also Duplication/Deletion (Dup/Del). Cytogenomic: a comprehensive genome-wide analysis of chromosomal and genetic abnormalities using molecular-based technologies. DNA methylation: the process of adding methyl groups to a DNA sequence, specifically adenine and cytosine nucleotides, thereby affecting transcription of that sequence. DNA hyper-methylation in a gene promoter typically represses gene transcription. DNA methylation serves as a regulatory mechanism in numerous scenarios including development, chromosome inactivation, and carcinogenesis. DNA methylation analysis: analytical protocols are designed to evaluate the degree of DNA methylation related to specific disease processes. This analysis has various applications, qualitative or quantitative, and could be gene specific or encompass global degrees of methylation. All assays employ specific maneuvers (eg, chemical, enzymatic) that allow for distinguishable evaluation of methylated and non-methylated sequences. Duplication/Deletion (Dup/Del): terms that are usually used together with the "/" to refer to molecular testing, which assesses the dosage of a particular genomic region. The region tested is typically of modest to substantial size-from several dozen to several million or more nucleotides. Normal gene dosage is two copies per cell, except for the sex chromosomes (X and Y). Thus, zero or one copy represents a deletion, and three (or more) copies represent a duplication. Dynamic mutation: polynucleotide (eg, trinucleotide) repeats that are in or associated with genes that can undergo disease-producing increases or decreases in the numbers of repeats within tissues and across generations. Exome: DNA sequences within the human genome that code for proteins (coding regions). Exon: typically, one of multiple nucleic acid sequences used to encode information for a gene product (polypeptide or protein). Exons are separated from each other by non-protein-coding sequences known as introns. Exons at the respective ends of a gene also contain nucleic acid sequence that does not code for the gene's protein product. Gene: a nucleic acid sequence that typically contains information for coding a protein as well as for the regulated expression of that protein. Human genes usually contain multiple protein coding regions (exons) separated by non-protein coding regions (introns). See also exon, intron, and polypeptide. Gene expression: the sequence of events that results in the production and assembly of a protein product corresponding to the information encoded in a specific gene. The process begins with the transcription of gene sequences to produce an mRNA intermediary, which is subsequently translated to produce a specific protein product. Genome: the total (nuclear) human genetic content. Heteroplasmy: the copy number of a variant within a cell; it is expressed as a percent. lay_term: The lab analyst performs the technical lab test to analyze the entire gene sequence for adenomatous polyposis coli, also known as APC. Explanation The lab analyst performs all technical steps, from extracting the nucleic acids by methods such as cell lysis and digestion, to increasing and stabilizing the quantity of nucleic acid for analysis by amplification, to detecting the target genes by methods such as nucleic acid probes. Code 81201 involves analyzing the full gene sequence for APC, not just common variations in the gene. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians may commonly order this test for patients with suspected familial adenomatosis polyposis, also known as FAP, or suspected attenuated FAP. These conditions are inherited disorders that involve formation of non–cancerous growths in the colon, called polyps, which often lead to colon cancer. Attenuated FAP is characterized by later onset, but both conditions involve the APC gene. Nucleic acid: DNA or RNA; sequence of specific biological chemicals, called nucleotides, that carry genetic information. Tips You may separately report prep work that precedes cell lysis, when documented. If the ordering clinician separately requests physician interpretation of the 81201 test and the pathologist renders an interpretation and writes a report, you can additionally report G0452 with modifier 26 to Medicare and perhaps other payers. An M.D. or D.O physician must perform the interpretation, not a PhD laboratory scientist, according to CMS. Don’t confuse testing for autosomal recessive familial adenomatous polyposis, also called MYH–associated polyposis, with FAP even though the names are similar. The former condition involves changes to the MUTYH gene rather than to the APC gene. Make sure to distinguish the 81201 test for the full APC gene sequence from the 81202 test for APC familial variants and from the 81203 test for APC duplication/deletion variants. Read Less

Explanation The lab analyst performs all technical steps, from extracting the nucleic acids by methods such as digestion and cell lysis, to increasing and stabilizing the quantity of nucleic acid for analysis by amplification (making more copies of the gene), to detecting the target genes by methods such as nucleic acid probes, using a specimen such as blood. Code 81176 involves analyzing a targeted gene sequence, such as exon 12, for ASXL1. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians may commonly order this test to help with diagnosis and prognosis for patients with conditions such as myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPN), myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS), and chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML). Terminology Amplification: Making more copies of desired gene for study by processes such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR) or transcription of DNA to RNA and reverse transcription from RNA to make an additional copy of the DNA. Exon: Nucleic acid sequence that includes at least part of the code for a specific product, such as a protein. Gene: Specific nucleic acid sequence associated with a unique function in the body such as production of a specific protein. Nucleic acid: A sequence of specific biological chemicals, called nucleotides, which carry genetic information; known as deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), or ribonucleic acid (RNA). Tips Some payers may pay separately for collecting the specimen using a code such as 36415. You should distinguish this code from other molecular pathology tests for the ASXL1 gene, such as 81175, which describes full gene sequence analysis. You may separately report prep work that precedes cell lysis, when documented. If the ordering clinician separately requests physician interpretation of the 81176 test and the pathologist renders an interpretation and writes a report, you can additionally report G0452, Molecular pathology procedure; physician interpretation and report, with modifier 26 to Medicare and perhaps other payers. An MD or DO physician must perform the interpretation, not a PhD laboratory scientist, according to CMS. Read Less
guidelines: Lab & Path Guidelines Section Specific Guideline Molecular pathology procedures are medical laboratory procedures involving the analyses of nucleic acid (ie, DNA, RNA) to detect variants in genes that may be indicative of germline (eg, constitutional disorders) or somatic (eg, neoplasia) conditions, or to test for histocompatibility antigens (eg, HLA). Code selection is typically based on the specific gene(s) that is being analyzed. Genes are described using Human Genome Organization (HUGO) approved gene names and are italicized in the code descriptors. Gene names were taken from tables of the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee (HGNC) at the time the CPT® codes were developed. For the most part, Human Genome Variation Society (HGVS) recommendations were followed for the names of specific molecular variants. The familiar name is used for some variants because defined criteria were not in place when the variant was first described or because HGVS recommendations were changed over time (eg, intronic variants, processed proteins). When the gene name is represented by an abbreviation, the abbreviation is listed first, followed by the full gene name italicized in parentheses (eg, "F5 [coagulation Factor V]"), except for the HLA series of codes. Proteins or diseases commonly associated with the genes are listed as examples in the code descriptors. The examples do not represent all conditions in which testing of the gene may be indicated. Codes that describe tests to assess for the presence of gene variants (see definitions) use common gene variant names. Typically, all of the listed variants would be tested. However, these lists are not exclusive. If other variants are also tested in the analysis, they would be included in the procedure and not reported separately. Full gene sequencing should not be reported using codes that assess for the presence of gene variants unless specifically stated in the code descriptor. The molecular pathology codes include all analytical services performed in the test (eg, cell lysis, nucleic acid stabilization, extraction, digestion, amplification, and detection). Any procedures required prior to cell lysis (eg, microdissection, codes 88380 and 88381) should be reported separately. The results of the procedure may require interpretation by a physician or other qualified health care professional. When only the interpretation and report are performed, modifier 26 may be appended to the specific molecular pathology code. All analyses are qualitative unless otherwise noted. For microbial identification, see 87149-87153 and 87471-87801, and 87900-87904. For in situ hybridization analyses, see 88271-88275 and 88365-88368. Molecular pathology procedures that are not specified in 81161, 81200-81383 should be reported using either the appropriate Tier 2 code (81400-81408) or the unlisted molecular pathology procedure code, 81479. Definitions For purposes of CPT® reporting, the following definitions apply: Abnormal allele: an alternative form of a gene that contains a disease-related variation from the normal sequence. Breakpoint: the region at which a chromosome breaks during a translocation (defined elsewhere). These regions are often consistent for a given translocation. Codon: a discrete unit of three nucleotides of a DNA or mRNA sequence that encodes a specific amino acid within, or signals the termination of, a polypeptide. Common variants: variants (as defined elsewhere) that are associated with compromised gene function and are interrogated in a single round of laboratory testing (in a single, typically multiplex, assay format or using more than one assay to encompass all variants to be tested). These variants typically fit the definition of a "mutation," and are usually the predominant ones causing disease. Testing for additional uncommon variants may provide additional limited value in assessment of a patient. Often there are professional society recommendations or guidelines for which variants are most appropriate to test (eg, American College of Medical Genetics/American College of Obstetrics and Gynecology guidelines for variants used in population screening for cystic fibrosis). Constitutional: synonymous with germline, often used in reference to the genetic code that is present at birth. Copy number variants (CNVs): structural changes in the genome composed of large deletions or duplications. CNVs can be found in the germline, but can also occur in somatic cells. See also Duplication/Deletion (Dup/Del). Cytogenomic: a comprehensive genome-wide analysis of chromosomal and genetic abnormalities using molecular-based technologies. DNA methylation: the process of adding methyl groups to a DNA sequence, specifically adenine and cytosine nucleotides, thereby affecting transcription of that sequence. DNA hyper-methylation in a gene promoter typically represses gene transcription. DNA methylation serves as a regulatory mechanism in numerous scenarios including development, chromosome inactivation, and carcinogenesis. DNA methylation analysis: analytical protocols are designed to evaluate the degree of DNA methylation related to specific disease processes. This analysis has various applications, qualitative or quantitative, and could be gene specific or encompass global degrees of methylation. All assays employ specific maneuvers (eg, chemical, enzymatic) that allow for distinguishable evaluation of methylated and non-methylated sequences. Duplication/Deletion (Dup/Del): terms that are usually used together with the "/" to refer to molecular testing, which assesses the dosage of a particular genomic region. The region tested is typically of modest to substantial size-from several dozen to several million or more nucleotides. Normal gene dosage is two copies per cell, except for the sex chromosomes (X and Y). Thus, zero or one copy represents a deletion, and three (or more) copies represent a duplication. Dynamic mutation: polynucleotide (eg, trinucleotide) repeats that are in or associated with genes that can undergo disease-producing increases or decreases in the numbers of repeats within tissues and across generations. Exome: DNA sequences within the human genome that code for proteins (coding regions). Exon: typically, one of multiple nucleic acid sequences used to encode information for a gene product (polypeptide or protein). Exons are separated from each other by non-protein-coding sequences known as introns. Exons at the respective ends of a gene also contain nucleic acid sequence that does not code for the gene's protein product. Gene: a nucleic acid sequence that typically contains information for coding a protein as well as for the regulated expression of that protein. Human genes usually contain multiple protein coding regions (exons) separated by non-protein coding regions (introns). See also exon, intron, and polypeptide. Gene expression: the sequence of events that results in the production and assembly of a protein product corresponding to the information encoded in a specific gene. The process begins with the transcription of gene sequences to produce an mRNA intermediary, which is subsequently translated to produce a specific protein product. Genome: the total (nuclear) human genetic content. Heteroplasmy: the copy number of a variant within a cell; it is expressed as a percent. It reflects the varied distribution and dosage of mutant mitochondria in tissues and organs (mitotic segregation). Intron: a nucleic acid sequence found between exons in human genes. An intron contains essential sequences for its proper removal (by a process known as splicing) to join exons together and thus facilitate production of a functional protein from a gene. An intron is sometimes referred to as an intervening sequence (IVS). Inversion: a defect in a chromosome in which a segment breaks and reinserts in the same place but in the opposite orientation. Loss of heterozygosity (LOH, allelic imbalance): an event that can occur in dividing cells that are heterozygous for one or more alleles, in which a daughter cell becomes hemizygous or homozygous for the allele(s) through mitotic recombination, deletion, or other chromosomal event. Low-pass sequencing: a method of genome sequencing intended for cytogenomic analysis of chromosomal abnormalities, such as that performed for trait mapping or copy number variation, typically performed to an average depth of sequencing ranging from 0.1 to 5X. Microarray: surface(s) on which multiple specific nucleic acid sequences are attached in a known arrangement. Sometimes referred to as a "gene chip." Examples of uses of microarrays include evaluation of a patient specimen for gains or losses of DNA sequences (copy number variants, CNVs), identification of the presence of specific nucleotide sequence variants (also known as single nucleotide polymorphisms, SNPs), mRNA expression levels, or DNA sequence analysis. Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA): DNA located in the mitochondria, which are cytoplasmic organelles involved with energy production. MtDNA contains 37 genes coding for oxidative phosphorylation enzymes, transfer RNAs (tRNAs) and ribosomal RNAs (rRNAs). Mutations: typically are variants associated with altered gene function that lead to functional deficits or disease (pathogenic). Mutation scanning: a technique (eg, single strand conformation polymorphism, temperature gradient gel electrophoresis, etc.) typically employed on multiple PCR amplicons to indicate the presence of DNA sequence variants by differences in physical properties compared to normal. Variants are then further characterized by DNA sequence analysis only in amplicons which demonstrate differences. Nuclear DNA: DNA located in the nucleus of a cell, generally packaged in chromosomes. Polymorphisms: typically are variants that do not compromise gene function or produce disease (benign). Polypeptide: a sequence of amino acids covalently linked in a specified order. Polypeptides alone or in combination with other polypeptide subunits are the building blocks of proteins. Promoter: a region of DNA associated with a gene (on the same strand) which regulates gene expression. Promoter regions can affect gene transcription through the binding of specific transcription factors. Short tandem repeat (STR): a region of DNA where a pattern of two or more nucleotides are repeated. The number of repeating segments can be used as genetic markers for human identity testing. Single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP): a DNA sequence variation existing at a significant frequency in the population, in which a single nucleotide (A, T, C, or G) differs between individuals and/or within an individual's paired chromosomes. Somatic: synonymous with acquired, referring to genetic code alterations that develop after birth (eg, occurring in neoplastic cells). Translocation: an abnormality resulting from the breakage of a chromosome and the relocation of a portion of that chromosome's DNA sequence to the same or another chromosome. Most common translocations involve a reciprocal exchange of DNA sequences between two differently numbered (ie, non-homologous) chromosomes, with or without a clinically significant loss of DNA. Uniparental disomy (UPD): abnormal inheritance of both members of a chromosome pair from one parent, with absence of the other parent's chromosome for the pair. Variant: a nucleotide sequence difference from the "normal" (predominant) sequence for a given region. Variants are typically of two types: substitutions of one nucleotide for another, and deletions or insertions of nucleotides. Occasionally, variants reflect several nucleotide sequence changes in reasonably close proximity on the same chromosomal strand of DNA (a haplotype). These nucleotide sequence variants often result in amino acid changes in the protein made by the gene. The term variant does not itself carry a functional implication for those protein changes. Variants in introns are typically described in one of two ways. The altered nucleotide(s) within a defined intervening sequence (eg, IVS3-2A>G) of a gene is listed with a "+" or "-" sign, which indicates the position relative to the first or last nucleotide of the intron. Or, the variant position is indicated relative to the last nucleotide of the preceding exon or first nucleotide of the following exon (eg, c.171+1G>A c.172-1G>T are single nucleotide changes at the first and last nucleotide of a given intron for a specific gene). The majority of the variants described here are listed by the amino acid change using the single letter amino acid code for the original amino acid followed by the numerical position in the protein product and the amino acid substitution, eg, for ASPA E285A, Glutamic acid (E) at position 285 is replaced with an alanine (A). A few of the variants are described by the DNA change using the numerical position followed by the original nucleotide, a greater than sign (>) and the new nucleotide, eg, MTHFR. 677C>T. A known familial variant is a specific mutation that has previously been identified within a patient's family. The following codes represent gene-specific and genomic procedures:

lay_term: The lab analyst performs the technical lab test to detect the presence of common changes in the gene for branched–chain keto acid dehydrogenase E1, beta polypeptide, also known as BCKDHB. Explanation The lab analyst performs all technical steps, from extracting the nucleic acids by methods such as cell lysis and digestion, to increasing and stabilizing the quantity of nucleic acid for analysis by amplification, to detecting the target genes by methods such as nucleic acid probes. A single unit of 81205 represents testing for any common changes in the BCKDHB gene, known as common variants. The test will typically include all variants listed in the code, R183P, G278S, E422X, and may include other, non–listed variants. Clinicians may commonly order this test for patients with suspected maple syrup urine disease, which is characterized by the toxic buildup of three chemicals called amino acids in the body: leucine, isoleucine, and valine. Because changes to the BCKDHB gene can interfere with the body’s ability to break down these chemicals, they can accumulate and cause damage to the nervous system leading to seizures, developmental delays, and other problems. Nucleic acid: DNA or RNA; sequence of specific biological chemicals, called nucleotides, that carry genetic information. Variant: Gene that differs from the usual nucleic acid sequence due to events such as nucleotide deletions/insertions or substitutions; may cause conditions such as genetic disorders or cancer. Tips You may separately report prep work that precedes cell lysis, when documented. If the ordering clinician separately requests physician interpretation of the 81205 test and the pathologist renders an interpretation and writes a report, you can additionally report G0452 with modifier 26 to Medicare and perhaps other payers. An M.D. or D.O physician must perform the interpretation, not a PhD laboratory scientist, according to CMS. Read Less

Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians may order this test for patients with a family history or who are diagnosed with breast, ovarian, or certain other cancers to establish their hereditary status. Both BRCA1 and BRCA2 are tumor suppressor genes, and many heritable changes to these genes are associated with breast and ovarian cancer, as well as other cancers such as prostate, pancreatic, and fallopian–tube cancer, and melanoma. Nucleic acid: A sequence of specific biological chemicals (nucleotides) that carry genetic information; known as deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) or ribonucleic acid (RNA). Code selection is typically based on the specific gene(s) that is being analyzed. Genes are described using Human Genome Organization (HUGO) approved gene names and are italicized in the code descriptors. Gene names were taken from tables of the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee (HGNC) at the time the CPT® codes were developed. For the most part, Human Genome Variation Society (HGVS) recommendations were followed for the names of specific molecular variants. The familiar name is used for some variants because defined criteria were not in place when the variant was first described or because HGVS recommendations were changed over time (eg, intronic variants, processed proteins). When the gene name is represented by an abbreviation, the abbreviation is listed first, followed by the full gene name italicized in parentheses (eg, "F5 [coagulation Factor V]"), except for the HLA series of codes. Proteins or diseases commonly associated with the genes are listed as examples in the code descriptors. The examples do not represent all conditions in which testing of the gene may be indicated. Codes that describe tests to assess for the presence of gene variants (see definitions) use common gene variant names. Typically, all of the listed variants would be tested. However, these lists are not exclusive. If other variants are also tested in the analysis, they would be included in the procedure and not reported separately. Full gene sequencing should not be reported using codes that assess for the presence of gene variants unless specifically stated in the code descriptor. The molecular pathology codes include all analytical services performed in the test (eg, cell lysis, nucleic acid stabilization, extraction, digestion, amplification, and detection). Any procedures required prior to cell lysis (eg, microdissection, codes 88380 and 88381) should be reported separately. The results of the procedure may require interpretation by a physician or other qualified health care professional. When only the interpretation and report are performed, modifier 26 may be appended to the specific molecular pathology code. All analyses are qualitative unless otherwise noted. For microbial identification, see 87149-87153 and 87471-87801, and 87900-87904. For in situ hybridization analyses, see 88271-88275 and 88365-88368. Molecular pathology procedures that are not specified in 81161, 81200-81383 should be reported using either the appropriate Tier 2 code (81400-81408) or the unlisted molecular pathology procedure code, 81479. Definitions For purposes of CPT® reporting, the following definitions apply: Abnormal allele: an alternative form of a gene that contains a disease-related variation from the normal sequence. Breakpoint: the region at which a chromosome breaks during a translocation (defined elsewhere). These regions are often consistent for a given translocation. Codon: a discrete unit of three nucleotides of a DNA or mRNA sequence that encodes a specific amino acid within, or signals the termination of, a polypeptide. Common variants: variants (as defined elsewhere) that are associated with compromised gene function and are interrogated in a single round of laboratory testing (in a single, typically multiplex, assay format or using more than one assay to encompass all variants to be tested). These variants typically fit the definition of a "mutation," and are usually the predominant ones causing disease. Testing for additional uncommon variants may provide additional limited value in assessment of a patient. Often there are professional society recommendations or guidelines for which variants are most appropriate to test (eg, American College of Medical Genetics/American College of Obstetrics and Gynecology guidelines for variants used in population screening for cystic fibrosis). Constitutional: synonymous with germline, often used in reference to the genetic code that is present at birth. Copy number variants (CNVs): structural changes in the genome composed of large deletions or duplications. CNVs can be found in the germline, but can also occur in somatic cells. See also Duplication/Deletion (Dup/Del). Cytogenomic: a comprehensive genome-wide analysis of chromosomal and genetic abnormalities using molecular-based technologies. DNA methylation: the process of adding methyl groups to a DNA sequence, specifically adenine and cytosine nucleotides, thereby affecting transcription of that sequence. DNA hyper-methylation in a gene promoter typically represses gene transcription. DNA methylation serves as a regulatory mechanism in numerous scenarios including development, chromosome inactivation, and carcinogenesis. DNA methylation analysis: analytical protocols are designed to evaluate the degree of DNA methylation related to specific disease processes. This analysis has various applications, qualitative or quantitative, and could be gene specific or encompass global degrees of methylation. All assays employ specific maneuvers (eg, chemical, enzymatic) that allow for distinguishable evaluation of methylated and non-methylated sequences. Duplication/Deletion (Dup/Del): terms that are usually used together with the "/" to refer to molecular testing, which assesses the dosage of a particular genomic region. The region tested is typically of modest to substantial size-from several dozen to several million or more nucleotides. Normal gene dosage is two copies per cell, except for the sex chromosomes (X and Y). Thus, zero or one copy represents a deletion, and three (or more) copies represent a duplication. Dynamic mutation: polynucleotide (eg, trinucleotide) repeats that are in or associated with genes that can undergo disease-producing increases or decreases in the numbers of repeats within tissues and across generations. Exome: DNA sequences within the human genome that code for proteins (coding regions). Exon: typically, one of multiple nucleic acid sequences used to encode information for a gene product (polypeptide or protein). Exons are separated from each other by non-protein-coding sequences known as introns. Exons at the respective ends of a gene also contain nucleic acid sequence that does not code for the gene's protein product. Gene: a nucleic acid sequence that typically contains information for coding a protein as well as for the regulated expression of that protein. Human genes usually contain multiple protein coding regions (exons) separated by non-protein coding regions (introns). See also exon, intron, and polypeptide. Gene expression: the sequence of events that results in the production and assembly of a protein product corresponding to the information encoded in a specific gene. The process begins with the transcription of gene sequences to produce an mRNA intermediary, which is subsequently translated to produce a specific protein product. Genome: the total (nuclear) human genetic content. Heteroplasmy: the copy number of a variant within a cell; it is expressed as a percent. It reflects the varied distribution and dosage of mutant mitochondria in tissues and organs (mitotic segregation). Intron: a nucleic acid sequence found between exons in human genes. An intron contains essential sequences for its proper removal (by a process known as splicing) to join exons together and thus facilitate production of a functional protein from a gene. An intron is sometimes referred to as an intervening sequence (IVS). Inversion: a defect in a chromosome in which a segment breaks and reinserts in the same place but in the opposite orientation. Loss of heterozygosity (LOH, allelic imbalance): an event that can occur in dividing cells that are heterozygous for one or more alleles, in which a daughter cell becomes hemizygous or homozygous for the allele(s) through mitotic recombination, deletion, or other chromosomal event. Low-pass sequencing: a method of genome sequencing intended for cytogenomic analysis of chromosomal abnormalities, such as that performed for trait mapping or copy number variation, typically performed to an average depth of sequencing ranging from 0.1 to 5X. Microarray: surface(s) on which multiple specific nucleic acid sequences are attached in a known arrangement. Sometimes referred to as a "gene chip." Examples of uses of microarrays include evaluation of a patient specimen for gains or losses of DNA sequences (copy number variants, CNVs), identification of the presence of specific nucleotide sequence variants (also known as single nucleotide polymorphisms, SNPs), mRNA expression levels, or DNA sequence analysis. Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA): DNA located in the mitochondria, which are cytoplasmic organelles involved with energy production. MtDNA contains 37 genes coding for oxidative phosphorylation enzymes, transfer RNAs (tRNAs) and ribosomal RNAs (rRNAs). Mutations: typically are variants associated with altered gene function that lead to functional deficits or disease (pathogenic). Mutation scanning: a technique (eg, single strand conformation polymorphism, temperature gradient gel electrophoresis, etc.) typically employed on multiple PCR amplicons to indicate the presence of DNA sequence variants by differences in physical properties compared to normal. Variants are then further characterized by DNA sequence analysis only in amplicons which demonstrate differences. Nuclear DNA: DNA located in the nucleus of a cell, generally packaged in chromosomes. Polymorphisms: typically are variants that do not compromise gene function or produce disease (benign). Polypeptide: a sequence of amino acids covalently linked in a specified order. Polypeptides alone or in combination with other polypeptide subunits are the building blocks of proteins. Promoter: a region of DNA associated with a gene (on the same strand) which regulates gene expression. Promoter regions can affect gene transcription through the binding of specific transcription factors. Short tandem repeat (STR): a region of DNA where a pattern of two or more nucleotides are repeated. The number of repeating segments can be used as genetic markers for human identity testing. Single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP): a DNA sequence variation existing at a significant frequency in the population, in which a single nucleotide (A, T, C, or G) differs between individuals and/or within an individual's paired chromosomes. Somatic: synonymous with acquired, referring to genetic code alterations that develop after birth (eg, occurring in neoplastic cells). Translocation: an abnormality resulting from the breakage of a chromosome and the relocation of a portion of that chromosome's DNA sequence to the same or another chromosome. Most common translocations involve a reciprocal exchange of DNA sequences between two differently numbered (ie, non-homologous) chromosomes, with or without a clinically significant loss of DNA. Uniparental disomy (UPD): abnormal inheritance of both members of a chromosome pair from one parent, with absence of the other parent's chromosome for the pair. Variant: a nucleotide sequence difference from the "normal" (predominant) sequence for a given region. Variants are typically of two types: substitutions of one nucleotide for another, and deletions or insertions of nucleotides. Occasionally, variants reflect several nucleotide sequence changes in reasonably close proximity on the same chromosomal strand of DNA (a haplotype). These nucleotide sequence variants often result in amino acid changes in the protein made by the gene. The term variant does not itself carry a functional implication for those protein changes. Variants in introns are typically described in one of two ways. The altered nucleotide(s) within a defined intervening sequence (eg, IVS3-2A>G) of a gene is listed with a "+" or "-" sign, which indicates the position relative to the first or last nucleotide of the intron. Or, the variant position is indicated relative to the last nucleotide of the preceding exon or first nucleotide of the following exon (eg, c.171+1G>A c.172-1G>T are single nucleotide changes at the first and last nucleotide of a given intron for a specific gene). The majority of the variants described here are listed by the amino acid change using the single letter amino acid code for the original amino acid followed by the numerical position in the protein product and the amino acid substitution, eg, for ASPA E285A, Glutamic acid (E) at position 285 is replaced with an alanine (A). A few of the variants are described by the DNA change using the numerical position followed by the original nucleotide, a greater than sign (>) and the new nucleotide, eg, MTHFR. 677C>T. A known familial variant is a specific mutation that has previously been identified within a patient's family. The following codes represent gene-specific and genomic procedures:

lay_term: The lab analyst performs the technical lab test to analyze the entire gene sequence for the BRCA1 DNA repair–associated gene, also known as BRCA1, and the BRCA2 DNA repair–associated gene, also known as BRCA2. Explanation The lab analyst performs all technical steps, using a specimen such as blood, from extracting the nucleic acids by methods such as cell lysis and digestion, to increasing and stabilizing the quantity of nucleic acid for analysis by amplification using a method such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR), to detecting the target genes. Code 81163 involves analyzing the BRCA1 and BRCA2 full gene sequences. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians may order this test for patients with a family history or who are diagnosed with breast, ovarian, or certain other cancers to establish their hereditary status. Both BRCA1 and BRCA2 are tumor suppressor genes, and many heritable changes to these genes are associated with breast and ovarian cancer, as well as other cancers such as prostate, pancreatic, and fallopian tube cancer, and melanoma. Terminology Amplification: Making more copies of a desired gene for study by processes such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR) or transcription of DNA to RNA and reverse transcription from RNA to make an additional copy of the DNA. Gene: Specific nucleic acid sequence associated with a unique function in the body such as production of a specific protein. Lysis: The act of breaking down a structure; destroying cells or tissue using an agent or substance. Mutation: An alteration in a deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) sequence that may lead to pathologic changes in the organism. Nucleic acid: A sequence of specific biological chemicals (nucleotides) that carry genetic information; known as deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) or ribonucleic acid (RNA). Reverse transcription: Generation of a complementary DNA sequence from a template of RNA. Ribonucleic acid (RNA): One of the essential building blocks of life, along with deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and proteins; RNA acts as a messenger (mRNA), carrying genetic information from DNA to proteins, helps regulate cellular processes, and, like enzymes, can speed up chemical reactions; RNA, rather than DNA, carries genetic information in some important viruses. Variant: Gene that differs from the usual nucleic acid sequence due to events such as nucleotide deletions or insertions or substitutions; may cause conditions such as genetic disorders or cancer. Tips Some payers may pay separately for collecting the specimen using a code such as 36415. You may separately report prep work that precedes cell lysis, when documented. If the ordering clinician separately requests physician interpretation of the 81163 test and the pathologist renders an interpretation and writes a report, you can additionally report G0452 with modifier 26 to Medicare and perhaps other payers. An MD or DO physician, not a PhD laboratory scientist, must perform the interpretation according to CMS. Make sure to distinguish tests for both the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes. Read Less

Code selection is typically based on the specific gene(s) that is being analyzed. Genes are described using Human Genome Organization (HUGO) approved gene names and are italicized in the code descriptors. Gene names were taken from tables of the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee (HGNC) at the time the CPT® codes were developed. For the most part, Human Genome Variation Society (HGVS) recommendations were followed for the names of specific molecular variants. The familiar name is used for some variants because defined criteria were not in place when the variant was first described or because HGVS recommendations were changed over time (eg, intronic variants, processed proteins). When the gene name is represented by an abbreviation, the abbreviation is listed first, followed by the full gene name italicized in parentheses (eg, "F5 [coagulation Factor V]"), except for the HLA series of codes. Proteins or diseases commonly associated with the genes are listed as examples in the code descriptors. The examples do not represent all conditions in which testing of the gene may be indicated. Codes that describe tests to assess for the presence of gene variants (see definitions) use common gene variant names. Typically, all of the listed variants would be tested. However, these lists are not exclusive. If other variants are also tested in the analysis, they would be included in the procedure and not reported separately. Full gene sequencing should not be reported using codes that assess for the presence of gene variants unless specifically stated in the code descriptor. The molecular pathology codes include all analytical services performed in the test (eg, cell lysis, nucleic acid stabilization, extraction, digestion, amplification, and detection). Any procedures required prior to cell lysis (eg, microdissection, codes 88380 and 88381) should be reported separately. The results of the procedure may require interpretation by a physician or other qualified health care professional. When only the interpretation and report are performed, modifier 26 may be appended to the specific molecular pathology code. All analyses are qualitative unless otherwise noted. For microbial identification, see 87149-87153 and 87471-87801, and 87900-87904. For in situ hybridization analyses, see 88271-88275 and 88365-88368. Breakpoint: the region at which a chromosome breaks during a translocation (defined elsewhere). These regions are often consistent for a given translocation. Codon: a discrete unit of three nucleotides of a DNA or mRNA sequence that encodes a specific amino acid within, or signals the termination of, a polypeptide. Common variants: variants (as defined elsewhere) that are associated with compromised gene function and are interrogated in a single round of laboratory testing (in a single, typically multiplex, assay format or using more than one assay to encompass all variants to be tested). These variants typically fit the definition of a "mutation," and are usually the predominant ones causing disease. Testing for additional uncommon variants may provide additional limited value in assessment of a patient. Often there are professional society recommendations or guidelines for which variants are most appropriate to test (eg, American College of Medical Genetics/American College of Obstetrics and Gynecology guidelines for variants used in population screening for cystic fibrosis). Constitutional: synonymous with germline, often used in reference to the genetic code that is present at birth. Copy number variants (CNVs): structural changes in the genome composed of large deletions or duplications. CNVs can be found in the germline, but can also occur in somatic cells. See also Duplication/Deletion (Dup/Del). Cytogenomic: a comprehensive genome-wide analysis of chromosomal and genetic abnormalities using molecular-based technologies. DNA hyper-methylation in a gene promoter typically represses gene transcription. DNA methylation serves as a regulatory mechanism in numerous scenarios including development, chromosome inactivation, and carcinogenesis. DNA methylation analysis: analytical protocols are designed to evaluate the degree of DNA methylation related to specific disease processes. This analysis has various applications, qualitative or quantitative, and could be gene specific or encompass global degrees of methylation. All assays employ specific maneuvers (eg, chemical, enzymatic) that allow for distinguishable evaluation of methylated and non-methylated sequences. Duplication/Deletion (Dup/Del): terms that are usually used together with the "/" to refer to molecular testing, which assesses the dosage of a particular genomic region. The region tested is typically of modest to substantial size-from several dozen to several million or more nucleotides. Dynamic mutation: polynucleotide (eg, trinucleotide) repeats that are in or associated with genes that can undergo disease-producing increases or decreases in the numbers of repeats within tissues and across generations. Exome: DNA sequences within the human genome that code for proteins (coding regions). Exon: typically, one of multiple nucleic acid sequences used to encode information for a gene product (polypeptide or protein). Exons are separated from each other by non-protein-coding sequences known as introns. Exons at the respective ends of a gene also contain nucleic acid sequence that does not code for the gene's protein product. Gene: a nucleic acid sequence that typically contains information for coding a protein as well as for the regulated expression of that protein. Human genes usually contain multiple protein coding regions (exons) separated by non-protein coding regions (introns). See also exon, intron, and polypeptide. Gene expression: the sequence of events that results in the production and assembly of a protein product corresponding to the information encoded in a specific gene. The process begins with the transcription of gene sequences to produce an mRNA intermediary, which is subsequently translated to produce a specific protein product. Genome: the total (nuclear) human genetic content. Heteroplasmy: the copy number of a variant within a cell; it is expressed as a percent. Mutations: typically are variants associated with altered gene function that lead to functional deficits or disease (pathogenic). Breakpoint: the region at which a chromosome breaks during a translocation (defined elsewhere). These regions are often consistent for a given translocation. Codon: a discrete unit of three nucleotides of a DNA or mRNA sequence that encodes a specific amino acid within, or signals the termination of, a polypeptide. Common variants: variants (as defined elsewhere) that are associated with compromised gene function and are interrogated in a single round of laboratory testing (in a single, typically multiplex, assay format or using more than one assay to encompass all variants to be tested). These variants typically fit the definition of a "mutation," and are usually the predominant ones causing disease. Testing for additional uncommon variants may provide additional limited value in assessment of a patient. Often there are professional society recommendations or guidelines for which variants are most appropriate to test (eg, American College of Medical Genetics/American College of Obstetrics and Gynecology guidelines for variants used in population screening for cystic fibrosis). Constitutional: synonymous with germline, often used in reference to the genetic code that is present at birth. Copy number variants (CNVs): structural changes in the genome composed of large deletions or duplications. CNVs can be found in the germline, but can also occur in somatic cells. DNA methylation serves as a regulatory mechanism in numerous scenarios including development, chromosome inactivation, and carcinogenesis. DNA methylation analysis: analytical protocols are designed to evaluate the degree of DNA methylation related to specific disease processes. All assays employ specific maneuvers (eg, chemical, enzymatic) that allow for distinguishable evaluation of methylated and non-methylated sequences. Exome: DNA sequences within the human genome that code for proteins (coding regions). Exon: typically, one of multiple nucleic acid sequences used to encode information for a gene product (polypeptide or protein). Exons are separated from each other by non-protein-coding sequences known as introns. Gene: a nucleic acid sequence that typically contains information for coding a protein as well as for the regulated expression of that protein. Gene expression: the sequence of events that results in the production and assembly of a protein product corresponding to the information encoded in a specific gene. lay_term: The lab analyst performs the technical lab test to analyze the common variants of the cytochrome P450 family 3 subfamily A member 4 gene (CYP3A4), such as *2, *22. Explanation The lab analyst performs all technical steps, from extracting the nucleic acids by methods such as digestion and cell lysis, to increasing and stabilizing the quantity of nucleic acid for analysis by amplification (making more copies of the gene), to detecting the target genes by methods such as nucleic acid probes, using a specimen such as blood. Code 81230 involves analyzing common variants of the CYP3A4 gene, such as *2, *22. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians may commonly order this test to help evaluate therapeutic drug dosing for certain medications. The CYP3A4 gene is involved in metabolism of certain drugs and can adversely affect bioavailability of the medication, such as some statins, which clinicians often use to treat high cholesterol. Nucleic acid: A sequence of specific biological chemicals, called nucleotides, which carry genetic information; known as deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), or ribonucleic acid (RNA). Variant: Gene that differs from the usual nucleic acid sequence due to events such as nucleotide deletions/insertions or substitutions; may cause conditions such as genetic disorders or cancer. Tips Some payers may pay separately for collecting the specimen using a code such as 36415. You may separately report prep work that precedes cell lysis, when documented. If the ordering clinician separately requests physician interpretation of the 81230 test and the pathologist renders an interpretation and writes a report, you can additionally report G0452, Molecular pathology procedure; physician interpretation and report, with modifier 26 to Medicare and perhaps other payers. lay_term: The lab analyst performs the technical lab test using comparative genomic hybridization (CGH) microarray, also referred to as chromosomal microarray (CMA) or molecular karyotype performed by microarray. The test is a high–resolution evaluation across the entire genome to detect variation in the number of copies of gene sequences, called copy–number variants (CNVs). This test also evaluates single–nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) that may indicate abnormalities such as long sequences of homozygous DNA. The test can identify genetic changes that may be associated with developmental delays or disabilities. Explanation The lab analyst extracts DNA from the specimen, such as blood, and amplifies (increases) the amount of DNA, then hybridizes the DNA to a microscopic array of short, single–stranded nucleic–acid targets across the entire genome. Hybridization is a process that joins complementary nucleotides to the nucleic acid targets. Computer image analysis allows high–resolution detection across the entire genome of copy–number variants (CNVs), such as deletions or duplications of specific nucleotide sequences, and single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) variants. The SNPs can help identify chromosomal abnormalities such as long sequences of homozygous DNA, which may indicate chromosomal abnormalities associated with known conditions. The homozygous DNA is sometimes called long contiguous stretches of homozygosity (LCSH), runs of homozygosity (ROH), or less commonly, loss of heterozygosity (LOH). Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians may order this test as an initial evaluation for children with signs of constitutional developmental delays, intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and/or congenital anomalies not indicative of a specific genetic disorder. Code 81229 evaluates a wider range of possible chromosomal abnormalities than the 81228 test, and is more specific than older cytogenetic tests such as karyotyping. The test broadly assess a wide range of possible genetic disorders across the entire genome, and helps narrow the focus for diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment for the condition. Gene: Specific nucleic acid sequence associated with a unique function in the body such as production of a specific protein. Genome: The entire genetic material of an organism, which means the entire DNA sequence. Hybridization: Forming a double–stranded DNA or RNA molecule by combining two complementary single strands, usually to identify a genetic mutation. Karyotype: Visual representation of chromosome number and appearance in the cell nucleus that can identify low–resolution abnormalities. Nucleic acid: DNA or RNA; sequence of specific biological chemicals, called nucleotides, that carry genetic information. Nucleotides: Biochemicals — sometimes called “bases” — that form the building blocks of nucleic acids, DNA and RNA; DNA is made up of four bases: adenine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G), and thymine (T), while RNA uses uracil (U) in place of T; each base will pair with only one specific “complementary” base when forming DNA or RNA strands. Single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP): Compared to the population, a difference in a single nucleotide in a nucleic acid sequence that may be associated with a specific disease or condition. Variant: A gene that differs from the usual nucleic acid sequence due to events such as nucleotide deletions or insertions or substitutions; may cause conditions such as genetic disorders or cancer. For a targeted cytogenomic analysis for chromosomal abnormalities that is not genome–wide, do not use a code from the 81228 family. lay_term: The lab analyst performs the technical lab test to analyze the entire gene sequence for the frataxin gene (FXN). Explanation The lab analyst performs all technical steps, using a specimen such as blood, from extracting the nucleic acids by methods such as cell lysis and digestion, to increasing and stabilizing the quantity of nucleic acid for analysis by amplification using a method such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR), to detecting the target genes. Code 81286 involves analyzing the FXN full gene sequence. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians may commonly order this test to aid in the diagnosis of Friedreich ataxia (FA), which is a heritable disease characterized by excessive muscle contraction (spasticity) with loss of control of body movements and reflexes, speech articulation difficulty, sensory loss, and possibly spinal curvature and heart–muscle thickening. Clinicians may also perform FXN testing to determine carrier status. Gene: Specific nucleic acid sequence associated with a unique function in the body such as production of a specific protein. Lysis: The act of breaking down a structure; destroying cells or tissue using an agent or substance. Mutation: An alteration in a deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) sequence that may lead to pathologic changes in the organism. Nucleic acid: A sequence of specific biological chemicals (nucleotides) that carry genetic information; known as deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) or ribonucleic acid (RNA). Reverse transcription: Generation of a complementary DNA sequence from a template of RNA. Ribonucleic acid (RNA): One of the essential building blocks of life, along with deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and proteins; RNA acts as a messenger (mRNA), carrying genetic information from DNA to proteins, helps regulate cellular processes, and, like enzymes, can speed up chemical reactions; RNA, rather than DNA, carries genetic information in some important viruses. Tips Some payers may pay separately for collecting the specimen using a code such as 36415. If the ordering clinician separately requests physician interpretation of the 81286 test and the pathologist renders an interpretation and writes a report, you can additionally report G0452 with modifier 26 to Medicare and perhaps other payers. An MD or DO physician, not a PhD laboratory scientist, must perform the interpretation according to CMS. Make sure to distinguish the four CPT®–listed tests for the FXN gene: 81284 for detection of abnormal alleles, 81285 for characterization of abnormal alleles, 81286 for full gene sequence analysis, and 81289 for known familial variants. lay_term: The lab analyst performs the technical lab test to detect the presence of specific changes in the alpha globin 1 and alpha globin 2 (HBA1/HBA) genes, which relate to alpha thalassemia and some structural hemoglobinopathies. The test specifically targets genetic variants known to occur in the patient’s family. Explanation The lab analyst performs all technical steps, from extracting the nucleic acids by methods such as digestion and cell lysis, to increasing and stabilizing the quantity of nucleic acid for analysis by amplification (making more copies of the gene), to detecting the target genes by methods such as nucleic acid probes, using a specimen such as blood. A single unit of 81258 represents testing for known familial variants in the HBA1/HBA2 genes. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians may commonly order this test for genetic counseling or to help evaluate symptomatic patients who have a relative with a known mutation in HBA1 or HBA2, which can result in conditions such as alpha thalassemia, characterized by decreased production of normal hemoglobin due to decreased alpha globins, or some hemoglobinopathies, which change the structure and often the function of hemoglobin. Alpha thalassemia takes several forms, depending largely on the number of inherited HBA1/HBA2 alleles exhibiting a mutation. The most severe form of the disease, Hb Bart syndrome, is due to deletion mutations in all four alleles, two from each parent, resulting in anemia, enlarged liver and spleen, and fetal fluid retention, called hydrops fetalis syndrome. Milder forms of alpha thalassemia, such as HbH disease, involve fewer damaged alleles and less severe symptoms. The HBA1/HBA2 variants involved in alpha thalassemia occur with varying frequency in different ethnic populations, which may impact interpretation of test results. Terminology Allele: Specific variant version of a gene at a specific locus. Amplification: Making more copies of desired gene for study by processes such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR) or transcription of DNA to RNA and reverse transcription from RNA to make an additional copy of the DNA. Deletion: Decrease in the normal copy number, which is two copies of a gene sequence. Gene: Specific nucleic acid sequence associated with a unique function in the body such as production of a specific protein. Hemoglobin: The red colored protein in the red blood cell that carries oxygen to the tissue and returns carbon dioxide to the lungs; when the amount is below normal, it indicates anemia. Lysis: To break down a structure or the act of breaking down a structure; destroy cells using an agent or substance. Mutation: Alteration in DNA sequence that may lead to pathologic changes in the organism. Nucleic acid: A sequence of specific biological chemicals, called nucleotides, which carry genetic information; known as deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) or ribonucleic acid (RNA). Variant: Gene that differs from the usual nucleic acid sequence due to events such as nucleotide deletions/insertions or substitutions; may cause conditions such as genetic disorders or cancer. Tips Some payers may pay separately for collecting the specimen using a code such as 36415. Code 81258 is part of the code family that describes HBA1/HBA2 genetic testing. Make sure to distinguish the codes in this family, including parent code 81257 for common deletions or variants, 81258 for known familial variants, 81259 for full gene sequence analysis, and 81269 for duplication deletion analysis. You may separately report prep work that precedes cell lysis, when documented. If the ordering clinician separately requests physician interpretation of the 81258 test and the pathologist renders an interpretation and writes a report, you can additionally report G0452 with modifier 26 to Medicare and perhaps other payers. lay_term: The lab analyst performs the technical lab test to analyze the genes of the two common alleles of Human Platelet Antigen 1 (HPA–1), also called CD61 or ITGB3, using a specimen such as blood or amniotic fluid. Explanation The lab analyst performs all technical steps, from extracting the nucleic acids by methods such as digestion and cell lysis, to increasing and stabilizing the quantity of nucleic acid for analysis by amplification (making more copies of the gene), to detecting the target genes, using a specimen such as blood. Specifically, this test commonly uses methods such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for multiple alleles, called multiplex PCR, and fluorescence or other marker to identify HPA–1 antigen alleles in the patient specimen, such as blood or amniotic fluid. A single unit of 81105 represents testing for the two common alleles of HPA–1, called HPA–1a and HPA–1b. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians may commonly order this test to help assess risk or aid in the diagnosis of neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia (NAIT) (sometimes called perinatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia [PAT]) and post–transfusion purpura (PTP) and thrombocytopenia. Specifically, the clinician may order the test to identify patient HPA–1 antigen genotype for fetuses or neonates with suspected NAIT, or for parents or prospective parents who have had an affected pregnancy to assess pregnancy risk, or for patients exhibiting PTP to aid in diagnosis of a potential transfusion reaction. Each HPA system is biallelic, meaning that each HPA antigen commonly exists in one of two forms (alleles), called “a” or “b.” As such, a person’s genotype may be homozygous (having two of the same alleles), aa or bb, or heterozygous (having one of each allele), ab. If the patient comes in contact with a different HPA antigen genotype, such as through maternal/fetal blood mixing or through blood transfusion, the patient may develop antibodies that result in an immune response that causes blood–related disorders such as thrombocytopenia (a low platelet count that interferes with blood clotting); purpura (skin blood spots); and internal hemorrhage (uncontrolled bleeding, possibly in the brain, gastrointestinal, and urinary tracts). Terminology Allele: Specific variant version of a gene at a specific locus. Amplification: Making more copies of desired gene for study by processes such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR) or transcription of DNA to RNA and reverse transcription from RNA to make an additional copy of the DNA. Antibody: A protein produced by the body as an immune–system response to a specific antigen, such as a bacteria or foreign substance; lab tests may utilize reactions between antibodies and antigens to identify a substance in a patient specimen. Antigen: A foreign substance that the body reacts to with an immune response, such as producing a specific antibody; lab tests may utilize reactions between antibodies and antigens to identify a substance in a patient specimen. Gene: Specific nucleic acid sequence associated with a unique function in the body such as production of a specific protein. Hemorrhage: Bleeding; typically refers to uncontrolled, rapid bleeding. Lysis: To break down a structure or the act of breaking down a structure; destroy cells using an agent or substance. Purpura: Bleeding under the skin due to ruptured vessels, resulting in red or purple spots. Thrombocytopenia: A deficiency of thrombocytes, or platelets, in the blood, which reduces the ability of the blood to clot. Variant: Gene that differs from the usual nucleic acid sequence due to events such as nucleotide deletions/insertions or substitutions; may cause conditions such as genetic disorders or cancer. Tips Some payers may pay separately for collecting the specimen using a code such as 36415. Distinguish 81105 from different HPA genotype tests described by different codes in the range 81105–81112. If the lab performs multiple HPA gene analyses for distinct HPA antigen systems, you may separately report the unique code for each test. If the ordering clinician separately requests physician interpretation of the 81105 test and the pathologist renders an interpretation and writes a report, you can additionally report G0452 with modifier 26 to Medicare and perhaps other payers. An MD or DO physician must perform the interpretation, not a PhD laboratory scientist, according to CMS. Read Less

Specifically, this test commonly uses methods such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for multiple alleles, called multiplex PCR, and fluorescence or other marker to identify HPA–15 antigen alleles in the patient specimen, such as blood or amniotic fluid. A single unit of 81106 represents testing for the two common alleles of HPA–15, called HPA–15a and HPA–15b. Genes are described using Human Genome Organization (HUGO) approved gene names and are italicized in the code descriptors. For the most part, Human Genome Variation Society (HGVS) recommendations were followed for the names of specific molecular variants. Proteins or diseases commonly associated with the genes are listed as examples in the code descriptors. The examples do not represent all conditions in which testing of the gene may be indicated. Codes that describe tests to assess for the presence of gene variants (see definitions) use common gene variant names. Typically, all of the listed variants would be tested. However, these lists are not exclusive. If other variants are also tested in the analysis, they would be included in the procedure and not reported separately. Any procedures required prior to cell lysis (eg, microdissection, codes 88380 and 88381) should be reported separately. The results of the procedure may require interpretation by a physician or other qualified health care professional. When only the interpretation and report are performed, modifier 26 may be appended to the specific molecular pathology code. All analyses are qualitative unless otherwise noted. For microbial identification, see 87149-87153 and 87471-87801, and 87900-87904. For in situ hybridization analyses, see 88271-88275 and 88365-88368. Breakpoint: the region at which a chromosome breaks during a translocation (defined elsewhere). These regions are often consistent for a given translocation. Codon: a discrete unit of three nucleotides of a DNA or mRNA sequence that encodes a specific amino acid within, or signals the termination of, a polypeptide. Common variants: variants (as defined elsewhere) that are associated with compromised gene function and are interrogated in a single round of laboratory testing (in a single, typically multiplex, assay format or using more than one assay to encompass all variants to be tested). Testing for additional uncommon variants may provide additional limited value in assessment of a patient. Often there are professional society recommendations or guidelines for which variants are most appropriate to test (eg, American College of Medical Genetics/American College of Obstetrics and Gynecology guidelines for variants used in population screening for cystic fibrosis). Constitutional: synonymous with germline, often used in reference to the genetic code that is present at birth. DNA methylation serves as a regulatory mechanism in numerous scenarios including development, chromosome inactivation, and carcinogenesis. Exome: DNA sequences within the human genome that code for proteins (coding regions). Exon: typically, one of multiple nucleic acid sequences used to encode information for a gene product (polypeptide or protein). lay_term: The lab analyst performs the technical lab test on a specimen such as blood, formalin–fixed paraffin embedded tissue (FFPE), or bone marrow to perform a translocation major breakpoint region (MBR) and minor cluster region (mcr) analysis for IGH@/BCL2 (t(14;18)), which is associated with follicular lymphoma (FL). Explanation The lab analyst performs all technical steps, using a specimen such as blood, formalin–fixed paraffin embedded tissue (FFPE), or bone marrow, from extracting the nucleic acids by methods such as cell lysis and digestion, to increasing and stabilizing the quantity of nucleic acid for analysis by amplification using a method such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR), to detecting the target genes. A single unit of 81278 evaluates the major breakpoint region (MBR) and minor cluster region (mcr) breakpoints for IGH@/BCL2 (t(14;18)), either as a qualitative test that identifies the presence of the fusion genes associated with MBR and mcr, or as a quantitative test using a method such as real–time PCR for quantitative detection of IGH@/BCL2 (t(14;18)) rearrangements. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians may order this test to confirm the diagnosis of follicular lymphoma (FL), monitor therapy efficacy, or detect residual disease. The IGH@/BCL2 (t(14;18)) MBR and mcr breakpoints are characteristic of follicular lymphoma, which is a type of non–Hodgkin lymphoma and is one of the most common types of low–grade lymphoma. Lysis: The act of breaking down a structure; destroying cells or tissue using an agent or substance; also, in vascular surgery, instilling a clot–dissolving drug to break up a clot. Nucleic acid: A sequence of specific biological chemicals (nucleotides) that carry genetic information; known as deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) or ribonucleic acid (RNA). Polymerase chain reaction (PCR): A rapid technique for making more copies (amplifying) of a DNA or RNA sequence used in the laboratory. Translocation: The process or genetic abnormality that occurs when disparate portions of one or more chromosomes become attached and create a hybrid segment, known as a fusion gene, inserted in one or both of the broken chromosomes. lay_term: The lab analyst performs the technical lab test on a specimen such as blood to analyze common variants of specific gene sequences of the MPL (MPL proto–oncogene, thrombopoietin receptor) gene, such as W515A, W515K, W515L, W515R, which may be associated with myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPN) such as essential thrombocythemia (ET) in JAK 2 V617F–negative patients. If the initial test is negative, the 81338 test may help detect MPL W515 mutations that could point toward MPN conditions such as primary myelofibrosis (PMF) or essential thrombocythemia (ET). Definitions For purposes of CPT® reporting, the following definitions apply: Abnormal allele: an alternative form of a gene that contains a disease-related variation from the normal sequence. Breakpoint: the region at which a chromosome breaks during a translocation (defined elsewhere). These regions are often consistent for a given translocation. Codon: a discrete unit of three nucleotides of a DNA or mRNA sequence that encodes a specific amino acid within, or signals the termination of, a polypeptide. Common variants: variants (as defined elsewhere) that are associated with compromised gene function and are interrogated in a single round of laboratory testing (in a single, typically multiplex, assay format or using more than one assay to encompass all variants to be tested). These variants typically fit the definition of a "mutation," and are usually the predominant ones causing disease. Testing for additional uncommon variants may provide additional limited value in assessment of a patient. Often there are professional society recommendations or guidelines for which variants are most appropriate to test (eg, American College of Medical Genetics/American College of Obstetrics and Gynecology guidelines for variants used in population screening for cystic fibrosis). Constitutional: synonymous with germline, often used in reference to the genetic code that is present at birth.
