Explanation Using a patient specimen, such as blood, the lab analyst performs a genomic sequence analysis of at least 15 genes related to severe inherited conditions, such as the 20 gene examples that the code descriptor lists. The procedure involves using specialized equipment such as a next generation gene sequencer, which is an automated instrument that determines the order of nucleotides in DNA. The instrument reports the sequence as a string of letters, called a read, which the analyst compares to a reference genome of the same genes, which is like a library of normal and variant gene sequences associated with certain conditions. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians may order this test as part of genetic counseling and evaluation of patients for susceptibility to certain severe, heritable conditions more common in people of Ashkenazi (German or Eastern European) Jewish descent, such as cystic fibrosis, characterized by thick, sticky mucus that blocks pancreatic ducts and clogs the lungs; Bloom syndrome, characterized by dilated blood vessels in a butterfly–shaped distribution on the face, light sensitivity and susceptibility to certain cancers, particularly leukemia; Canavan disease, characterized by a loss of white matter in the brain, starting in infancy, and leading to death; Fanconi anemia group C, an inherited blood disorder that results in dwarfism and susceptibility to certain cancers; Gaucher disease, characterized by spleen and liver enlargement and anemia; Tay–Sachs disease, characterized by build–up of fatty proteins in the brain that causes spasticity, loss of sight and hearing, and death in childhood; and mucolipidosis type IV, characterized by vision loss and delayed mental and motor skills often leading to blindness and inability to walk or talk. The test also interrogates genes for the basis of conditions such as beta hemoglobinopathies, phenylketonuria, and galactosemia. Terminology Gene: Specific nucleic acid sequence associated with a unique function in the body such as production of a specific protein. Mutation: An alteration in a deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) sequence that may lead to pathologic changes in the organism. Nucleic acid: A sequence of specific biological chemicals (nucleotides) that carry genetic information; known as deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) or ribonucleic acid (RNA). Variant: Gene that differs from the usual nucleic acid sequence due to events such as nucleotide deletions or insertions or substitutions; may cause conditions such as genetic disorders or cancer. Tips Some payers may pay separately for collecting the specimen using a code such as 36415. CPT® provides multiple other codes that describe individual gene sequence analyses that might be part of the 81443 panel, such as 81200 for ASPA, 81209 for BLM, 81220–81224 for CFTR, 81242 for FANCC, 81250 for G6PC, 81251 for GBA, 81361–81364 for HBB, 81255 for HEXA, 81260 for IKBKAP, and 81290 for MCOLN1, as well as Tier 2 molecular pathology codes for ACADM, ARSA, ATP7B, BCKDHA, BCKDHB, DHCR7, GAA, GALT, and PAH. Code 81443 describes the entire panel, and you should not separately report the individual codes in addition to 81443. Be sure to distinguish 81443 from code 81412, which involves testing for nine genes for Ashkenazi–Jewish–associated disorders, many of which code 81443 also includes. Read Less
guidelines: Lab & Path Guidelines Range Specific Guideline Genomic sequencing procedures (GSPs) and other molecular multianalyte assays are DNA and/or RNA sequence analysis methods that simultaneously assay multiple genes or genetic regions relevant to a clinical situation. They may target specific combinations of genes or genetic material, or they may assay the exome or genome. The technology typically used for genomic sequencing is massively parallel sequencing (MPS) (eg, next-generation sequencing [NGS]) although other technologies may be employed. GSPs are performed on nucleic acids from germline or neoplastic samples. Examples of applications include aneuploidy analysis of cell-free circulating fetal DNA, gene panels for somatic alterations in neoplasms, and sequence analysis of the exome or genome to determine the cause of developmental delay. Exome and genome procedures are designed to evaluate the genetic material in totality or near totality. Although commonly used to identify sequence (base) changes, they can also be used to identify copy number, structural changes, and abnormal zygosity patterns, and these analyses may be performed in combination or as separate and distinct studies. Another unique feature of GSPs is the ability to "re-query" or re-evaluate the sequence data (eg, complex phenotype such as developmental delay is reassessed when new genetic knowledge is attained, or for a separate unrelated clinical indication). The analyses below are often performed using NGS/MPS technology; however, they may also be performed using molecular techniques (eg, polymerase chain reaction [PCR] methods and microarrays). These codes should be used when the components of the descriptor(s) are fulfilled regardless of the technique used for analysis, unless specifically noted in the code descriptor. When a GSP assay includes gene(s) that is listed in more than one code descriptor, the code for the most specific test for the primary disorder sought should be reported, rather than reporting multiple codes for the same gene(s). When all of the components of the descriptor are not performed, use individual Tier 1 codes, Tier 2 codes, or 81479 (Unlisted molecular pathology procedure). Testing for somatic alterations in neoplasms may be reported differently depending on whether combined or separate methods and analyses are used for both DNA and RNA analytes. Procedures for somatic alterations in neoplasms which include DNA analysis or DNA and RNA analysis using a single combined method are reported with 81445, 81450, 81455, 81457, 81458, 81459, 81462, 81463, 81464. RNA analysis performed using a separate method is reported with 81449, 81451, 81456. When evaluation for tumor mutation burden (TMB) and/or microsatellite instability (MSI) is performed as part of the same test for somatic alterations in neoplasms, report 81457, 81458, 81459. When a genomic sequencing procedure (GSP) is performed on cell-free nucleic acid (eg, plasma), sometimes referred to as a liquid biopsy, report 81462, 81463, 81464. Definitions Cell-free nucleic acid: DNA or RNA released into the blood and other body fluids. Cell-free nucleic acid released from fetal cells can be sampled for non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) while that released from tumor cells can be sampled for cancer, sometimes referred to as tumor liquid biopsy. Copy number variants (CNVs): structural changes in the genome which are composed of large deletions or duplications. CNVs can be found in the germline but can also occur in somatic cells. See also Duplication/Deletion (Dup/Del). Duplications may also be referred to as amplifications. Duplication/Deletion (Dup/Del): terms that are usually used together with the "/" to refer to molecular testing, which assesses the dosage of a particular genomic region. The region tested is typically of modest to substantial size, from several dozen to several million or more nucleotides. Normal gene dosage is two copies per cell, except for the sex chromosomes (X and Y). Thus, zero or one copy represents a deletion and three (or more) copies represent a duplication. Low-pass sequencing: a method of genome sequencing intended for cytogenomic analysis of chromosomal abnormalities, such as that performed for trait mapping or copy number variation, typically performed to an average depth of sequencing ranging from 0.1 to 5X. Massively parallel sequencing (MPS): high-throughput method used to determine a portion of the nucleotide sequences in an individual patient's genome, utilizing advanced (non-Sanger) sequencing technologies that are capable of processing multiple DNA and/or RNA sequences in parallel. While other technologies exist, next-generation sequencing (NGS) is a common technique used to achieve MPS. Microsatellite instability (MSI): a type of DNA hypermutation or predisposition to mutation in which replication errors are not corrected due to defective DNA mismatch repair (dMMR) mechanism. MSI manifests as insertions or deletions in short tandem repeat (STR) (defined in the molecular pathology guidelines) alleles and can be identified by changes in the DNA repeat sequence length. Rearrangements: structural chromosomal variations such as deletions, insertions, inversions (defined in the molecular pathology guidelines), or translocations (defined in the molecular pathology guidelines) that bring together genetic material that is not normally adjacent in the unmodified genome. It can manifest as abnormal gene expression or as an abnormal fusion product at the RNA and/or protein level. Rearrangement can also refer to the process by which immunoglobulin and T cell receptor genes are normally modified. Tumor mutational burden (TMB): the number of somatic mutations detected per million bases (Mb) of genomic sequence investigated from a cancer specimen. It is usually obtained from analysis using a next generation sequencing method. It is considered a biomarker to guide immunotherapy decisions for patients with cancer. The assays in this section represent discrete genetic values, properties, or characteristics in which the measurement or analysis of each analyte is potentially of independent medical significance or useful in medical management. In contrast to multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAAs), the assays in this section do not represent algorithmically combined results to obtain a risk score or other value, which in itself represents a new and distinct medical property that is of independent medical significance relative to the individual, component test results. (For cytogenomic [genome-wide] analysis for constitutional chromosomal abnormalities, see 81228, 81229, 81349, 81405, 81406) View Table For this Range

short_description: Genome (eg, unexplained constitutional or heritable disorder or syndrome); sequence analysis
lay_term: The lab analyst performs a gene sequence analysis of the entire patient genome to look for genetic changes that could account for an unexplained disorder or syndrome. Explanation Using a patient specimen, such as blood, the lab analyst performs a whole genome sequence analysis. The procedure involves using specialized equipment such as a next generation gene sequencer, which is an automated instrument that determines the order of nucleotides in DNA. The gene sequencer reports the patient genome gene sequence as a string of letters, called a read, which the analyst compares to a reference genome. The goal of this test is to compare the patient genome to family member genomes as the reference. Each genome gene sequencing test for a family member warrants a separate code: +81426, Genome e.g., unexplained constitutional or heritable disorder or syndrome; sequence analysis, each comparator exome, e.g., parents, siblings, List separately in addition to code for primary procedure. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians may order this test to aid in the diagnosis of an unexplained set of patient symptoms that could be associated with a constitutional or genetic disorder or syndrome, particularly if some family members evidence similar symptoms with no evident diagnosis. Terminology Exome: Portion of the genome made up of exons, which are DNA sequences that transcribe to mature RNA, also called mature messenger RNA or mRNA, which remains in cells and produces proteins through a process called translation; the human exome constitutes about 1 to 2 percent of the human genome. Gene: Specific nucleic acid sequence associated with a unique function in the body such as production of a specific protein. Genome: The entire genetic material of an organism, which means a person’s entire DNA sequence. Mutation: Alteration in DNA sequence that may lead to pathologic changes in the organism. Nucleic acid: DNA or RNA; sequence of specific biological chemicals, called nucleotides, that carry genetic information. Syndrome: A condition characterized by a specific group of symptoms that often occur together. Variant: Gene that differs from the usual nucleic acid sequence due to events such as nucleotide deletions or insertions or substitutions; may cause conditions such as genetic disorders or cancer. Tips Some payers may pay separately for collecting the specimen using a code such as 36415, Collection of venous blood by venipuncture. Code 81425 is in a family with +81426 to 81427, and you may report any or all of the codes together depending on the various tests that the lab analyst performs. Make sure to distinguish the 81415 to 81417 code family for an exome analysis from the 81425 to 81427 family for a whole genome analysis. Read Less

The service includes interrogation for sequence variants and copy number variants. Explanation Using a patient specimen, such as blood, the lab analyst performs a genomic sequence analysis of at least five genes. The procedure involves using specialized equipment such as a next generation gene sequencer, which is an automated instrument that determines the order of nucleotides in DNA. The instrument reports the sequence as a string of letters, called a read, which the analyst compares to a reference genome of the same genes, which is like a library of normal and variant gene sequences associated with certain conditions. The service includes interrogation for sequence variants and copy number variants. Sequence variants are small changes in the DNA code. Copy number variants involve sections of DNA that are either missing or have extra copies. Clinicians may order this test as part of genetic counseling and evaluation of patients for susceptibility to certain heritable neuroendocrine tumor–related disorders such as medullary thyroid cancer, parathyroid cancer, and malignant pheochromocytoma or paraganglioma, tumors that release bursts of too much adrenalin, the “fight or flight” hormone. Terminology Endocrine system: Organs and other structures in the body that secret hormones or hormonelike substances essential for metabolism and other processes such as reproduction; the system includes the pituitary (the "master" gland), thyroid, parathyroid, adrenal glands, sex glands (gonads), the pancreas, paraganglia (cells that secrete epinephrine or norepinephrine, substances that in response to stress raise blood pressure and increase heart rate), and the pineal body; the intestines and lungs also secrete hormonelike substances. Gene: Specific nucleic acid sequence associated with a unique function in the body such as production of a specific protein. Nucleic acid: DNA or RNA; sequence of specific biological chemicals, called nucleotides, that carry genetic information. Parathyroid: A small paired gland that sits next to the thyroid glands in the neck and secretes the hormone responsible for calcium and phosphorus regulation. Thyroid: A gland in the neck that secretes hormones regulating growth and development. Variant: Gene that differs from the usual nucleic acid sequence due to events such as nucleotide deletions/insertions or substitutions; may cause conditions such as genetic disorders or cancer. Tips Some payers may pay separately for collecting the specimen. Read Less
guidelines: Lab & Path Guidelines Range Specific Guideline Genomic sequencing procedures (GSPs) and other molecular multianalyte assays are DNA and/or RNA sequence analysis methods that simultaneously assay multiple genes or genetic regions relevant to a clinical situation. They may target specific combinations of genes or genetic material, or they may assay the exome or genome. The technology typically used for genomic sequencing is massively parallel sequencing (MPS) (eg, next-generation sequencing [NGS]) although other technologies may be employed. GSPs are performed on nucleic acids from germline or neoplastic samples. Examples of applications include aneuploidy analysis of cell-free circulating fetal DNA, gene panels for somatic alterations in neoplasms, and sequence analysis of the exome or genome to determine the cause of developmental delay. Exome and genome procedures are designed to evaluate the genetic material in totality or near totality. Although commonly used to identify sequence (base) changes, they can also be used to identify copy number, structural changes, and abnormal zygosity patterns, and these analyses may be performed in combination or as separate and distinct studies. Another unique feature of GSPs is the ability to "re-query" or re-evaluate the sequence data (eg, complex phenotype such as developmental delay is reassessed when new genetic knowledge is attained, or for a separate unrelated clinical indication). The analyses below are often performed using NGS/MPS technology; however, they may also be performed using molecular techniques (eg, polymerase chain reaction [PCR] methods and microarrays). These codes should be used when the components of the descriptor(s) are fulfilled regardless of the technique used for analysis, unless specifically noted in the code descriptor. When a GSP assay includes gene(s) that is listed in more than one code descriptor, the code for the most specific test for the primary disorder sought should be reported, rather than reporting multiple codes for the same gene(s). When all of the components of the descriptor are not performed, use individual Tier 1 codes, Tier 2 codes, or 81479 (Unlisted molecular pathology procedure). Testing for somatic alterations in neoplasms may be reported differently depending on whether combined or separate methods and analyses are used for both DNA and RNA analytes. Procedures for somatic alterations in neoplasms which include DNA analysis or DNA and RNA analysis using a single combined method are reported with 81445, 81450, 81455, 81457, 81458, 81459, 81462, 81463, 81464. RNA analysis performed using a separate method is reported with 81449, 81451, 81456. When evaluation for tumor mutation burden (TMB) and/or microsatellite instability (MSI) is performed as part of the same test for somatic alterations in neoplasms, report 81457, 81458, 81459. When a genomic sequencing procedure (GSP) is performed on cell-free nucleic acid (eg, plasma), sometimes referred to as a liquid biopsy, report 81462, 81463, 81464. Definitions Cell-free nucleic acid: DNA or RNA released into the blood and other body fluids. Cell-free nucleic acid released from fetal cells can be sampled for non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) while that released from tumor cells can be sampled for cancer, sometimes referred to as tumor liquid biopsy. Copy number variants (CNVs): structural changes in the genome which are composed of large deletions or duplications. CNVs can be found in the germline but can also occur in somatic cells. See also Duplication/Deletion (Dup/Del). Duplications may also be referred to as amplifications. Duplication/Deletion (Dup/Del): terms that are usually used together with the "/" to refer to molecular testing, which assesses the dosage of a particular genomic region. The region tested is typically of modest to substantial size, from several dozen to several million or more nucleotides. Normal gene dosage is two copies per cell, except for the sex chromosomes (X and Y). Thus, zero or one copy represents a deletion and three (or more) copies represent a duplication. Low-pass sequencing: a method of genome sequencing intended for cytogenomic analysis of chromosomal abnormalities, such as that performed for trait mapping or copy number variation, typically performed to an average depth of sequencing ranging from 0.1 to 5X. Massively parallel sequencing (MPS): high-throughput method used to determine a portion of the nucleotide sequences in an individual patient's genome, utilizing advanced (non-Sanger) sequencing technologies that are capable of processing multiple DNA and/or RNA sequences in parallel. While other technologies exist, next-generation sequencing (NGS) is a common technique used to achieve MPS. Microsatellite instability (MSI): a type of DNA hypermutation or predisposition to mutation in which replication errors are not corrected due to defective DNA mismatch repair (dMMR) mechanism. MSI manifests as insertions or deletions in short tandem repeat (STR) (defined in the molecular pathology guidelines) alleles and can be identified by changes in the DNA repeat sequence length. Rearrangements: structural chromosomal variations such as deletions, insertions, inversions (defined in the molecular pathology guidelines), or translocations (defined in the molecular pathology guidelines) that bring together genetic material that is not normally adjacent in the unmodified genome. It can manifest as abnormal gene expression or as an abnormal fusion product at the RNA and/or protein level. Rearrangement can also refer to the process by which immunoglobulin and T cell receptor genes are normally modified. Tumor mutational burden (TMB): the number of somatic mutations detected per million bases (Mb) of genomic sequence investigated from a cancer specimen. It is usually obtained from analysis using a next generation sequencing method. It is considered a biomarker to guide immunotherapy decisions for patients with cancer. The assays in this section represent discrete genetic values, properties, or characteristics in which the measurement or analysis of each analyte is potentially of independent medical significance or useful in medical management. In contrast to multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAAs), the assays in this section do not represent algorithmically combined results to obtain a risk score or other value, which in itself represents a new and distinct medical property that is of independent medical significance relative to the individual, component test results. (For cytogenomic [genome-wide] analysis for constitutional chromosomal abnormalities, see 81228, 81229, 81349, 81405, 81406) View Table For this Range

lay_term: The lab analyst performs a genomic sequence analysis panel to evaluate the patient specimen for genetic sequences of at least five cardiomyopathy–related genes, possibly from the examples that the code descriptor lists. The tested genes may relate to hereditary cardiomyopathy conditions such as hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, dilated cardiomyopathy, or arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy. Explanation Using a patient specimen, such as blood, the lab analyst performs a genomic sequence analysis of at least five cardiomyopathy–related genes, possibly from the examples that the code descriptor lists. The procedure involves using specialized equipment such as a next generation gene sequencer, which is an automated instrument that determines the order of nucleotides in DNA. The instrument reports the sequence as a string of letters, called a read, which the analyst compares to a reference genome of the same genes, which is like a library of normal and variant gene sequences associated with certain conditions. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians may order this test to help identify any potential genetic component to cardiomyopathy, which is chronic disease of the heart muscle. The test results can aid in diagnosis, allow individualized disease management, and indicate modified surveillance and risk management for genetically susceptible individuals. Terminology Cardiomyopathy: Abnormality of the heart muscle that impairs the pumping function and can result in heart failure. Gene: Specific nucleic acid sequence associated with a unique function in the body such as production of a specific protein. Tips Some payers may pay separately for collecting the specimen using a code such as 36415. CPT® provides various other molecular pathology codes for tests involving most of the genes included in the 81439 test. Because 81439 includes gene sequencing of each of the genes, you should not additionally report a code for the single gene analysis. Read Less

short_description: Inherited bone marrow failure syndromes (IBMFS) (eg, Fanconi anemia, dyskeratosis congenita, Diamond-Blackfan anemia, Shwachman-Diamond syndrome, GATA2 deficiency syndrome, congenital amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia) sequence analysis panel, must include sequencing of at least 30 genes, including BRCA2, BRIP1, DKC1, FANCA, FANCB, FANCC, FANCD2, FANCE, FANCF, FANCG, FANCI, FANCL, GATA1, GATA2, MPL, NHP2, NOP10, PALB2, RAD51C, RPL11, RPL35A, RPL5, RPS10, RPS19, RPS24, RPS26, RPS7, SBDS, TERT, and TINF2
lay_term: Code 81441 describes analyzing a blood specimen for at least 30 genes, including those listed in the code, to evaluate mutations associated with inherited bone marrow failure syndromes (IBMFS). These are blood disorders involving failure of the bone marrow to produce blood cells. Most patients with IBMFS have a family history of a certain condition listed in the code, such as Fanconi anemia. Explanation Using a patient specimen, such as blood, the lab analyst performs a genomic sequence analysis of at least 30 genes, including those listed in the code, related to inherited bone marrow failure syndromes (IBMFS). The lab analyst processes the specimen to extract nucleic acids, then creates more copies (amplifies) the target DNA using a procedure such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR). The lab analyst evaluates the nucleic acids with next generation sequencing (NGS), which uses an automated instrument that can simultaneously determine the order of DNA or RNA nucleotides in many genes from the patient specimen and use bioinformatics to interpret the results relative to genetic changes associated with certain conditions. Clinicians may order this test for patients with symptoms or a family history of an IBMFS, such as Fanconi anemia that results in dwarfism and susceptibility to certain cancers, or Shwachman–Diamond syndrome characterized by low white blood cell production that may lead to poor growth and skeletal abnormalities. Terminology Anemia: Decrease in the number of red blood cells, which results in a lack of oxygen in the blood; anemia can result from excessive blood loss or a disease process that destroys red blood cells. Gene: Specific nucleic acid sequence associated with a unique function in the body such as production of a specific protein. Genomic sequencing procedures (GSPs): Tests that use germline or neoplastic specimens to simultaneously analyze DNA or RNA sequences, typically for a combination of many genes or even an entire exome or genome; the tests often employ technology such as next generation sequencing (NGS) to identify changes to nucleic acid sequences or possibly other variations such as copy number or chromosomal structure, and then use bioinformatics to compare the findings to known genetic changes relevant to a specific clinical condition. Mutation: An alteration in a deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) sequence that may lead to pathologic changes in the organism. Nucleic acid: A sequence of specific biological chemicals (nucleotides) that carry genetic information; known as deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) or ribonucleic acid (RNA). Variant: Gene that differs from the usual nucleic acid sequence due to events such as nucleotide deletions or insertions or substitutions; may cause conditions such as genetic disorders or cancer. Tips Some payers may pay separately for collecting the specimen. CPT® provides multiple other codes that describe evaluation of individual genes that might be part of the 81441 panel, such as 81242 for FANCC. Code 81441 describes the entire panel, and you should not separately report the individual gene codes in addition to 81441. Read Less

Variant: Gene that differs from the usual nucleic acid sequence due to events such as nucleotide deletions/insertions or substitutions; may cause conditions such as genetic disorders or cancer. lay_term: The lab analyst performs a genomic sequence analysis panel to evaluate the entire mitochondrial genome from the patient specimen for large deletions, which are missing sections of DNA, that relate to nerve or muscle pathologies such as those that the code descriptor lists. The test includes heteroplasmy detection, if the analyst performs it, which means identifying if some mitochondrial DNA exhibits mutation, while some remains normal. Explanation Using a patient specimen, such as blood, the lab analyst performs a deletion analysis panel for the entire mitochondrial genome, possibly including detection of differences in mitochondrial DNA that harbor mutations in some mitochondria but not others, called heteroplasmy. The lab analyst may perform a method such as Multiplex Ligation dependent Probe Amplification, or MLPA, which is a test designed to detect duplications and deletions in nucleotide sequences that normal DNA sequencing methods do not detect. Mitochondria are organelles inside cells that process energy. Mitochondria have their own DNA, called mDNA, which is different from the DNA contained in the nucleus of cells throughout the body. Only the mother effectively passes mDNA to the child. However, the majority of the compounds that mitochondria need to function come from DNA found in the nucleus, not in the mitochondria itself. Clinicians may request studies involving relevant DNA from the mitochondria or in the nucleus, but this test involves only the mitochondrial DNA. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians may order this test to help evaluate disorders of the mitochondria, which can affect nerve and muscle function. Symptoms of mitochondrial disorders vary widely, from asymptomatic to fatal, but often involve muscle weakness, organ diseases such as liver, kidney, heart, and lungs, neurological problems, and vision or hearing loss. Clinicians may order this test to evaluate specific conditions such as Kearns Sayre syndrome and others that the code descriptor lists. Although most mutations associated with mitochondrial DNA disorders will show up on the full gene sequence analysis, some patients have large deletion mutations that normal sequencing methods don’t detect. Terminology Duplication or deletion: Increase or decrease in the normal copy number, which is two copies of a gene sequence. Gene: Specific nucleic acid sequence associated with a unique function in the body such as production of a specific protein. Mutation: Alteration in DNA sequence that may lead to pathologic changes in the organism. Nucleic acid: DNA or RNA; sequence of specific biological chemicals, called nucleotides, that carry genetic information. Syndrome: A condition characterized by a specific group of symptoms that often occur together. Variant: Gene that differs from the usual nucleic acid sequence due to events such as nucleotide deletions or insertions or substitutions; may cause conditions such as genetic disorders or cancer. Tips Some payers may pay separately for collecting the specimen using a code such as 36415, Collection of venous blood by venipuncture. This code describes a large deletion panel that evaluates the entire mitochondrial DNA. For a full genome sequencing of mitochondrial DNA, use 81460. For gene analysis of nuclear encoded mitochondrial DNA, select an appropriate code such as 81440, Nuclear encoded mitochondrial genes, e.g., neurologic or myopathic phenotypes, genomic sequence panel, must include analysis of at least 100 genes, including BCS1L, C10orf2, COQ2, COX10, DGUOK, MPV17, OPA1, PDSS2, POLG, POLG2, RRM2B, SCO1, SCO2, SLC25A4, SUCLA2, SUCLG1, TAZ, TK2, and TYMP. lay_term: Code 81523 describes a next–generation sequence (NGS) analysis using a formalin–fixed paraffin–embedded (FFPE) breast tumor tissue specimen. The test is a Multianalyte Assay with Algorithmic Analysis (MAAA) that evaluates mRNA gene expression profile of 70 content genes with 31 housekeeping genes, and uses an algorithmic analysis of the results plus patient data to report an index related to the risk of breast cancer distant metastasis (spread). Explanation The lab analyst performs the technical lab test on formalin–fixed paraffin–embedded (FFPE) breast tumor tissue by extracting nucleic acids by methods such as cell lysis and digestion, and stabilizing and increasing the quantity of 70 target (content) mRNA nucleic acid markers and 31 housekeeping (control) markers. The lab analyst uses next–generation sequencing (NGS) to evaluate gene expression, which is the execution of DNA instructions through RNA to produce a functional substance, such as a protein. NGS uses an automated instrument that can simultaneously determine the order of DNA or RNA nucleotides in many genes from the patient specimen and use bioinformatics to interpret the results relative to variant gene sequences associated with certain conditions. The expression of the content genes in this test involves substances relevant to breast cancer metastasis (secondary cancerous growth at a distant site), while the housekeeping genes serve as a control of uniformly expressed reference genes. The assay includes an algorithmic analysis of the findings to report an index score related to the risk of breast cancer distant metastasis. Code 81523 is a multianalyte assay with algorithmic analysis (MAAA) test, meaning that the code includes performing all technical lab test(s), gathering relevant patient data, carrying out the algorithmic analysis, and reporting the results. Clinicians may order this test to help assess the likelihood that a breast tumor will result in distant metastasis. Gene expression profiling evaluates mRNA, as opposed to just identifying DNA gene sequences, which means the test is a measure of which genes are actively expressed or “turned on.” By measuring the activity of multiple target genes in the cancerous cells, the clinician can evaluate how to proceed with further treatment. Terminology Algorithm: A specific set of step–by–step calculations using defined inputs at each step to produce a useful output; for multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAA), the output involves some sort of diagnostic or prognostic information about treatment options or disease outcomes. Bioinformatics: Discipline used to gather, store and evaluate biological data, such as gene sequences, using computer systems. Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA): A form of nucleic acid that consists of a sequence of specific biological chemicals (nucleotides) which carry genetic information. Formalin: Diluted formaldehyde used to preserve biologic tissue for laboratory analysis. Gene: Specific nucleic acid sequence associated with a unique function in the body such as production of a specific protein. Gene expression: The two–step process by which cells generate messenger RNA m(RNA) from a DNA template (transcription), then generate a protein from the mRNA template (translation). Lysis: The act of breaking down a structure; destroying cells or tissue using an agent or substance; also, in vascular surgery, instilling a clot–dissolving drug to break up a clot. Multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAA): A set of codes generally unique to a single clinical laboratory or manufacture; they typically list all the analytic and algorithmic analysis for a type of disease, such cancer; the type and number of analytes, such as proteins; the lab methods, such as immunoassay; the specimen type, such as blood; and the result type, such as prognostic risk score. Next–generation sequencing (NGS): A general term for number of different modern DNA and RNA sequencing technologies that are quicker and cheaper than the previous methods; also known as high–throughput sequencing Nucleotides: Biochemicals — sometimes called “bases” — that form the building blocks of nucleic acids, DNA and RNA; DNA is made up of four bases: adenine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G), and thymine (T), while RNA uses uracil (U) in place of T; each base will pair with only one specific “complementary” base when forming DNA or RNA strands. Ribonucleic acid (RNA): One of the essential building blocks of life, along with deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and proteins; RNA acts as a messenger (mRNA), carrying genetic information from DNA to proteins, helps regulate cellular processes, and, like enzymes, can speed up chemical reactions; RNA, rather than DNA, carries genetic information in some important viruses. Variant: A gene that differs from the usual nucleic acid sequence due to events such as nucleotide deletions or insertions or substitutions; may cause conditions such as genetic disorders or cancer. short_description: Oncology (thyroid), mRNA, gene expression analysis of 10,196 genes, utilizing fine needle aspirate, algorithm reported as a categorical result (eg, benign or suspicious)
lay_term: The lab analyst performs the technical lab tests on a thyroid fine needle aspiration (FNA) specimen for mRNA gene expression profiling of 10,196 genes and carries out an algorithmic analysis using patient data and the lab–test results to report a categorical result of “benign” or “suspicious” for thyroid cancer. Explanation The lab analyst performs technical lab tests on a fine needle aspiration (FNA) thyroid specimen sample by extracting nucleic acids by methods such as cell lysis and digestion, and stabilizing and increasing the quantity of 10,196 nucleic acid markers. A common procedure for the test may be next generation sequencing, which uses an automated instrument that simultaneously determines the order of nucleotides in many genes. The process may involve reverse transcription PCR (RT–PCR) to create copy DNA (cDNA) from the specimen mRNA, and amplification and quantification of genes by methods such as real–time (quantitative) PCR (qPCR). Processing the lab test result and patient data with a computer algorithm, the lab provides the test findings as a category for the specimen as “benign” or “suspicious” for thyroid cancer. Code 81546 is a multianalyte assay with algorithmic analysis (MAAA) test, meaning that the code includes performing all technical lab test(s), gathering relevant patient data, carrying out the algorithmic analysis, and reporting the results. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians may order this test using a thyroid FNA specimen to help assess whether the specimen is benign or suspicious for thyroid cancer. Gene expression profiling evaluates mRNA, as opposed to just identifying DNA gene sequences, which means the test is a measure of which genes are actively expressed or “turned on.” By measuring the activity of multiple target genes in the cancerous cells, the clinician can evaluate how to proceed with further treatment, such as surgery. Terminology Algorithm: A specific set of step–by–step calculations using defined inputs at each step to produce a useful output; for multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAA), the output involves some sort of diagnostic or prognostic information about treatment options or disease outcomes. Gene: Specific nucleic acid sequence associated with a unique function in the body such as production of a specific protein. Lysis: The act of breaking down a structure; destroying cells or tissue using an agent or substance; also, in vascular surgery, instilling a clot–dissolving drug to break up a clot. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR): A rapid technique for making more copies (amplifying) of a DNA or RNA sequence used in the laboratory. Ribonucleic acid (RNA): One of the essential building blocks of life, along with deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and proteins; RNA acts as a messenger (mRNA), carrying genetic information from DNA to proteins, helps regulate cellular processes, and, like enzymes, can speed up chemical reactions; RNA, rather than DNA, carries genetic information in some important viruses. MAAAs are typically unique to a single clinical laboratory or manufacturer. The results of individual component procedure(s) that are inputs to the MAAAs may be provided on the associated laboratory report; however, these assays are not separately reported using additional codes. The format for the code descriptors of MAAAs usually include (in order): Disease type (eg, oncology, autoimmune, tissue rejection), Material(s) analyzed (eg, DNA, RNA, protein, antibody), Number of markers (eg, number of genes, number of proteins), Methodology(ies) (eg, microarray, real-time [RT]-PCR, in situ hybridization [ISH], enzyme linked immunosorbent assays [ELISA]), Number of functional domains (if indicated), Specimen type (eg, blood, fresh tissue, formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded), Algorithm result type (eg, prognostic, diagnostic), Report (eg, probability index, risk score) In contrast to GSPs and other molecular multianalyte assays, the assays in this section represent algorithmically combined results of analyses of multiple analytes to obtain a risk score or other value which in itself represents a new and distinct medical property that is of independent medical significance relative to the individual component test results in clinical context in which the assay is performed. MAAAs, including those that do not have a Category I code, may be found in Appendix O. MAAAs that do not have a Category I code are identified in Appendix O by a four-digit number followed by the letter "M." The Category I MAAA codes that are included in this subsection are also included in Appendix O. All MAAA codes are listed in Appendix O along with the procedure's proprietary name. In order to report an MAAA code, the analysis performed must fulfill the code descriptor and, if proprietary, must be the test represented by the proprietary name listed in Appendix O. When a specific MAAA procedure is not listed below or in Appendix O, the procedure must be reported using the Category I MAAA unlisted code (81599). These codes encompass all analytical services required (eg, cell lysis, nucleic acid stabilization, extraction, digestion, amplification, hybridization, and detection) in addition to the algorithmic analysis itself. Procedures that are required prior to cell lysis (eg, microdissection, codes 88380 and 88381) should be reported separately.

short_description: Transplantation medicine (allograft rejection, pediatric liver and small bowel), measurement of donor and third-party-induced CD154+T-cytotoxic memory cells, utilizing whole peripheral blood, algorithm reported as a rejection risk score Notes: (Do not report 81560 in conjunction with 85032, 86353, 86821, 88184, 88185, 88187, 88230, 88240, 88241, 0018M)
lay_term: The lab analyst performs a blood test to evaluate allograft rejection for a pediatric liver or small–bowel transplant patient. The test measures the level of CD154+T–cytotoxic memory cells in response to incubating the patient blood specimen with organ–donor and third–party leukocytes. As with all MAAAs, the code describes both the lab test as well as an algorithm that uses the test results and possibly other patient data to calculate a probability or risk score. In this case, the MAAA establishes a score that indicates the risk of liver or small bowel rejection for a pediatric transplant patient. Explanation The lab analyst performs the technical lab test using a blood specimen from a pediatric small–bowel or liver transplant patient. The test involves a procedure such as a mixed leukocyte response assay (MLA), which involves incubating the prepared patient blood specimen with leukocytes (white blood cells) from the organ donor and a third–party donor, and inserting a label for cell types that proliferate (multiply) as an immune response to the donor cells. Specifically, the test reveals the ratio of donor–induced to third–party donor–induced CD154+T–cytotoxic memory cells. The assay includes an algorithmic analysis of the findings to report a score that indicates the risk of transplanted organ rejection. Code 81560 is a multianalyte assay with algorithmic analysis (MAAA) test, meaning that the code includes performing all technical lab test(s), gathering relevant patient data, carrying out the algorithmic analysis, and reporting the results. Clinicians may order this test to help assess the likelihood of liver or small–bowel transplant rejection in pediatric patients. The test is less invasive than tissue biopsy, which is another way clinicians may assess the likelihood of transplant rejection, and provides an opportunity for earlier clinical intervention to avoid rejection. Terminology Algorithm: A specific set of step–by–step calculations using defined inputs at each step to produce a useful output; for multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAA), the output involves some sort of diagnostic or prognostic information about treatment options or disease outcomes. Allograft: A tissue graft or organ harvested from one person for another; donors include cadavers and living individuals related or unrelated to the recipient; also known as an allogeneic graft or homograft. Leukocyte: One of the three main cell types in blood, also known as white blood cells (WBCs) that are part of the immune system and help defend the body against infectious agents. Multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAA): A set of codes generally unique to a single clinical laboratory or manufacture; they typically list all the analytic and algorithmic analysis for a type of disease, such cancer; the type and number of analytes, such as proteins; the lab methods, such as immunoassay; the specimen type, such as blood; and the result type, such as prognostic risk score. Transplant: Tissue or organs removed from one person (donor) and placed in another (recipient), also transplantation, allotransplantation; tissue moved from within one location in the body to another, also allograft, autotransplantation; (verb) to transfer aforementioned tissue or organs. Tips Don’t separately report any technical lab tests, such as leukocyte antibody assay, because MAAA codes always include the underlying lab tests. Some payers may pay separately for collecting the specimen. In addition to Category I codes for MAAA tests, CPT® lists additional MAAA “administrative codes” in an appendix for tests that have not been assigned a Category I code. Use the unlisted MAAA code, 81599, only when the there is no Category I or administrative code for a given MAAA test. Read Less

Tips CPT® guidelines instruct that you should not choose a code that merely approximates the service provided. short_description: Ketone body(s) (eg, acetone, acetoacetic acid, beta-hydroxybutyrate); qualitative
lay_term: This testing is for the qualitative determination of ketone bodies. Clinicians frequently order ketone body tests for diabetic patients, but also for patients who are dehydrated or are on diets where the body is using fat as its source of energy. Explanation Lab personnel qualitatively test for the presence of ketone bodies using a manual stick or tablet reagent. Alternatively, the lab personnel may use an automated instrument. The test identifies ketone bodies in urine or other fluid samples. An older term for this test is the nitroprusside test because most methods of measurement use the nitroprusside reaction for detection, such as using a test strip impregnated with nitroprusside and checking the color change when the analyst adds the sample to the strip. Terminology Ketones; ketone bodies: Byproducts produced when the liver breaks down fat (rather than glucose) for energy, which can lead to ketoacidosis in diabetics. Qualitative testing: Test to determine the presence or absence of a substance in the specimen. Quantitative measurement: Test to measure the specific quantity of a substance in the specimen. Tips To report a quantitative ketone body test, use 82010. If the analyst performs the quantitative level test on a measured urine specimen, 81050 may be a possible addition. As noted in the descriptor, the various ketone bodies include not just acetone but also acetoacetic acid and beta–hydroxybutyrate as well, meaning you can use this code for any or all of the qualitative ketone bodies. Personnel testing patient specimens for ketone bodies should also recognize that there may be false–positive test results due to substances such as certain drugs and vitamin C, as well as false negatives due to other causes. The level of the ketone body beta–hydroxybutyrate may be present but not be identified until later when the ketone levels are measurable. Read Less
guidelines: Lab & Path Guidelines Range Specific Guideline The material for examination may be from any source unless otherwise specified in the code descriptor. When an analyte is measured in multiple specimens from different sources, or in specimens that are obtained at different times, the analyte is reported separately for each source and for each specimen. The examination is quantitative unless specified. To report an organ or disease oriented panel, see codes 80048-80076. Clinical information or mathematically calculated values, which are not specifically requested by the ordering physician and are derived from the results of other ordered or performed laboratory tests, are considered part of the ordered test procedure(s) and therefore are not separately reportable service(s). When the requested analyte result is derived using a calculation that requires values from nonrequested laboratory analyses, only the requested analyte code should be reported. When the calculated analyte determination requires values derived from other requested and nonrequested laboratory analyses, the requested analyte codes (including those calculated) should be reported. An exception to the above is when an analyte (eg, urinary creatinine) is performed to compensate for variations in urine concentration (eg, microalbumin, thromboxane metabolites) in random urine samples; the appropriate CPT® code is reported for both the ordered analyte and the additional required analyte. When the calculated result(s) represent an algorithmically derived numeric score or probability, see the appropriate multianalyte assay with algorithmic analyses (MAAA) code or the MAAA unlisted code (81599). Analytes that are not specified by either an analyte-specific or method-specific code in the Chemistry (82009-84830) subsection may be reported using the unlisted chemistry procedure code 84999.

short_description: Acylcarnitines; quantitative, each specimen Notes: (For carnitine, use 82379)
lay_term: This test is for the analysis of quantitative acylcarnitines, which clinicians use to diagnose various fatty acid metabolic disorders. The clinician may also use this testing to help determine the diagnosis of many organic acidurias. Explanation The lab analyst may use various methodologies for the analysis of acylcarnitines including enzymatic, chromatographic, or mass spectroscopy methods. The sample type is usually serum or urine. Many metabolic disorders are associated with an increase of acylcarnitines, and this testing is helpful in determining many fatty acid disorders that are amenable to treatment if diagnosed early in the disease state. Other uses for this testing are the diagnosis of other fatty acid disorders such as Zellweger’s syndrome and many inborn disorders of metabolism. Providers may determine many organic acidurias, such as ones that cause sudden death, with the help of acylcarnitine level testing. Terminology Aciduria: The presence of acid in urine, particularly in abnormal amounts. Chromatography: A lab technique that separates the components of a mixture; the mixture passes through various materials and the components pass through at different rates depending on their nature. Mass spectroscopy: A lab technique that separates the components of a sample based on their mass. Tips See 82016 if the test is for qualitative acylcarnitines. Report one unit for each specimen the lab analyst tests. Read Less

short_description: Aldosterone Notes: (Alkaline phosphatase, see 84075, 84080) (Alphaketoglutarate, see 82009, 82010) (Alpha tocopherol [Vitamin E], use 84446)
lay_term: The lab analyst performs a quantitative measurement, typically on serum, plasma, or urine, to determine the level of aldosterone. Providers order this test primarily for the determination of primary or secondary hyperaldosteronism. Aldosterone is the primary mineralocorticoid that is produced in the adrenal cortex, located on the upper pole of the kidney; it helps with water and sodium retention and potassium excretion Explanation The analyst performs laboratory testing by using sensitive instrumentation, such as by radioimmunoassay or more commonly by liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry. Radioimmunoassay, commonly abbreviated as RIA, uses a gamma–radioactive isotope for the precise measurement of minute quantities of an analyte. The test involves using a tagged antigen to measure the quantity of the analyte from the patient’s sample by using a gamma counter. Liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry quantitatively measures aldosterone in a process where the analyst injects the sample into the chromatography instrument for separation and analysis and then into a second instrument for mass spectrometry where sensitive detectors are able to quantitate the amount of aldosterone present. Terminology Mineralocorticoid: A steroid hormone class that influences salt and water balances in the body. Tips You may see patient position and time of collection noted in the documentation for this test. The provider takes special care to collect the proper specimen by following lab collection instructions on the position of the patient prior to and during the collection, as the position of the patient will affect the level of the aldosterone. Also, the time of the day the provider takes the collection needs to be established and carefully scheduled as aldosterone levels vary over the 24 hour period. See code 80408 if the testing is for an aldosterone suppression evaluation panel, as this panel includes the performance of two aldosterone and two renin tests. The provider performs the tests to evaluate a patient with a particular problem, where the use of this saline infusion test adds valuable diagnostic information that a single test does not give. short_description: Aminolevulinic acid, delta (ALA)
lay_term: The lab analyst performs a delta aminolevulinic acid test to diagnose porphyrias, a genetic disorder in which there is a problem in production of heme, or blood in the body. Explanation The lab analyst performs a test to measure the aminolevulinic acid, or ALA, concentration in the patient’s body. The aminolevulinic acid is a precursor of heme and the excretion of aminolevulinic acid increases in the body due to porphyrias. A typical specimen is urine. The lab analyst may use a methodology such as column chromatography or spectrophotometry to perform the test. Spectrophotometry is a method in which the lab analyst calculates the concentration of a substance in a solution by determining the amount of light absorbed. He uses a spectrophotometer to accurately measure the amount of light at a particular wavelength that the sample absorbs after a chemical reaction. This process determines the amount of the tested analyte. Column chromatography is a method in which the substances for segregation are distributed in two phases in a solid stationary phase and a mobile fluid phase. A glass column serves as the solid stationary phase and a solvent serves as the fluid mobile phase. The analyst introduces a tissue sample into a glass column with a glass filter at the bottom. A suitable solvent is poured to the top of the column to dissolve the tissue sample and is lowered down slowly into the column. The analyst then separates the dissolved components, as to their relative similarity towards the solvent and their own specific gravity. Finally, the analyst removes the impurities and separates the elements the analyst desires. These constituents are available for study later. Terminology Heme: An iron compound that makes up the deep red pigment portion, or protein free part of the blood. short_description: Ammonia
lay_term: The lab analyst performs a measurement of the ammonia in the blood, plasma, or other body fluids. Elevated levels of ammonia in the blood are frequently indicative of an infectious process. Explanation The lab analyst performs a quantitative measurement of the ammonia, commonly using an ion–selective electrode. This is a method where a sensitive instrument called a potentiometer measures the voltage from a transducer, which converts energy from one form to another. In this case, the transducer converts the activity of a single ion’s electrical potential to measure the amount of a specific analyte in a solution. Providers consider this test to be a liver function test. Symptoms of ammonia increase can present as seizures, vomiting, hyperventilation, irritability, neurologic disorders, and epilepsy. The liver usually breaks down ammonia, which is then converted to urea, which is excreted in the urine. Increased protein intake may also increase the ammonia level. Tips It is critical to follow special collection and handling of the specimen when testing for ammonia. Providers frequently order ammonia testing as NH3, the common abbreviation. Read Less

short_description: Androstenedione
lay_term: The lab analyst measures the quantitative level of the androgenic hormone androstenedione. The test is of use in addition to other hormone tests in the clinical workup of hyperandrogenism, meaning excess androgen, or adrenal hyperplasia, a disorder in which the adrenal glands produce excess androgen. This hormone is primarily produced by the adrenal glands and gonads. Explanation The lab analyst quantitatively measures the androstenedione level primarily by a radioimmunoassay methodology. This method uses a gamma–radioactive isotope that can precisely measure minute quantities of an analyte using a tagged antigen, which a gamma counter then quantitates. Lab analysts perform the test on serum, whole blood, amniotic fluid, or saliva. This hormone is produced in the adrenal glands and gonads and serves as a precursor for other hormones. Providers order the test in the clinical setting for the evaluation of patients suspected of Cushing’s syndrome and other conditions related to the management and treatment of adrenal disorders. Terminology Cushing’s syndrome: A condition where the body produces too much cortisol or is subjected to too much corticosteroid medication, which can result in visible signs or symptoms such as puffy face, diabetic symptoms, and elevated blood pressure. short_description: Arsenic Notes: (For heavy metal screening, use 83015)
lay_term: The analyst measures the level of arsenic, which is a toxic metallic chemical element with symbol As and atomic number 33. Explanation The lab analyst quantitatively determines the amount of this toxic metal. The preferred specimen is a 24 hour urine specimen. Methodology is commonly by a form of mass spectroscopy where the sample is bombarded with electrons, which are then subjected to an electric or magnetic field, allowing the arsenic to be identified by its mass or the characteristic fragmentation pattern. This substance has been used for thousands of years as a therapeutic agent and as a poison. The Nobel laureate, physician, and chemist Paul Ehrlich developed Salvarsan, an organic arsenical, used in the treatment of syphilis, and even today providers use it in the treatment of trypanosomiasis. Toxic exposure today is primarily from inorganic arsenic in drinking water. Arsenic is prevalent in drinking water in certain localities and providers order this test to determine whether the patient has a toxic level. Organic arsenic is less harmful and quickly eliminated from the body while nonorganic arsenic is toxic. Eating shellfish will raise the level of arsenic, but this being an organic arsenic substance, it is not harmful. Inorganic arsenic is used in industry for hardening metals and for treating wood products and also in the production of insecticides, herbicides, and pesticides. Terminology Trypanosomiasis: Disease caused by the parasitic protozoan organism of the genus Trypanosoma, earlier known as sleeping sickness, now known as African trypanosomiasis or Chagas disease when found on the American continent, primarily in Latin America. short_description: Beta-2 microglobulin Notes: (Bicarbonate, use 82374)
lay_term: The lab analyst measures the level of beta–2 microglobulin, typically in serum, cerebral spinal fluid, or urine. This test is useful in the evaluation of renal disease, the activity of certain leukemias, and checking for increases seen in Crohn’s disease, sarcoidosis, viral infections, and certain malignancies. Explanation The lab analyst quantitatively measures the beta–2 microglobulin, usually in serum, spinal fluid, or urine, most commonly by radioimmunoassay. This is a technique using a gamma–radioactive tagged isotope that allows a precise measurement using a gamma counter. Beta–2 microglobulin is useful in the evaluation of, or following the progression of, many different disease conditions, such as renal disease, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, hepatitis, and other malignancies. Beta–2 microglobulin is an amino acid peptide and is a small polymorphic protein that is a component of the class I HLA complex, which is part of the immune system. Tips Providers may abbreviate this test as B2–M, B–2M, or Beta2M. Read Less

short_description: Bile acids; total
lay_term: The lab analyst performs an analysis, primarily on serum, for total bile acids, which are essentially formed from cholesterol in the liver. These bile acids are stored and concentrated in the gall bladder and are secreted into the intestine to help emulsify ingested fats to aid digestion. Explanation The lab analyst quantitates the total bile acids, usually with an enzymatic method in which the analyte molecules are oxidized and reduced by an enzyme and then detected and recorded at a specific wavelength by a spectrophotometer. This bile acid, which aids in the digestion and absorption of dietary fat, is a steroid acid and is an organic compound that also has hormonal actions throughout the body. This determination aids in the assessment of hepatic dysfunction due to chemical and environmental insult or injury. Testing is also useful to assess histologic improvement for patients with chronic hepatitis who are undergoing treatment, as well as for patients with cirrhosis, drug induced liver injury, and alcoholic liver disease. short_description: Bile acids; cholylglycine Notes: (For bile pigments, urine, see 81000-81005)
lay_term: The lab analyst measures the level of cholylglycine, typically in serum. Cholylglycine is a glycine conjugate of cholic acid, meaning the two substances join together. Cholylglycine is a fractional part of the total bile acids, which acts as a detergent to solubilize fats for absorption and is itself absorbed in the process. Explanation The lab analyst quantitatively measures the amount of cholylglycine, which is a portion of the total bile acids. The usual method is radioimmunoassay, which uses a gamma–radioactive tagged isotope that allows a precise measurement using a gamma counter. Cholylglycine determinations aid in the diagnosis of hepatocellular disease as the ratio of this analyte to other bile acid fractions is a significant factor. This test is of importance when used to monitor bile acid therapy or aid in the determination of inborn errors of bile metabolism. Tips Providers may order this test as glycocholic acid, which is the closest synonym. Analysts usually perform testing for multiple bile acid fractions using high performance liquid chromatography and mass spectrometry. For those tests, base the billing code on the particular methodology used. See 82239 for total bile acids. Read Less

short_description: Bilirubin; feces, qualitative
lay_term: The lab analyst determines the qualitative presence of bilirubin in the feces specimen. Bilirubin is not generally present in normal conditions. short_description: Biotinidase, each specimen
lay_term: The lab analyst performs a measurement of the enzyme biotinidase, typically on a blood sample. This enzyme test is useful for the identification of a deficiency of biotinidase and also for the follow–up testing for a previously positive screen for this enzyme. Symptoms commonly seen with this disease are irritability, seizures, vomiting, and loss of appetite. Explanation The lab analyst performs a quantitative measurement for the enzyme biotinidase. Analysts commonly use spectrophotometric instrumentation to accurately measure the amount of light at a particular wavelength that the sample absorbs after a chemical reaction. This difference allows for calculation and reporting of the amount of the analyte. Serum or whole blood is the common sample used for testing. Biotinidase deficiency testing is important to allow treatment for affected individuals early during the disease. Providers identify many biotinidase deficiencies using the newborn screening program that states have in place. Providers primarily use this testing to confirm and better define this inherited metabolic autosomal recessive disorder that affects the recycling of biotin, a vitamin B complex. The deficiency of this enzyme affects the production of certain fats and carbohydrates. Tips Biotinidase’s parent substance is biotin. Vitamin B7 is the common term used. The billing code for this is 84591, which applies to testing for vitamins not otherwise specified. New molecular tests are available for mutation analysis and for confirmatory or carrier testing for biotinidase deficiency as well as for the full gene analysis that can identify at–risk family members to enable early identification and treatment. Use the proper molecular test code for those tests. Read Less

short_description: Blood, occult, by peroxidase activity (eg, guaiac), qualitative, feces, 1-3 simultaneous determinations, performed for other than colorectal neoplasm screening Notes: (Blood urea nitrogen [BUN], see 84520, 84525)
lay_term: The lab analyst uses a peroxidase activity method to perform a test for the presence of hidden blood in a fecal specimen that the patient collects from three consecutive bowel movements, or that the clinician acquires through a method such as a digital rectal exam. Explanation The clinician may acquire the specimen through a digital rectal exam and provide a single smear to the lab. Or the clinician may provide the patient with a triple card or three separate cards for a stool sample smear from three consecutive bowel movements, and the patient submits the cards to the laboratory. If the smear changes rapidly to an intense blue color, that is a positive result, indicating the presence of blood in the stool as a qualitative result. The test is sometimes called a guaiac test because the paper for the fecal smear test card comes from an extract of the guaiacum tree, which reacts with blood in the presence of hydrogen peroxide to turn blue. The clinician orders this test to help diagnose or rule out a condition such as bleeding ulcers. This test is not a colorectal cancer screening test. short_description: Bradykinin
lay_term: The lab analyst measures the bradykinin level in blood, plasma, or other biologic fluids. The test for this biologically active peptide is primarily a research–use–only procedure. Bradykinin is involved in many allergy–like diseases or swelling disorders and researchers are studying its effect on smooth muscle. Explanation The lab analyst, primarily in a research facility, performs quantitative measurements of bradykinin. A typical method involves using an enzyme–linked immunosorbent test using an antigen–antibody reaction and a color change to determine the endpoint and quantitative peptide level. This is a biologically active peptide that activates sensory fibers. It functions by affecting smooth muscle and is involved in conditions such as asthma and inflammation. It also functions as a vasodilation agent that affects blood pressure and the release of cytokines. Testing currently is performed at research facilities as bradykinin testing is not available for routine clinical use. Terminology Cytokine: A substance secreted by certain cells of the immune system capable of having an effect on other cells. Tips The bradykinin test, primarily a research–use–only test, has limited application in clinical laboratories, as most payers will not pay for this testing. Read Less

short_description: Cadmium
lay_term: The lab analyst measures this element, typically in a blood sample when acute intoxication is expected or in a 24 hour urine specimen if the provider suspects chronic exposure to cadmium. Cadmium is a toxic heavy metal primarily used in industry and manufacturing. Explanation The lab analyst quantitatively measures this heavy metal, usually in blood or urine, usually by a method such as atomic absorption spectroscopy. In this test the analyst measures the cadmium in the sample by utilizing the absorption of spectral radiation by free atoms in a gaseous state. This metal is a chemical element with the atomic number 48 and the symbol Cd, and it is a frequent source of toxic contamination from burning coal or oil and the incineration of municipal waste. Tips Analysts should not perform testing within 96 hours after the patient receives a contrast medium such as gadolinium or iodine containing solutions such as those used with certain imaging contrast studies in radiology imaging departments. short_description: Vitamin D; 25 hydroxy, includes fraction(s), if performed
lay_term: The lab analyst measures the vitamin D level, typically on a serum specimen. This analyte, commonly known as vitamin D, is not really a vitamin, but is an important steroid hormone that is produced by the liver. It is commonly known as the sunshine vitamin, with sunlight on the skin being a common source of this important vitamin. Explanation The lab analyst quantifies this vitamin, usually on a serum specimen and commonly by immunoassay with a bioanalytical method. This test depends on the reaction of an antigen, which is the analyte, and an antibody to accurately measure this hormone. This analysis measures the major circulating form of vitamin D that helps regulate calcium and phosphorus. Vitamin D has many other diverse effects that are mediated by receptors; these help regulate hundreds of genes. Practitioners test for vitamin D to diagnose and treat vitamin D deficiency, malabsorption, and a host of related disorders. This is the most common vitamin D test practitioners order when they suspect deficiency or when following the patient on vitamin D supplementation. Tips Code 82306 is appropriate when the analyst measures the total vitamin D only. But this code 82306 also includes the fractions vitamin D2 and/or vitamin D3 if performed. The fractions are not separately billable. Providers may also order this test as 25–OH vitamin D, 25–hydroxycholecalciferol, 25(OH)D, calcifediol, and calcidiol. For testing of 1, 25–dihydroxy vitamin D, see 82652. Read Less

short_description: Calcitonin
lay_term: The lab analyst measures calcitonin, typically on serum or plasma. This hormone calcitonin is a polypeptide secreted by specialized cells in the thyroid gland. Calcitonin is elevated primarily in the presence of tumors located in the thyroid calcitonin cells, also known as parafollicular cells. Explanation The lab analyst quantitatively measures the calcitonin level, commonly using a chemiluminescent immunoassay method. This method accurately measures the luminescence as a result of a chemical reaction. Calcitonin’s main function is to inhibit bone resorption by having a regulatory effect on bone osteoclasts. Their function is to remove old bone prior to the osteoblasts remodeling or adding new bone. Malignant processes such as medullary thyroid carcinoma will usually produce an increase in the calcitonin level. Tips Clinicians may order a calcitonin stimulation test after calcium infusion. The provider gives the patient a calcium–pentagastrin infusion, followed by two additional calcitonin tests performed after the infusion. The billing code for each test performed is 82308. See 82331 for measurement of calcium after the calcium infusion test. Read Less

short_description: Calcium; total

Providers rarely order calcium testing as a single test unless it is to follow–up on a previous value that is out of the normal range. short_description: Calcium; ionized
lay_term: The lab analyst measures this ionized form of calcium primarily on serum, blood, or a capillary sample. short_description: Calcium; urine quantitative, timed specimen
lay_term: The lab analyst performs the technical lab test to analyze the quantitative value of calcium in the timed urine specimen. Explanation The lab analyst performs all technical steps to measure the amount of calcium in a timed specimen of urine. Providers often order timed urine specimens when the provider is looking for the concentration of a specific substance. In this way, the value is more reliable than just one specimen taken at one point in time. This test does provide a quantitative, number value, not just a positive or negative result. Typically, the patient will rise in the morning and discard the first urine specimen, and then collect every drop of urine for the next 24 hours, including the next morning when he rises. He turns this sample in to the laboratory. The lab analyst measures the volume and tests for the concentration of calcium commonly by spectrophotometry, which measures the amount of light at a particular wavelength that the sample absorbs after a chemical reaction, allowing measurement of the analyte. Typically, if a patient has a higher than normal amount of calcium in the urine, called hypercalciuria, it can be from ingesting larger than normal amounts of calcium–containing foods, the gastrointestinal system absorbing high amounts of calcium, or the bones demineralizing and adding free calcium back into the circulation, which the kidneys filter into the urine. High amounts of calcium over a long period of time in the urine can lead to kidney stones, kidney disease, and failure. Additionally, the parathyroid gland controls the levels of calcium in the body, so providers can use urine calcium to monitor any parathyroid problems. Low amounts of calcium in the urine, called hypocalciuria, can be due to insufficient dietary intake, increased urination, for example, if the patient is taking a diuretic, and parathyroid abnormalities. Also, calcium requires vitamin D for absorption and so low calcium levels may also be linked to low vitamin D levels. Terminology Diuretic: A medication that helps a patient to excrete excess fluid in the body, some patients call this a water pill. Parathyroid: Small paired glands that sit next to the thyroid gland in the neck and secrete parathyroid hormone, the substance responsible for calcium and phosphorus regulation. Tips See 82310 to 82331 to review other calcium test codes. Read Less

lay_term: The lab analyst determines the composition of the calculus or stone performing a chemical analysis, which determines the quantitative chemical composition. short_description: Carboxyhemoglobin; quantitative
lay_term: The lab analyst measures the carboxyhemoglobin, more commonly known as a complex of hemoglobin and carbon monoxide, which is a colorless, odorless, poisonous gas, primarily derived from the combustion or burning of a variety of fuels. Explanation The lab analyst quantitatively determines the level of this gas in a blood sample, commonly using a spectrophotometer. This instrument accurately measures the amount of light at a particular wavelength that the sample absorbs after a chemical reaction, which then quantitates the carbon monoxide. Analysts also can measure this analyte on an instrument called a co–oximeter, which measures various blood gases and blood pH. Clinicians order this test on persons suspected of carbon monoxide poisoning from a variety of sources, especially those with prolonged contact with vehicle exhaust in an enclosed space, or fire victims. The great danger of carbon monoxide exposure is that the affinity of hemoglobin to carbon monoxide is greater than it is for oxygen, and the carbon monoxide bond to hemoglobin is more permanent, replacing the affected hemoglobin and making it useless for oxygen transport to the tissue. Levels greater than 60 percent to 70 percent usually result in death. Carbon monoxide poisoning is a leading cause of death by poisoning and thousands die from this condition every year. Terminology Carbon monoxide poisoning: The condition of the hemoglobin in the blood having an abnormally high level of carbon monoxide with a resultant decrease in the ability of the hemoglobin to receive the oxygen atom; can result in death when the lethal level is attained. Tips Common abbreviations include CO and COHb. Use code 82376 for the screening test for carboxyhemoglobin. Read Less

short_description: Carboxyhemoglobin; qualitative Notes: (For transcutaneous measurement of carboxyhemoglobin, use 88740)
lay_term: The lab analyst performs testing to determine if carboxyhemoglobin or carbon monoxide is present. This poisonous, colorless, odorless gas causes thousands of deaths each year and is a leading cause of death by poisoning. Explanation The lab analyst tests for the presence of carboxyhemoglobin or carbon monoxide, CO, in the blood, commonly using a spectrophotometer. short_description: Carnitine (total and free), quantitative, each specimen Notes: (For acylcarnitine, see 82016, 82017)
lay_term: The lab analyst measures both the total and free carnitine on serum, plasma, urine, or tissue specimens. Total carnitine includes both the free carnitine and all the acylcarnitines. Carnitines are important carriers that shuttle long–chain fatty acids into the mitochondria where the fatty acids are used as cellular fuel. Practitioners may order carnitine testing when a newborn screen tested positive on the blood spot test. Explanation The lab analyst quantitatively measures the level of both the free and total carnitine using an instrument such as a tandem mass spectroscope, which is capable of separating the components of a sample based on their mass and fragmentation pattern. Carnitine deficiency causes a decrease in cellular oxidation of fatty acids in the mitochondria and a decrease in ketone production. Practitioners order carnitine testing to determine both primary genetic conditions and secondary fatty acid oxidation disorders, both of which can be treated with supplements. Providers may also order the testing on muscle tissue, in addition to blood levels, due to muscle levels being much higher than serum or plasma levels. Tips See code 82016 for acylcarnitines, qualitative, and 82017 for acylcarnitines, quantitative. Report only one unit for code 82379 for carnitine, total and free, for each specimen the analyst tests. Read Less

short_description: Carotene
lay_term: The lab analyst measures this photosynthetic orange pigment, also known as beta–carotene, typically in a serum specimen. Carotene is a fat–soluble provitamin converted to vitamin A in the liver. Explanation The lab analyst quantitatively measures the carotene level, typically in serum. Practitioners consider this test controversial as the level of carotene does not add much diagnostic information because it is primarily a pigment.
