short_description: Catecholamines; fractionated Notes: (For urine metabolites, see 83835, 84585)
lay_term: The analyst measures the catecholamines, which includes fractionation for epinephrine, norepinephrine, and dopamine, typically from a 24–hour urine or a plasma sample. Explanation The lab analyst quantitatively determines the catecholamines fractions, usually using a method such as high pressure liquid chromatography. This method utilizes a combination of a pressurized liquid and the sample forced though a sorbent column and then separated by a sensitive detector. Practitioners may order this test to workup patients with unexplained or persistent hypertension, or for suspected adrenal or neuroendocrine tumors. This test fractionates the catecholamines into the three component parts, epinephrine, norepinephrine and dopamine. In contrast, the total catecholamines test on blood or urine, gives only a total of all three as one result. The clinician is interested in learning whether any of the three fractions are increased, as each fraction is of diagnostic significance. short_description: Ceruloplasmin

short_description: Chloride; other source Notes: (For sweat collection by iontophoresis, use 89230)
lay_term: The lab analyst measures the amount of chloride in the cerebrospinal fluid, called CSF, in sweat, or from another source other than blood or urine. Chloride is one of the important ions needed to maintain the electrolyte balance in the body. Explanation The lab analyst quantitatively measures the chloride, commonly in spinal fluid or sweat, using a method known as ion selective electrode. In this method, a sensitive potentiometer measures the voltage from a transducer, which converts energy from one form to another. In this case the transducer converts the activity of a single ion’s electric potential to measure the amount of chloride in the solution. Clinicians order sweat chloride by iontophoresis, and the lab analyst performs the testing which measures the chloride in the collected sweat. Patients with cystic fibrosis may have elevated chloride levels. Terminology Iontophoresis: The clinician or lab analyst uses the drug pilocarpine to induce sweating using an iontophoresis apparatus consisting of two small electrodes placed on the skin; the electrodes create a tiny electrical current that stimulates sweat, which is collected and analyzed for the chloride level. Tips See 82435 for blood chloride, 82436 for urine chloride, and 89230 for the sweat collection procedure by iontophoresis. Read Less

short_description: Chondroitin B sulfate, quantitative Notes: (Chorionic gonadotropin, see gonadotropin, 84702, 84703)
lay_term: The lab analyst measures the level of chondroitin B sulfate in a patient specimen. Chondroitin sulfate is a chemical found in the cartilage, the flexible connective tissue around the joints. Explanation Chondroitin sulfate is a major constituent in the cartilage surrounding the joint and is important in maintaining the connective tissue function. It is also found in blood vessels, heart valves, and the lungs. It plays a valuable role in the functioning of the articular cartilage. Chondroitin B sulfate is also known as dermatan sulfate. The lab analyst usually uses a 24 hour urine collection kit for testing of chondroitin B sulfate. However, depending upon the patient's condition, the specimen may be body fluids like blood, plasma, serum, or even different body tissues, or muscles. The lab analyst may use a methodology such as high performance liquid chromatography, or HPLC. This method forces a combination of a pressurized liquid and the specimen through a specially designed column. This method separates the analyte, which is the substance the analyst is measuring, from the mixture, allowing a sensitive detector to quantitate the analyte. Quantitation refers to measuring the exact amount of a substance. The clinician uses chondroitin sulfate for the treatment of various chronic diseases such as degenerative arthritis and cirrhosis. He also uses it as dietary supplement for treatment of osteoarthritis. Terminology Articular cartilage: Fibrous connective tissue covering the bony surfaces of a joint. Arthritis: An inflammatory condition affecting one or more of the body’s joints, resulting in pain, swelling, and limitation of movement. Cirrhosis: A disease in which scar tissue replaces the normal liver tissue. Serum: The clear liquid portion of blood that is not cellular and contains important components such as antibodies, or proteins produced in blood that are activated as part of the immune response to neutralize specific invaders such as bacteria or viruses. short_description: Collagen cross links, any method
lay_term: The lab analyst performs collagen cross–linking, a technique that he uses for various medical conditions. Collagen cross–links are reliable markers of bone resorption because they are stable in serum and urine. This test is helpful to monitor, assess, and determine the rate of bone loss and treatment effectiveness during osteoporosis and osteopenia. Explanation The lab analyst performs a collagen cross–linking test that he uses for various medical conditions. A typical specimen may be urine or serum. One of the methods is called N Telopeptide, in which urine is the sample. This test is useful for the diagnosis of medical interlinked conditions, with increased bone turnover. In this method, the lab analyst collects a 24–hour urine specimen and keeps it cold by refrigeration that helps to evaluate the amount of collagen cross–links present in the body. He may implement various techniques to perform this test such as quantitative electrochemiluminescent immunoassay, Vitros® ECi competitive assay, enzymatic colorimetric assay, and Vitros® N terminal telopeptide (NTx) assay. Terminology Immunoassay: Chemical tests used to detect or quantify a specific substance, known as the analyte, in a blood or body fluid sample, using an immunological reaction, or the interaction of antigens with specific antibodies. Osteopenia: A condition less severe than osteoporosis in which the protein and mineral content of bone tissue gets reduced. Osteoporosis: A thinning of the bones with reduction in bone mass due to depletion of calcium and bone protein commonly occurring as a result of hormonal changes, or a deficiency of calcium or vitamin D. Photosensitizing agent: A category of topical or systemic drugs or chemicals a provider uses to treat various skin diseases and neoplasms; they are pharmacologically inactive, but when exposed to ultraviolet radiation or sunlight they convert to an active metabolite to produce a beneficial reaction affecting the diseased tissue. Serum: The clear liquid portion of blood that is not cellular and contains important components such as antibodies, proteins produced in the blood that are activated as part of the immune response to neutralize specific invaders such as bacteria or viruses. Ultraviolet light: A part of light not visible to the eye that is able to break some chemical bonds. Read Less

short_description: Cryoglobulin, qualitative or semi-quantitative (eg, cryocrit) Notes: (For quantitative, cryoglobulin, see 82784, 82785) (Crystals, pyrophosphate vs urate, use 89060)
lay_term: The lab analyst measures the amount of cryoglobulin, an abnormal blood protein such as cryocrit, in a patient specimen, using qualitative or semi–quantitative analysis. Cryocrit is cryoglobulin sediment after cold centrifugation of the serum. Explanation The lab analyst performs a test to measure the amount of cryoglobulins or cryocrit in a patient specimen. A typical specimen is blood. For the testing of cryoglobulins or cryocrit, the lab analyst usually draws the blood sample through a prewarmed syringe. After obtaining the blood, he then transfers it to a pre–warmed blue tube containing sodium citrate, a sodium salt of citric acid, and keeps it at room temperature. The lab analyst may use a methodology such as qualitative analysis or semiquantitative analysis. Qualitative analysis identifies the presence or absence of cryoglobulins whereas semiquantitative is an approximate calculation of the amount of cryoglobulins. A common method to perform this test is quantization and qualitative typing precipitation at one degree Celsius. Cryoglobulin is an abnormal blood protein that separates a substance from a solution as a solid upon cooling to 4 degrees centigrade and redissolves at 37 degrees centigrade when warmed to room temperature. Cryoglobulins are interlinked with plasma cells, and clinicians mainly perform this test to analyze symptoms occurring with cold exposure such as collagen vascular diseases, vasculitis, hepatitis C, glomerulonephritis, and other disorders. Terminology Glomerulonephritis: A disease of the clusters of blood vessels in the kidneys with small pores that filter blood; leads to body tissue swelling or edema, high blood pressure, and the presence of red blood cells in the urine of the patient; also called nephritic syndrome. Hepatitis: Inflammation or swelling of the liver. Tips Some payers may pay separately for collecting the specimen using a code such as 36415, Collection of venous blood by venipuncture. Read Less

short_description: Cystatin C
lay_term: The lab analyst performs the technical lab test to measure the amount of a protein, typically in the blood, called cystatin C. Explanation The lab analyst performs all technical steps to mix the patient’s specimen, typically serum, with reagents to obtain a cystatin C level. Typically, the analyst performs an agglutination type test; the analyst mixes the reagents from the assay with the patient’s serum or plasma, and clumping occurs making the sample cloudy. The amount of cloudiness is proportional to the amount of cystatin C in the sample and allows quantification. Clinicians may order this test instead of creatinine for renal function. Some patients have another disorder that affects the creatinine value, making it useless for detecting renal function. Cystatin C may be more sensitive than creatinine, thereby increasing earlier than creatinine to indicate early kidney dysfunction. Cystatin C is a good indication of glomerular filtration rate (GFR). Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians may order cystatin C as a screen for kidney disease, but also may use the test for cardiovascular disease and some brain disorders. Terminology Assay: A laboratory test to find or measure the quantity of some entity, called the analyte, or to find or measure some property of the analyte, such as functional activity. Glomerular filtration rate (GFR): The rate at which the kidneys can process the elements in the blood so they can be eliminated through urine. Plasma: The liquid portion of blood that typically suspends blood cells; plasma accounts for about 55 percent of blood volume and contains important components such as proteins, electrolytes, hormones, and coagulation factors. Reagent: A substance used in a lab test to bring about a desired change or reaction, often to reveal the presence or quantity of another substance that is the focus of the test. Serum: The clear liquid portion of blood that is not cellular and contains important components such as antibodies, proteins produced in the blood that are activated as part of the immune response to neutralize specific invaders such as bacteria or viruses. Tips Serum concentration of cystatin C is a good marker for renal function as other conditions such as inflammation, body mass, or diet don’t affect cystatin C. Although clinicians may also use serum creatinine and blood urea nitrogen, or BUN, as indicators of kidney function, they're not likely to order those tests and cystatin C at the same time solely to assess renal status. You should check with your payers for coverage rules regarding these tests. Cystatin C is sometimes called gamma trace, post gamma globulin, or neuroendocrine basic polypeptide. Some payers may pay separately for collecting the specimen using a code such as 36415, Collection of venous blood by venipuncture. Read Less

short_description: Dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) Notes: (Do not report 82626 in conjunction with 80327, 80328 to identify anabolic steroid testing for testosterone)
lay_term: The lab analyst performs an analysis of dehydroepiandrosterone, known as an unconjugated form of DHEA. It is a major precursor of 17–ketosteroids, which the body forms when it breaks down certain hormones. Lab analysts commonly perform the test on a serum specimen. Clinicians primarily use the testing to determine adrenal gland function. Explanation The lab analyst performs a quantitative measurement of the dehydroepiandrosterone, primarily on serum, using a methodology such as radioimmunoassay. This method uses a gamma–radioactive tagged isotope, which allows a precise measurement using a gamma counter. Clinicians use this procedure to diagnose delayed puberty and hirsutism as well as other conditions such as neoplasm of the adrenal gland, ovarian disorders, and Cushing’s disease. Decreased levels may be found in adrenal hypoplasia. Terminology Hirsutism: Condition presenting with increased hairiness in women, in locations where such stiff, pigmented hair is not normally present. Unconjugated: The free form of a compound, not joined by two or more chemical compounds. Tips See code 82627 for dehydroepiandrosterone–S. Review the requisition request closely, if the letter "S" follows the DHEA order, the request is actually for a dehydroepiandrosterone–S test, which has now become the more commonly ordered of these two tests. short_description: Elastase, pancreatic (EL-1), fecal; qualitative or semi-quantitative
lay_term: Code 82656 describes a test for pancreatic elastase (EL–1) in a fecal specimen. A common lab method for this test is a qualitative or semi–quantitative enzyme–linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Clinicians may use this test to evaluate conditions such as cystic fibrosis and pancreatic inflammation or tumors. Explanation The lab analyst performs a qualitative or semi–quantitative lab test such as an enzyme–linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) to identify pancreatic elastase (EL–1) in a fecal specimen. ELISA uses an enzyme–labeled antigen or antibody that will react with a specific target causing a measurable change (such as color) that identifies the presence and possibly the level of the target in the specimen. Clinicians may order this test to evaluate conditions such as cystic fibrosis and pancreatic inflammation or tumors. Terminology Antibody: A protein produced by the body as an immune–system response to a specific antigen, such as a bacteria or foreign substance; lab tests may utilize reactions between antibodies and antigens to identify a substance in a patient specimen; may also be referred to as immunoglobulin. Antigen: A substance that the body reacts to with an immune response, such as by producing a specific antibody; lab tests may utilize reactions between antibodies and antigens to identify a substance in a patient specimen. Cystic fibrosis: An inherited disorder characterized by the production of thick, sticky mucus that blocks pancreatic ducts and clogs the lungs. Enzyme: A biological compound that acts as a selective catalyst to increase the rate and specificity of certain biochemical reactions, such as breaking down a specific compound. Enzyme–linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA): A laboratory testing method using an enzyme attached to an antigen or antibody used as a marker to detect a specific substance, such as another antigen or antibody. Pancreas: An organ in the abdomen that produces enzymes to aid in digestion and control of blood sugar; islets cells scattered through the pancreas secrete a variety of hormones, including glucagon and insulin. short_description: Estrogens; fractionated
lay_term: The lab analyst measures the fractions of estrogen, primarily estradiol and estrone. A third lesser fraction is estriol, produced in significant amount only during pregnancy. The first two represent the major fractions found in serum. Estrogens are the major sex hormone in females, being produced primarily in the ovaries. Explanation The lab analyst quantitates the level of the major fractions of estrogen, typically estradiol and estrone, in serum or urine. Methodology is commonly by liquid mass spectroscopy, in which electrons bombard atoms or molecules from the sample. The instrument then subjects the electrons to an electric or magnetic field, and identifies the resulting hormones by their masses or by their characteristic fragmentation pattern. short_description: Ethylene glycol
lay_term: The lab analyst measures the sample’s level of ethylene glycol, a very toxic, sweet tasting compound. This solution is very dangerous, and the lab test report, if positive, should be a panic value, meaning one that the lab urgently reports to the clinician. Ethylene glycol is the primary component in antifreeze, used in the coolant systems of most automobiles. Explanation The lab analyst quantitates the serum or plasma sample’s level of ethylene glycol, a very toxic, sweet tasting, odorless fluid. Gas–liquid chromatography is one of the most frequent methods lab analysts use. The method involves a liquid compound and an inert gas pushing the analyte through an adsorbent tube. The instrument identifies the amount of the analyte by the migration rate and vapor pressure. Clinicians order emergency testing primarily for poisoning or inadvertent ingestion of ethylene glycol. This sweet tasting liquid can be enticing for children or pets, or mistaken for the alcohol ethanol, but ethylene glycol is very toxic, and a patient who ingests it requires quick medical intervention. Tips Clinicians may request this test as 1,2–ethanediol. With ethylene glycol ingestion, chemistry tests, electrolytes, and blood gases are frequently markedly abnormal, and in the urine, the lab analyst may observe the presence of oxalate crystals. The term ethylene glycol has similar terminology and characteristics to the food grade propylene glycol and drink–safe antifreeze. But despite this similarity, the effects of ethylene glycol are very different, and can be lethal. Read Less

short_description: Etiocholanolone Notes: (For fractionation of ketosteroids, use 83593)

short_description: Fat or lipids, feces; qualitative
lay_term: The lab analyst performs an analysis on the stool specimen to determine the relative amount of fat in the fecal sample. Malabsorption, maldigestion, and celiac disease are the primary causes of an abnormal increase of fat in the stool. Explanation The lab analyst performs a microscopic study on a random stool specimen to determine the presence of steatorrhea. The lab analyst performs the technique by mixing the fecal material with water, adding Sudan III stain, and observing microscopically to determine the amount of neutral fat or fatty acids present. The analyst reports the observation of fat globules and their size as a semiquantitative analysis, which he may report using a scale from zero to 4–plus. Clinicians order this assay for the presence of an abnormal amount of fecal fat, which is an indication of malabsorption or maldigestion, and also celiac disease. Terminology Steatorrhea: Presence of an increased level of fat in the stool. Tips Also see codes 82710 for quantitative fecal fats, 82715 for fat differential testing, 82725 for nonesterified fatty acids, and 82726 for very long chain fatty acids. In addition, see 89125 for fat stain feces, urine, or respiratory secretions. The patient should receive instructions on how to collect the sample and how to prevent contamination to ensure a valid specimen. The patient also should receive instructions to consume an adequate intake of fat for at least 3–5 days prior to the collection. Read Less

short_description: Ferritin Notes: (Fetal hemoglobin, see hemoglobin 83030, 83033, and 85460) (Fetoprotein, alpha-1, see 82105, 82106)
lay_term: The lab analyst measures the level of ferritin, an important protein composed of about 20 percent iron. Ferritin also acts as an iron reserve in the body, and is present in serum in only minute quantities, but it reflects the iron stores in the body. Explanation The lab analyst quantitates the ferritin in serum, commonly using an immunoassay technique which uses an antigen–antibody response to measure this analyte. Ferritin is present in almost all tissue, including the iron producing cells, and is present in only minute quantities in serum, but is still able to act as an iron reserve for the body. Clinicians depend on ferritin to distinguish between iron deficiency anemia, in which the ferritin level will be diminished, and anemia of chronic disease, in which the ferritin level is usually normal or elevated. A high serum ferritin is also indicative of hemochromatosis, a very serious condition of iron overload, which is treatable if identified. Terminology Anemia of chronic disease: An anemia of inflammatory response, a natural protective mechanism whereby the body is able to sequester or isolate a portion of the iron to prevent it from being available to nourish pathogens. Tips Clinicians frequently order ferritin when also testing for serum iron, code 83540, and iron binding capacity, code 83550. Read Less

short_description: Fluoride Notes: (Foam stability test, use 83662)
lay_term: The lab analyst measures the fluoride in a sample such as plasma, serum, or urine. Fluoride is a substance frequently added to water supplies, in locations where the natural fluoride content is low, with the aim of enhancing dental health. Explanation The lab analyst quantitates the level of fluoride in serum, plasma, urine, or other specimens, using a method such as an ion specific electrode, which employs a sensor that converts the ion’s activity in a solution into an electric potential, which a sensitive voltmeter then measures. Fluoride, described by the National Research Council as an endocrine disrupter in the broad sense, may negatively affect bones, the thyroid gland, the brain, and other glands and organs. Clinicians order fluoride testing when concerned about the toxic level in patients that are exposed to, or ingest, high levels of fluoride, or for patients being treated with anti–fungal medication that includes fluoride. Terminology Endocrine disrupter: A chemical that at a certain dose may interfere with hormone synthesis, transport, secretion, or hormonal action in the body. Tips Fluoride is a common additive to many municipal water supplies to aid in dental health. Recently many cities have discontinued the use of this substance because of concern over studies indicating harmful effects, such as pitted teeth in children consuming fluoride treated water. short_description: Gases, blood, any combination of pH, pCO2, pO2, CO2, HCO3 (including calculated O2 saturation) Notes: (Use 82803 for 2 or more of the above listed analytes)
lay_term: The lab analyst performs blood gas analysis to measure at least two of the listed parameters. He typically performs an arterial blood gas analysis, called an ABG, using arterial blood inserted into a blood gas analyzer that measures several parameters to assess respiratory status including pH, pCO2, pO2, CO2, HCO3, and calculated O2 saturation. These tests indicate the amount of oxygen and carbon dioxide as well as acid and base balance in the blood. Explanation The lab analyst typically receives a heparinized arterial blood specimen that he or another collector obtains by arterial puncture or withdrawal from an arterial catheter from the patient. The analyst then performs all technical steps, from inserting the sample into the blood gas machine to interpreting the acceptability of the results. The blood gas analyzer uses specific electrodes to directly measure pH, pCO2, and pO2, and calculates HCO3 and O2 saturation. He verifies that the blood is arterial and not venous because blood gas values vary with the blood source. Blood gas analytes indicate the partial pressure of carbon dioxide, called pCO2, and partial pressure of oxygen, called pO2. Partial pressure refers to the amount dissolved in the blood. HCO3 is bicarbonate, the most common form of CO2 in blood, created when CO2 and H2O combine. Oxygen saturation, O2 sat, is the percentage of hemoglobin carrying oxygen molecules, and pH is the measure of acid and base balance. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians may order this test all together or in combinations to evaluate respiratory condition, organ function, metabolic status, or other conditions. Terminology Electrode: A device used to transmit electrical impulses. Hemoglobin: The red colored protein in the red blood cell that carries oxygen to the tissue and returns carbon dioxide to the lungs; when the amount is below normal, it may indicate anemia. Heparin: A group of biochemicals that inactivate clotting factors such as thrombin and factor Xa by enhancing the activity of a protein that inhibits coagulation, or clotting. Tips This code is appropriate to use if the analyst measures two or more of the listed gases. Some payers may provide separate reimbursement for drawing the sample, such as 36600, Arterial puncture, withdrawal of blood for diagnosis. Read Less

lay_term: The lab analyst measures the gastric specimen for total acid by chemical testing, by use of a pH meter, or both. This testing is performed on each specimen, and each specimen represents one unit. The patient may also have gastric analysis testing after a stimulation test; in that case the provider obtains fractional specimens over a 1 to 1.5 hour period for testing as described above. Explanation The lab analyst performs the technical steps for gastric acid analysis, including measuring the volume of each specimen, measuring the gastric acidity as shown by pH, or both. The methodology is primarily by using a pH meter, which accurately measures the acidity or alkalinity of a liquid, such as gastric fluid. There is a direct readout on the meter of the actual pH. Many labs today record only the pH for the acidity present. The stimulation test when requested will require an injection of that stimulant and the collection of fractional gastric specimens for a period of 1 to 1.5 hours after stimulation. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians typically order gastric acid analysis for conditions of obscure stomach pain, weight loss, loss of appetite, suspected stomach ulcer, and other similar reasons. Clinicians will frequently order a gastric stimulation test if the initial testing does not reveal information that is diagnostic. Terminology Gastric acid stimulation test: Injection of a stimulant such as secretin or pentagastrin, followed by fractional specimens tested at intervals for 1 to 1.5 hours for gastric acidity level. Tips Report 82930 once for each specimen tested. For example, a gastric analysis may include testing of four separate specimens. Report each as one unit of 82930, for a total of 4 units. short_description: Glucose; quantitative, blood (except reagent strip)
lay_term: The lab analyst performs a test to measure the amount of glucose in a patient's blood using a method other than a reagent strip. Explanation The lab analyst tests patient blood to determine the amount of glucose present, typically after the patient has fasted for at least eight hours. Clinicians sometimes call this a fasting glucose test or a blood sugar test. The lab analyst uses a method such as an enzyme assay, typically using a specialized chemistry analyzer instrument. For instance, the lab analyst may add a reagent containing an enzyme that reacts with glucose in the specimen, causing a change that the analyst can measure using an instrument such as a spectrophotometer. Although the lab analyst, or even the patient, can determine blood glucose level using a simple reagent test strip method, code 82947 specifically excludes that type of test. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians often order this test as an initial step in the diagnosis of carbohydrate metabolism disorders, such as diabetes mellitus, idiopathic hypoglycemia, which is unexplained low blood sugar, or pancreatic islet cell cancer. Terminology Assay: A laboratory test to find or measure the quantity of some entity, called the analyte, or to find or measure some property of the analyte, such as functional activity. Enzymes: Biological compounds that act as selective catalysts to increase the rate and specificity of certain biochemical reactions, such as breaking down a specific compound. Glucose: The main type of sugar in the blood; the major source of energy for the body’s cells. Reagent: A substance used in a lab test to bring about a desired change or reaction, often to reveal the presence or quantity of another substance that is the focus of the test. Spectrophotometry: A quantitative analysis procedure that uses a spectrophotometer, a type of colorimeter, to measure the light intensity of a specific wavelength that a sample transmits; light absorption is the basis of the measure of quantity. Tips Some payers may pay separately for collecting the specimen using a code such as 36415, Collection of venous blood by venipuncture. Distinguish 82947 for fasting blood glucose using a method such as a chemistry analyzer from other glucose test codes in the range 82948 to 82952. Clinicians may order this test more than once in the same day, and some payers will cover multiple units of 82947only if you bill the subsequent test with a modifier such as 91, Repeat clinical diagnostic test. short_description: Helicobacter pylori, blood test analysis for urease activity, non-radioactive isotope (eg, C-13) Notes: (For H. pylori, breath test analysis for urease activity, see 83013, 83014)
lay_term: The lab analyst measures the Helicobacter pylori urease activity, typically in a blood sample. Analysts use this test to determine the presence of Helicobacter pylori in the stomach. The organism is a cause of stomach and duodenal ulcers. Explanation The lab analyst performs the technical steps to determine the presence of the bacteria, Helicobacter pylori, typically from a blood sample drawn 30 minutes after staff administers a non–radioactive isotope, for instance containing C–13, to the patient. Methodology is typically by gas isotope ratio mass spectroscopy, which bombards the sample with electrons. Then, these ionized particles separate according to their charge ratio and accelerate. The instrument then subjects the particles to an electric or magnetic field, where the instrument identifies the tagged molecules, by their masses, using their characteristic fragmentation pattern. The presence of the tagged molecules reveals urease activity. Clinicians order the Helicobacter pylori urease test primarily on patients with symptoms of a stomach ulcer or duodenal ulcer to determine the presence of the usual causative agent, Helicobacter pylori. This non–invasive technique does not require a costly surgical procedure, and the test is usually sufficient for the clinician to make a diagnosis. Terminology C–13: An abbreviation for the non–radioactive isotope carbon–13, one of the 15 known isotopes of carbon, frequently used for clinical laboratory testing purposes. Duodenum: The first part of the small intestine, just beyond the stomach. Helicobacter pylori: This Gram negative, comma or spiral shaped organism is implicated as the causative agent of most stomach and duodenal ulcers. Urease activity: Helicobacter pylori is a bacteria that produces urease, an enzyme that breaks down urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide. Tips For Helicobacter pylori breath test analysis for urease activity, see 83013 and 83014. For Helicobacter pylori antigen test on a stool specimen, see 87338. For Helicobacter pylori antigen test on a serum sample, see 87339. For Helicobacter pylori nuclear medicine liquid scintillation counter C–14 urea breath test, see 78267 and 78268. For Helicobacter pylori CLO test, previously known as Campylobacter–Like Organism test, see 87077 or 87081. Helicobacter pylori was previously known as Campylobacter pylori. lay_term: The lab analyst administers drugs for helicobacter pylori bacteria testing. H. pylori is most commonly present in the stomach and mainly affects the mucosal lining of the stomach. Explanation After the patient is prepped, the lab analyst begins the drug administration phase of the test for urease activity. He initiates the procedure with collection of a breath sample for measuring the baseline. The lab analyst administers a drug to the patient that consists of urea chemically attached to an isotope, typically carbon 13, or C13. H. pylori break this urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide. Blood absorbs the carbon dioxide gas along with radiolabeled C13. The analyst collects this breath air in an airbag to test the presence of C13. The analyst takes several breath samples at regular intervals for further analysis during the separately reportable breath test analysis. Terminology Helicobacter pylori: Gram negative bacteria present in the stomach and duodenum, which is the first part of the small intestine; H. pylori can cause ulcers; its presence mainly occurs due to poor sanitation. Isotopes: Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons in their nuclei; they are chemically the same. Urea: A waste product made in the liver that contains ammonia and nitrogen and is eliminated in urine. Urease: Enzyme that breaks down urea to carbon dioxide and ammonia. Tips For the breath test analysis, use 83013, Helicobacter pylori; breath test analysis for urease activity, nonradioactive isotope. Read Less

short_description: Hemoglobin; by copper sulfate method, non-automated
lay_term: The lab analyst performs a non–automated determination of the hemoglobin content, typically in the blood, using a copper sulfate solution. Up until recently, lab analysts used this technique primarily to screen blood donors. Now, lab analysts use more precise, automated methods for determining hemoglobin. Explanation The lab analyst performs the technical steps to estimate or quantitate the hemoglobin, typically in a blood sample from a finger, ear lobe, or venous sample. This non–automated, or manual, technique utilizes a copper sulfate solution of a specific gravity. The analyst drops a drop of the sample into the solution. If it slowly sinks to the bottom, the hemoglobin level is greater than the specific gravity of the solution. Analysts have used this old, crude, yet reasonably reliable technique for many years to screen donors before a blood donation. Analysts also used this method to measure the hemoglobin level, using copper sulfate solutions in a range of different specific gravity concentrations, in different containers. The analyst places a sample drop into each and then records in which container the sample drop first sank to the bottom. This test is not currently in general use. Clinicians now have available more precise and reliable techniques for measuring the hemoglobin in a blood sample. Terminology Copper sulfate: A bluish solution composed of copper and sulfur, of a precise specific gravity, used in a manual technique to determine hemoglobin in blood. Hemoglobin: The red colored protein in the red blood cell that carries oxygen to the tissue and returns carbon dioxide to the lungs. Specific gravity: The ratio of the density of a substance compared to the density of a standard, such as water. Tips This test provides quick analysis. For instance, the copper sulfate hemoglobin technique was developed during World War II, and was a lifesaving test used on soldiers in the battlefield, as the blood could be analyzed quickly. Some payers may pay separately for collecting the specimen using a code such as 36415, if staff collects the specimen by venipuncture. Read Less

short_description: Hemoglobin; methemoglobin, qualitative
lay_term: The lab analyst determines the presence of methemoglobin, typically in a whole blood sample. This different form of hemoglobin, which gives the blood a brownish color, can be due to a genetic defect or can also be caused by certain drugs or chemicals. Explanation The lab analyst performs the technical steps to determine the presence of methemoglobin in a blood sample. The lab analyst commonly measures methemoglobin by using a co–oximeter. This instrument uses a spectrophotometer to measure different wavelengths of light to differentiate methemoglobin from other hemoglobins. This form of hemoglobin, methemoglobin, is actually a brownish color instead of being a red, normal color when in the blood. Normal blood does not include methemoglobin, and possible reasons for its presence include a genetic defect; medications such as sulfonamides, anesthetic agents, or pain relievers such as phenazopyridine; or ingestion of nitrites found in many processed meats. Clinicians order testing to screen for the genetic defect, changes due to certain medications, or foods that can cause a methemoglobin increase in the blood. Patients may present with a bluish skin color when methemoglobin is present. Terminology Co–oximeter: An instrument, usually located in the respiratory therapy department or blood gas lab, which measures the different blood gas levels and hemoglobin types. Hemoglobin: The oxygen–carrying red pigment in red blood cells; function is to carry oxygen to the cells and return carbon dioxide to the lungs. Sulfonamides: A large class of antibiotics. Tips Clinicians usually order the quantitative methemoglobin test 83050, as most labs do not offer the qualitative test. short_description: b-Hexosaminidase, each assay
lay_term: The lab analyst measures the amount of the beta–hexosaminidase A or B that is present, typically in a serum specimen. These two enzymes are deficient in conditions such as Tay–Sachs disease or Sandhoff disease. When this enzyme is deficient, waste products accumulate and cause severe central nervous system degeneration and eventual death. (The b in b–hexosaminidase stands for the Greek character for beta.) Explanation The lab analyst determines the quantitative amount of the enzyme beta–hexosaminidase, typically in a serum sample. The methodology is frequently by use of a chemistry analyzer having two fluorometers capable of accurately measuring the two fractions of beta–hexosaminidase, a necessary enzyme in the body, deficiency of which causes a malfunction with serious central nervous system degeneration. Individuals with an enzyme activity that is moderately low will have less severe clinical symptoms and may not show this disease until later in life. This testing is primarily limited to two genetic diseases Tay–Sachs or Sandhoff disease, which are disorders of lysosomal storage. Another name for these disorders is GM2 gangliosidoses. Deficiency of the enzymes beta–hexosaminidase A or B causes the disorders. Clinicians may order this test for either or both the A and B beta–hexosaminidases. For the performance of both, report a separate unit for each. Terminology Assay: The analysis or performance of a clinical laboratory procedure or test that results in a specific report, usually stated in terms of milligrams per deciliter or an exact number, for a particular analyte. Enzyme: A protein molecule that activates or increases the rate of a chemical reaction yet is not destroyed in the process. Fluorometer: An instrument used in biochemical analysis to measure the intensity of fluorescence, or the glowing of a chemical reaction, as in the example of fireflies, whose light is produced by a chemical fluorescence. Lysosome: A membrane–bound unit within the cell containing an enzyme that breaks down food molecules. Lysosomal storage disease: An inherited disease where the lysosomes are overloaded due to a specific enzyme deficiency. Sandhoff disease: A genetic disease caused by a deficiency of both beta–hexosaminidase A and B enzymes, which causes central nervous system degeneration. Serum: The liquid portion of blood, which is separated from the cellular portion after the blood has been allowed to form a clot. Tay–Sachs disease: A genetic disease caused by a deficiency of the beta–hexosaminidase A enzyme resulting in central nervous system degeneration. Tips GM2 gangliosidoses is another name for genetic disorders caused by beta–hexosaminidase deficiency. Both beta–hexosaminidase A and beta–hexosaminidase B are listed as beta–hexosaminidase. Although there is an A subunit and a B subunit, each subunit is still a beta–amyloid–hexosaminidase. Clinicians may order this test as beta–hexosaminidase, as the b stands for beta. As noted, when the clinician orders both the b–hexosaminidase A and b–hexosaminidase B, the lab performing the test should report two units. The reason is that the description of this procedure indicates it represents each assay. Some payers may pay separately for collecting the specimen using a code such as 36415 for venipuncture. short_description: Immunoassay for analyte other than infectious agent antibody or infectious agent antigen; qualitative or semiquantitative, multiple step method
lay_term: The lab analyst performs the technical immunoassay test involving several steps to detect and measure an analyte of a noninfectious nature. The results show as positive or negative, or in semiquantitative numerical format to indicate normal and abnormal results. Explanation The lab analyst performs multiple technical steps in processing and testing the appropriate specimen, commonly blood or urine, for the specified noninfectious analyte using immunoassay methods. These assays typically involve specimen pretreatment, incubation, centrifugation, automated instrumentation, and result interpretation. Immunoassay is a test methodology that involves an antigen antibody response to detect the particular target. Results appear in qualitative form, indicating the presence or absence of the analyte, or semiquantitative form, using a numeric value to indicate positive and negative results with less specificity than a quantitative result. Terminology Antibody: Also called immunoglobulins, these are proteins produced in blood that are activated as part of the immune response to neutralize specific invaders such as bacteria or viruses. Antigen: Foreign bodies, such as bacteria, that enter the human body or substances that form within the body that cause an immune response and possibly infection. Assay: A laboratory test to find or measure the quantity of some entity, called the analyte, or to find or measure some property of the analyte, such as functional activity. Read Less

short_description: Immunoglobulin light chains (ie, kappa, lambda), free, each
lay_term: The lab analyst performs a chemistry test to measure the level of each immunoglobulin light chain, kappa or lambda, in a serum specimen. A common lab method for this test is turbidimetry, which uses light absorption to measure the level of a targeted solid suspended in a liquid. Levels of free (unbound) kappa and lambda in a serum specimen can help clinicians diagnose and monitor certain plasma–cell disorders such as multiple myeloma (MM) and primary amyloidosis (AL). Explanation The lab analyst performs a lab test such as turbidimetry to measure the level of free kappa or lambda in a serum specimen and allow determination of the ratio of the two light chains. The lab test involves reacting the liquid serum specimen with an antiserum specific to the light chain of interest, such as kappa, so that it forms a solid. With the solid suspended in the liquid specimen, a spectrophotometer measures the light that passes through the specimen and determines the concentration of the target light chain in the serum specimen. Clinicians may order two units of this test, for kappa and lambda, to aid in the diagnosis of and to monitor treatment of plasma–cell disorders such as the blood cancer multiple myeloma (MM) or monoclonal light chain (primary) amyloidosis (AL). The results may also aid in diagnosis of other conditions such as monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS). The body produces antibodies by combining a pair of light chain and a pair of heavy chain proteins to form an immunoglobulin (antibody), which means that the light chain is bound, not free in the serum. An abnormal level of free light chains in the serum may indicate an overabundance or deficit of the type of plasma cell(s) that produce that light chain, leading to plasma–cell disorders. Terminology Amyloidosis: Buildup of amyloid, an abnormal protein produced in the bone marrow, that can be deposited in any organ in the body; amyloidosis can affect the nervous system (brain and spinal cord), heart, kidneys, liver, spleen, and gastrointestinal tract. Immunoglobulins: Proteins (IgA, IgD, IgE, IgG, and IgM) produced in the body to react against a specific disease–causing substance; a protein formed by certain white blood cells (B cells lymphocytes) and plasma cells in response to foreign substances in the body; clinicians may identify different immunoglobulin classes to provide different diagnostic information; also known as antibodies. Light chain: One small protein subunit that is part of a pair that joins with a pair of larger subunits (heavy chains) to form an immunoglobulin molecule (antibody). Serum: The clear liquid portion of blood that is not cellular and contains important components such as antibodies, proteins produced in blood that are activated as part of the immune response to neutralize specific invaders such as bacteria or viruses. Turbidimetry: A lab procedure to measure the turbidity (level of cloudiness) of a liquid that contains suspended solid particles. Tips One unit of 83521 describes testing for a single free light chain, such as kappa or lambda. Some payers may pay separately for collecting the specimen. Read Less

short_description: Interleukin-6 (IL-6)
lay_term: Code 83529 describes a chemistry test to measure the level of interleukin–6 (IL–6) in a specimen such as serum or plasma. A common lab method for this test is immunoassay, which uses an antibody/antigen reaction to measure the IL–6 level in the specimen. IL–6 is a cytokine involved in the body’s immune response and may be elevated in patients with inflammation related to infection, cardiovascular disease, autoimmune disorders, or some cancers. Explanation The lab analyst performs an immunoassay lab test such as electrochemiluminescence (ECL) using a specimen such as serum or plasma. A common procedure involves mixing dilutions of the specimen with an antibody specific to interleukin–6 (IL–6), then conjugating (joining) an electrochemiluminescent label to any bound antibody/IL–6 complex and measuring the intensity of emitted light to correlate with IL–6 level in the specimen. IL–6 is a cytokine involved in the body’s immune response and may be elevated in patients with inflammation. Clinicians may order this test to evaluate the level of inflammation in a number of clinical situations. For instance, IL–6 may be elevated in cardiovascular disease, some cancers, or autoimmune disorders such as rheumatoid arthritis (RA). For RA patients, this test may indicate the value of the drug tocilizumab, which blocks IL–6 action and reduces inflammation. Clinicians also may look for elevated IL–6 in patients with infections, using the test to identify severe inflammation in COVID–19 patients to help evaluate risks associated with ventilator use. Terminology Antibody: A protein produced by the body as an immune–system response to a specific antigen, such as a bacteria or foreign substance; lab tests may utilize reactions between antibodies and antigens to identify a substance in a patient specimen; may also be referred to as immunoglobulin. Antigen: A substance that the body reacts to with an immune response, such as by producing a specific antibody; lab tests may utilize reactions between antibodies and antigens to identify a substance in a patient specimen. Cytokines: Small proteins, such as interferons and interleukins, involved in controlling the activity of the immune system. Immunoassay: A biochemical test that uses an antibody/antigen reaction to detect and possibly quantify a specific substance present in the specimen, such as blood. Inflammation: The physiologic response of body tissues to protect itself from injury or infection, including pain, heat, redness, and swelling. Plasma: The liquid portion of blood that typically suspends blood cells; plasma accounts for about 55 percent of blood volume and contains important components such as proteins, electrolytes, hormones, and coagulation factors. Serum: The clear liquid portion of blood that is not cellular and contains important components such as antibodies, proteins produced in blood that are activated as part of the immune response to neutralize specific invaders such as bacteria or viruses. Tips Some payers may pay separately for collecting the specimen. Read Less

short_description: Lactoferrin, fecal; quantitative
lay_term: The lab analyst performs the technical lab test to analyze a stool specimen for the quantity of lactoferrin, an indicator of inflammation of the intestinal tract. Explanation The lab analyst performs all technical steps, typically using an enzyme linked immunosorbent assay method, called ELISA, to measure the amount of lactoferrin in a stool specimen. ELISA uses an enzyme linked to a specific protein, such as an antigen or antibody, as a marker to identify and quantitate the analyte. Lactoferrin is a protein produced and released by certain types of white blood cells, called neutrophils, in response to bacterial infection and inflammation. Lactoferrin is a marker for inflammatory bowel disease, known as IBD, as well as intestinal infection and colon cancer. Low levels of lactoferrin indicate noninflammatory conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome, called IBS, or viral infection. Patients in the early stages of IBD may have highly elevated levels. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, the provider may order a quantitative lactoferrin test when a patient has bloody or watery diarrhea that persists for several days. The quantitative test is useful to monitor the severity and treatment response of IBD. Terminology Antibody: Also called immunoglobulins, these are proteins produced in blood that are activated as part of the immune response to neutralize specific invaders such as bacteria or viruses. Antigen: Foreign bodies, such as bacteria, that enter the human body or substances that form within the body that cause an immune response and possibly infection. Irritable bowel disease: Inflammatory disorders of the intestine including Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis. Neutrophils: The most abundant form of white blood cells, neutrophils originate from stem cells in the bone marrow, are short lived, and are essential to functioning of the immune system. Qualitative test: A test used to determine the presence or absence of an analyte. Quantitative test: A test used to determine the amount of an analyte present. Tips Use 83630 for Lactoferrin, fecal; qualitative. Read Less

short_description: Fetal lung maturity assessment; lecithin sphingomyelin (L/S) ratio
lay_term: The lab analyst performs a test to assess the maturity of fetal lungs using the lecithin sphingomyelin ratio for an indication of whether the organ system will be able to support life outside the uterus. Explanation The lab analyst assesses the lecithin sphingomyelin ratio to evaluate the relative amount of lecithin and sphingomyelin in amniotic fluid. The levels of the two are similar at 32 to 33 weeks of pregnancy. After that, the lecithin typically increases. A ratio of roughly two to one may indicate lung maturity. A typical specimen may be amniotic fluid that the provider collects via amniocentesis. The lab analyst may use a methodology such as thin layer chromatography, which involves placing the specimen on a special flat plate and adding a liquid that moves the specimen up the plate, dividing the constituents of the specimen because they travel at different rates. The lab analyst evaluates the plate for the presence of the analyte that separates out from the specimen. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians may order this test to evaluate the maturity of fetal lungs in a patient expected to deliver early. The immaturity of lungs may cause respiratory distress syndrome, RDS, which occurs due to insufficient pulmonary surfactant, lipoproteins that help prevent the lung’s air sacs from collapsing. Terminology Amniocentesis: Obtaining a sample of amniotic fluid by inserting a needle in the uterus to examine any abnormality in the fetus. Amniotic fluid: Clear yellow fluid that is present in the amniotic sac and covers the fetus during pregnancy. Lipoproteins: Group of soluble proteins that combine with lipid, or fat, and carry it to its correct destination. Respiratory distress syndrome or RDS: Disease of newborn premature infants in which there is a defect in the surfactant layer over the inner surface of lungs that can cause difficulty in breathing. Surfactant: A substance that decreases the surface tension of the liquid after dissolving in to it. Uterus: A hollow, muscular, pear shaped organ located between the base of the bladder and the rectum; it bends forward at its narrowest part, called the isthmus, and rests on the bladder; the body of the uterus is the widest part, and it lies above the isthmus; the cervix forms the lower part of the uterus and is below the isthmus and juts into the vaginal canal. Tips If the provider performs a foam stability test to test the maturity of lungs, use 83662, Fetal lung assessment; foam stability test. If the provider performs fluorescence polarization to test the maturity of lungs, use 83663, Fetal lung maturity; fluorescence polarization. If the provider assesses the lamellar body density to determine the maturity of lungs, use 83664, Fetal lung maturity; lamellar body density. Read Less

short_description: Lipoprotein, blood; high resolution fractionation and quantitation of lipoproteins including lipoprotein subclasses when performed (eg, electrophoresis, ultracentrifugation)
lay_term: The lab analyst performs high resolution fractionation and measures the amount of blood lipoprotein in a patient specimen. The test may include lipoprotein subclasses, as well. Explanation The lab analyst performs a test that involves high resolution fractionation and measures the amount of blood lipoprotein, and possibly lipoprotein subclasses, in a patient blood specimen. The lab analyst may use a methodology such as ultracentrifugation for fractionation and measurement of the lipoproteins. The basic principle of the test is separation of lipoproteins based on their densities and floating rates. The lipoproteins form a rigid uniform layer at the top of the centrifuge tube after 20 to 24 hours of centrifugation, which involves spinning. The analyst adds soluble materials to raise the density of the solution containing the sample, and then spins this mixture, subjecting it to high centrifugal force, called ultracentrifugation. The various lipoproteins gather on the top of the centrifuge tube according to their densities. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians may order this test to evaluate patients with atherosclerosis for an increase in the level of lipoprotein associated phospholipase enzyme, which may further increase the risk of stroke or heart attack. This test may follow other lipoprotein tests as it provides greater specificity. Terminology Atherosclerosis: Deposition of a thick layer of fat on the inner walls of the arteries that may lead to blockage of the arteries. Enzymes: Biological compounds that act as selective catalysts to increase the rate and specificity of certain biochemical reactions, such as breaking down a specific compound. Lipoprotein: Complex of fat and protein molecules that move cholesterol in blood. Myocardial infarction: A loss of circulation to a part of the heart muscle due to a blood clot or other mass lodging in a coronary artery; a heart attack. Stroke: Deprivation of blood supply in the brain that may cause death of the brain cells. short_description: Lipoprotein, blood; quantitation of lipoprotein particle number(s) (eg, by nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy), includes lipoprotein particle subclass(es), when performed
lay_term: The lab analyst performs a test to measure the lipoprotein particle numbers and possibly lipoprotein particle subclasses in blood. Explanation The lab analyst performs a test to measure the number of one or more types of lipoprotein particles in blood, such as low density lipoproteins (LDL) and high density lipoproteins (HDL). If the lab analyst also measures the particle number for lipoprotein subclasses, such as HDL subclasses HDL2 and HDL3 or LDL subclasses, that work is also included in the code. The lab analyst may use a methodology such as nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy. The analyst adds the purified sample and buffer solution to a thin walled glass tube. Pulses of electromagnetic energy result in magnetization of the sample and create a chemical shift in the sample. The analyst uses the help of a spectrometer to detect the chemical shift. This radiation varies according to the structure and amount of specific components present in the sample. Spectroscopic differences naturally exist among lipoprotein particles of different sizes. The analyst uses specialized software to complete the quantitation. Although not limited to testing specific condition, clinicians may order this test to evaluate patients with atherosclerosis or other risk factors for cardiovascular disease or stroke to determine the level of specific classes or subclasses of lipoprotein in blood that may indicate a further risk factor for stroke or heart attack. Terminology Atherosclerosis: Buildup of plaque, or fatty deposits, on the walls of an artery; hardening and thickening the artery walls, which can lead to coronary artery disease; sometimes used interchangeably with arteriosclerosis, thickening and hardening of the walls of the arteries. Lipoprotein: A biochemical assemblage of lipids, or fats, such as cholesterol, that are bound to proteins, which allows fats to move inside and outside of cells through water–based substrates such as blood. Stroke: A neurological condition that occurs when the blood supply is interrupted or reduced to the brain causing a lack of oxygen and blood; also known as a brain stroke or brain attack. short_description: Organic acids; total, quantitative, each specimen
lay_term: The lab analyst measures the total organic acids, with a 24 hour urine being the preferred specimen. Organic acids are a byproduct of metabolism and derive from many sources, such as, fatty acids, amino acids, carbohydrates, steroids, and hormones. Explanation The lab analyst performs the technical steps to quantitate the total organic acids in whichever specimen type he tests, with a 24 hour urine being the preferred specimen. This specimen type involves the patient collecting all urine over a 24 hour period. The methodology analysts commonly use is liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry, which bombards the sample with electrons before a second mass spectrometer sorts, weighs, and identifies the particles by their specific fragmentation pattern. This testing is not for any particular analyte, but for the total organic acids the patient excretes as a byproduct of metabolism. The specimen type is typically urine, as the kidneys are the primary organ of metabolic excretion of measurable organic acids. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians may use total organic acids testing to determine abnormal genetic, organic, or metabolic disorders, based on the results of the metabolic byproducts revealed. Terminology Metabolism: The sum of all the physical and chemical processes going on within our bodies. Tips Clinicians rarely order total organic acids, as testing for a specific single organic acid is of more clinical importance. For qualitative organic acids, see 83919, Organic acids; qualitative, each specimen. For a single quantitative organic acid, see 83921, Organic acid, single, quantitative. Some payers may pay separately for the volume measurement for timed urine collection, when performed. For that service see 81050, Volume measurement for timed collection, each. The term each specimen listed in the code descriptor for total quantitative organic acids clarifies that you may report only one unit of service for all analytes the analyst identifies from one specimen tested. You should not report one unit of service for each reported analyte. Read Less

short_description: Infectious disease, bacterial vaginosis and vaginitis, real-time PCR amplification of DNA markers for Atopobium vaginae, Atopobium species, Megasphaera type 1, and Bacterial Vaginosis Associated Bacteria-2 (BVAB-2), utilizing vaginal-fluid specimens, algorithm reported as positive or negative for high likelihood of bacterial vaginosis, includes separate detection of Trichomonas vaginalis and Candida species (C. albicans, C. tropicalis, C. parapsilosis, C. dubliniensis), Candida glabrata/Candida krusei, when reported
lay_term: The lab analyst performs the technical lab tests on a vaginal fluid specimen for real–time polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplification of DNA markers for bacterial species listed in the code descriptor and carries out an algorithmic analysis using patient data and the lab test results to report positive or negative for a high likelihood of bacterial vaginosis (BV). The test may additionally report detection of other organisms such as Trichomonas vaginalis and Candida species. Explanation The lab analyst performs a technical lab test on a vaginal fluid specimen by extracting nucleic acids by methods such as cell lysis and digestion and stabilizing and increasing the quantity of target DNA markers for bacterial species: Atopobium vaginae, Atopobium species, Megasphaera type 1, and Bacterial Vaginosis Associated Bacteria–2 (BVAB–2). The test uses real–time (quantitative) PCR (qPCR) for amplification and quantification of DNA targets. Processing the lab test result and patient data with a computer algorithm, the lab provides the findings as positive or negative for a high likelihood of bacterial vaginosis (BV) and may additionally report detection of other organisms such as Trichomonas vaginalis and Candida species. Code 81515 is a multianalyte assay with algorithmic analysis (MAAA) test, meaning that the code includes performing all technical lab test(s), gathering relevant patient data, carrying out the algorithmic analysis, and reporting the results. Clinicians may order this test for patients with symptoms of vaginitis and BV, such as abnormal vaginal discharge. BV is a common cause of vaginal discharge, sexually transmitted infections, and pelvic inflammatory disease. Terminology Algorithm: A specific set of step–by–step calculations using defined inputs at each step to produce a useful output; for multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAA), the output involves some sort of diagnostic or prognostic information about treatment options or disease outcomes. Amplification: Making more copies of a desired gene for study by processes such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR) or transcription of DNA to RNA and reverse transcription from RNA to make an additional copy of the DNA. Multianalyte assays with algorithmic analyses (MAAA): A set of codes generally unique to a single clinical laboratory or manufacture; they typically list all the analytic and algorithmic analysis for a type of disease, such cancer; the type and number of analytes, such as proteins; the lab methods, such as immunoassay; the specimen type, such as blood; and the result type, such as prognostic risk score. Nucleic acid: A sequence of specific biological chemicals (nucleotides) that carry genetic information; known as deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) or ribonucleic acid (RNA). Real–time polymerase chain reaction (real–time PCR): A laboratory technique that monitors the progress of a PCR reaction in real time and allows quantification (counting) of PCR product (DNA, cDNA, or RNA) from a relatively small amount; sometimes called quantitative PCR (qPCR). Vaginitis: Inflammation of the vagina. Tips Don’t separately report technical lab tests, because MAAA codes always include the underlying lab tests. Some payers may pay separately for collecting the specimen. In addition to Category I codes for MAAA tests, CPT® lists additional MAAA “administrative codes” in an appendix for tests that have not been assigned a Category I code. Use the unlisted MAAA code, 81599, only when the there is no Category I or administrative code for a given MAAA test. Read Less
guidelines: Lab & Path Guidelines Range Specific Guideline Multianalyte Assays with Algorithmic Analyses (MAAAs) are procedures that utilize multiple results derived from panels of analyses of various types, including molecular pathology assays, fluorescent in situ hybridization assays, and non-nucleic acid based assays (eg, proteins, polypeptides, lipids, carbohydrates). Algorithmic analysis using the results of these assays as well as other patient information (if used) is then performed and typically reported as a numeric score(s) or as a probability. MAAAs are typically unique to a single clinical laboratory or manufacturer. The results of individual component procedure(s) that are inputs to the MAAAs may be provided on the associated laboratory report; however, these assays are not separately reported using additional codes. The format for the code descriptors of MAAAs usually include (in order): Disease type (eg, oncology, autoimmune, tissue rejection), Material(s) analyzed (eg, DNA, RNA, protein, antibody), Number of markers (eg, number of genes, number of proteins), Methodology(ies) (eg, microarray, real-time [RT]-PCR, in situ hybridization [ISH], enzyme linked immunosorbent assays [ELISA]), Number of functional domains (if indicated), Specimen type (eg, blood, fresh tissue, formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded), Algorithm result type (eg, prognostic, diagnostic), Report (eg, probability index, risk score) In contrast to GSPs and other molecular multianalyte assays, the assays in this section represent algorithmically combined results of analyses of multiple analytes to obtain a risk score or other value which in itself represents a new and distinct medical property that is of independent medical significance relative to the individual component test results in clinical context in which the assay is performed. MAAAs, including those that do not have a Category I code, may be found in Appendix O. MAAAs that do not have a Category I code are identified in Appendix O by a four-digit number followed by the letter "M." The Category I MAAA codes that are included in this subsection are also included in Appendix O. All MAAA codes are listed in Appendix O along with the procedure's proprietary name. In order to report an MAAA code, the analysis performed must fulfill the code descriptor and, if proprietary, must be the test represented by the proprietary name listed in Appendix O. When a specific MAAA procedure is not listed below or in Appendix O, the procedure must be reported using the Category I MAAA unlisted code (81599). These codes encompass all analytical services required (eg, cell lysis, nucleic acid stabilization, extraction, digestion, amplification, hybridization, and detection) in addition to the algorithmic analysis itself. Procedures that are required prior to cell lysis (eg, microdissection, codes 88380 and 88381) should be reported separately.

short_description: Osteocalcin (bone g1a protein)
lay_term: The lab analyst performs technical steps, typically on serum or plasma, using laboratory methods to detect the amount of osteocalcin. Osteocalcin is a protein that is essential for bone formation and analysis may indicate bone density and response to bone building drug therapy. short_description: pH; body fluid, not otherwise specified
lay_term: The analyst performs the technical lab test to measure the pH, meaning the acidity or alkalinity, of a body fluid not represented by another code. The analyst may use methods such as a pH meter, blood gas analyzer, or litmus paper. Explanation The analyst performs all testing on one of a wide variety of fluids to evaluate acidity or alkalinity using various methods, depending upon the specific laboratory protocol and type of fluid the analyst will test. Types of body fluids analyzed include peritoneal, which is fluid in the abdominal cavity; pericardial, which is fluid surrounding the heart; pleural, which is fluid around the lungs; cerebral spinal fluid, which is fluid in the spinal column; synovial, which is joint fluid; and amniotic, which is fluid from the sac surrounding a developing fetus. Many laboratories use blood gas machines to test the pH of these fluids with a dedicated electrode for measuring pH. Other labs use pH specific meters with electrodes or chemically reactive reagent strips that measure pH when immersed in fluid. Fluid pH can assist the provider in determining if the fluid is an exudate, originating from inflammation, or a transudate, often found in congestive heart failure and cirrhosis. In certain cases, nitrazine paper, a type of litmus paper containing blue dye, helps the clinician determine if the amniotic sac has ruptured because amniotic fluid has higher pH than vaginal fluid. Explanation Following a separate lab test such as 84075, Phosphatase, alkaline, that demonstrates an elevated alkaline phosphatase level in the patient specimen, the clinician may order this test for heat stable alkaline phosphatase. Alkaline phosphatase occurs in many body tissues, especially in the liver, bile duct, bone, and placenta. It is an enzyme that removes phosphate groups from many molecules. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians may order this test following an elevated alkaline phosphatase test to help distinguish between liver or bone disease as the cause of elevated patient ALP. guidelines: Lab & Path Guidelines Range Specific Guideline Multianalyte Assays with Algorithmic Analyses (MAAAs) are procedures that utilize multiple results derived from panels of analyses of various types, including molecular pathology assays, fluorescent in situ hybridization assays, and non-nucleic acid based assays (eg, proteins, polypeptides, lipids, carbohydrates). Algorithmic analysis using the results of these assays as well as other patient information (if used) is then performed and typically reported as a numeric score(s) or as a probability. MAAAs are typically unique to a single clinical laboratory or manufacturer. The results of individual component procedure(s) that are inputs to the MAAAs may be provided on the associated laboratory report; however, these assays are not separately reported using additional codes. The format for the code descriptors of MAAAs usually include (in order): Disease type (eg, oncology, autoimmune, tissue rejection), Material(s) analyzed (eg, DNA, RNA, protein, antibody), Number of markers (eg, number of genes, number of proteins), Methodology(ies) (eg, microarray, real-time [RT]-PCR, in situ hybridization [ISH], enzyme linked immunosorbent assays [ELISA]), Number of functional domains (if indicated), Specimen type (eg, blood, fresh tissue, formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded), Algorithm result type (eg, prognostic, diagnostic), Report (eg, probability index, risk score) In contrast to GSPs and other molecular multianalyte assays, the assays in this section represent algorithmically combined results of analyses of multiple analytes to obtain a risk score or other value which in itself represents a new and distinct medical property that is of independent medical significance relative to the individual component test results in clinical context in which the assay is performed. MAAAs, including those that do not have a Category I code, may be found in Appendix O. MAAAs that do not have a Category I code are identified in Appendix O by a four-digit number followed by the letter "M." The Category I MAAA codes that are included in this subsection are also included in Appendix O. All MAAA codes are listed in Appendix O along with the procedure's proprietary name. In order to report an MAAA code, the analysis performed must fulfill the code descriptor and, if proprietary, must be the test represented by the proprietary name listed in Appendix O. When a specific MAAA procedure is not listed below or in Appendix O, the procedure must be reported using the Category I MAAA unlisted code (81599). These codes encompass all analytical services required (eg, cell lysis, nucleic acid stabilization, extraction, digestion, amplification, hybridization, and detection) in addition to the algorithmic analysis itself. Procedures that are required prior to cell lysis (eg, microdissection, codes 88380 and 88381) should be reported separately.

short_description: Prostaglandin, each
lay_term: The lab analyst performs a test to evaluate the level of a prostaglandin in a patient specimen such as a random or 24 hour urine specimen. Explanation The lab analyst performs a test on a patient specimen such as a random or 24 hour urine collection to measure levels of one of a family of compounds called prostaglandins. Prostaglandins are fatty compounds that function much like a hormone, but with local action, to regulate body functions such as muscle contraction. The lab analyst may use procedures such as an immunoassay that uses antibodies specific to the prostaglandin of interest to form an antigen and antibody complex that produces a colorimetric change. The lab analyst can use a colorimeter to determine levels of the prostaglandin of interest in the specimen by measuring the amount of light of a specific wavelength the sample absorbs. If the lab analyst evaluates the level of more than one prostaglandin in the specimen, report multiple units of this code. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians may order this test as an early, noninvasive indicator of systemic mast cell disease. Specifically, clinicians may use this test to evaluate 11 Beta prostaglandin F2 alpha, which is a prostaglandin that is a common breakdown product of prostaglandin D2, called PGD2. Elevated levels of PGD2 occur in systemic mast cell disease, so elevated levels of 11 Beta prostaglandin F2 alpha in urine may indicate that the patient has the condition. Systemic mast cell disease, also called systemic mastocytosis, results in a build–up of mast cells within the body, resulting in symptoms such as itching, flushing, rapid heartbeat, and lightheadedness. Terminology Antibody: Also called immunoglobulin; a protein that the body produces in the blood as part of the immune response to neutralize specific invaders such as bacteria or viruses, but occasionally reacts to the patient’s own body; lab tests may utilize reactions between antibodies and antigens to identify a substance in a patient specimen. Antigen: Foreign bodies, such as bacteria, that enter the human body, or substances that form within the body, that cause an immune response, such as antibody production, and possibly infection; lab tests may utilize reactions between antibodies and antigens to identify a substance in a patient specimen. Immunoassay: A biochemical test that detects an antigen antibody reaction. Tips Report one unit of this code for evaluating a single prostaglandin level in the specimen. Read Less

short_description: Prostate specific antigen (PSA); total
lay_term: The lab analyst performs testing for total prostate specific antigen, PSA, typically on serum or plasma samples using laboratory analyzers. PSA is a protein the prostate gland produces, and clinicians may use PSA levels to screen for prostate cancer and follow disease progression. Explanation The lab analyst performs all technical steps of the testing process, choosing from various methods to quantitate total PSA. Possible methods include immunoenzymatic assay, which uses antigen antibody reactions, and electrochemiluminescence immunoassay, or ECLIA, a method using antibody antigen particles reacting by electric charge and chemical properties to produce a color change, with automated laboratory equipment. The typical specimen is serum or plasma. No special preparation is required of the patient for sample collection, however, blood collection usually takes place before a digital rectal exam as prostate manipulation may elevate PSA levels in the blood. Providers typically order a total PSA test on patients experiencing difficult, painful, or frequent urination, back pain or, depending on the provider, as a routine health screening test. Elevated results are common in prostatitis, which is inflammation of the prostate, benign prostate hyperplasia, called BPH, and prostate cancer. A total PSA test may aid in monitoring patients to check disease progression when the cancer is slow growing. Terminology Antibody: Proteins produced in blood that are activated as part of the immune response to neutralize specific invaders such as bacteria or viruses, also called immunoglobulin. Antigen: Foreign bodies, such as bacteria, that enter the human body or substances that form within the body that cause an immune response and possibly infection. Prostate: A small gland, part of the reproductive system in males, that secretes prostatic fluid, a component of semen. Tips For PSA testing to screen a Medicare patient for prostate cancer, see G0103, Prostate cancer screening; prostate specific antigen test, PSA. Other payers also may require you to use G0103 for screening. Read Less
