short_description: Infectious agent genotype analysis by nucleic acid (DNA or RNA); severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) (coronavirus disease [COVID-19]), mutation identification in targeted region(s) Notes: (For infectious agent detection by nucleic acid [DNA or RNA] for severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 [SARS-CoV-2] [coronavirus disease {COVID-19}], see 87635, 87636, 87637) (For SARS-CoV-2 variant analysis, use 87913)
lay_term: Code 87913 describes genotype analysis using a specimen from a patient with confirmed severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS–CoV–2) infection. The test uses next–generation sequencing to identify virus mutations that could impact disease transmissibility or severity. Explanation The lab analyst processes a specimen such as a nasopharyngeal swab for mutation analysis of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS–CoV–2). After extracting specimen viral nucleic acids, an automated platform amplifies (increases the number of) gene sequences in targeted regions using reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT–PCR). The platform continues with next–generation sequencing (NGS) to compare the specimen to multiple reference mutations such as alterations of the viral spike (S) protein. NGS uses an automated instrument that can simultaneously determine the order of DNA or RNA nucleotides in many genes, and uses bioinformatics to interpret the results. Clinicians may order this test for patients with a positive SARS–CoV–2 PCR test to guide patient treatment in certain cases, such as to help distinguish between a persistent infection versus reinfection with a new viral strain, or to identify mutations that could reduce efficacy of certain antiviral medications or vaccine–induced antibodies. SARS–CoV–2 is the virus that causes COVID–19. Terminology Amplification: Making more copies of a desired gene for study by processes such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR) or transcription of DNA to RNA and reverse transcription from RNA to make an additional copy of the DNA. Antibody: A protein produced by the body as an immune–system response to a specific antigen, such as a bacteria or foreign substance; lab tests may utilize reactions between antibodies and antigens to identify a substance in a patient specimen; may also be referred to as immunoglobulin. Bioinformatics: Discipline used to gather, store, and evaluate biological data, such as gene sequences, using computer systems. COVID–19: Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID–19) is a disease caused by a novel coronavirus, SARS–CoV–2, that resulted in declaration of a global pandemic beginning in March 2020. Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA): A form of nucleic acid that consists of a sequence of specific biological chemicals (nucleotides) which carry genetic information. Genotype: The genetic, internally coded information of a particular organism or person, distinct from the expressed features or the phenotype. Mutation: An alteration in a nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) sequence that may lead to pathologic changes in the organism. Nasopharyngeal specimen: A specimen for laboratory testing obtained from the portion of the throat that is open to the nasal cavity, usually by means of a long swab passed through the nose; it is necessary to collect cells from the airway to be able to identify viral respiratory pathogens such as respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), influenza virus A and B, parainfluenza virus, or coronavirus. Next–generation sequencing (NGS): A general term for a number of different modern DNA and RNA sequencing technologies that are quicker and cheaper than the previous methods; also known as high–throughput sequencing. Nucleic acid: A sequence of specific biological chemicals (nucleotides) that carry genetic information; known as deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) or ribonucleic acid (RNA). Nucleotides: Biochemicals — sometimes called “bases” — that form the building blocks of nucleic acids, DNA and RNA; DNA is made up of four bases: adenine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G), and thymine (T), while RNA uses uracil (U) in place of T; each base will pair with only one specific “complementary” base when forming DNA or RNA strands. Reverse transcription–polymerase chain reaction (RT–PCR): A technique to measure specimen RNA levels by reacting RNA with the enzyme reverse transcriptase to produce complementary DNA (cDNA), which is more stable than RNA, and then create more copies of the DNA by polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Ribonucleic acid (RNA): One of the essential building blocks of life, along with deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and proteins; RNA acts as a messenger (mRNA), carrying genetic information from DNA to proteins, helps regulate cellular processes, and, like enzymes, can speed up chemical reactions; RNA, rather than DNA, carries genetic information in some important viruses. Tips Report one unit of this code for a single specimen analyzed on a single date of service. short_description: Cytopathology, in situ hybridization (eg, FISH), urinary tract specimen with morphometric analysis, 3-5 molecular probes, each specimen; manual
lay_term: The lab analyst performs a technical lab test on a urinary tract specimen using in situ hybridization and three to five molecular probes for manual morphometric analysis, looking at the number and form of the structures in the cells. Explanation The lab analyst performs all technical steps to analyze a specimen from the urinary tract, most commonly urine, using in situ hybridization, ISH, involving three to five molecular probes and manual morphometric analysis. The typical method of fluorescent in situ hybridization, FISH, allows the lab analyst to find the positions of specific DNA sequences on specific chromosomes, which are DNA containing structures in cells. The analyst fixes the urinary tract specimen to a slide. He mixes the specimen with a nucleic acid probe, which is a fabricated single strand sequence of DNA or RNA that joins with the complementary sequence in the specimen through a process called hybridization. The nucleic acid probe includes a label, such as a radioactive or chemical tag, that allows the lab analyst to visualize the hybridization product, if present. This test involves using three to five fluorescent labeled probes to detect the specific DNA sequences. The analyst then uses an enzyme to detect the fluorescent labeled probes coupled with the sequences of DNA. For example, if the clinician performs a bronchoscopy, he passes a very small scope down the throat and into the lungs to directly examine and possibly biopsy lung tissue. While the bronchoscope is inserted, he may flush saline through specific areas of the lungs and collect this fluid to try to obtain cellular material. This cytopathology specimen is not a smear, so you would not use this code. short_description: Tissue culture for non-neoplastic disorders; amniotic fluid or chorionic villus cells
lay_term: The lab analyst prepares a tissue culture for nonneoplastic disorders using amniotic fluid or chorionic villus cells. In this process, fetal cells in amniotic fluid, which is fluid surrounding the developing fetus, and in the chorionic villi, which are the tiny projections on the outer layer of the fetal sac, multiply in a tissue culture for subsequent use in chromosome analysis. Explanation The lab analyst performs a procedure to culture fetal cells recovered from amniotic fluid or chorionic villus that will increase the number of cells available for genetic testing. The analyst receives the sample, collected by a clinician, in a syringe or sterile container and processes amniotic fluid by centrifugation, which essentially involves rapidly spinning to concentrate the cells, or by sorting a chorionic villus sample to remove maternal tissue. The analyst places the amniotic sediment or villus cells in a flask or petri dish with growth media, a substance composed of vitamins and amino acids, that nourishes and encourages the cells to divide and multiply. The cells incubate for about 14 days. During this time, fetal cells multiply in a process called mitosis, or cell division. The chromosomes line up, replicate, and form new cells. If the analyst did not culture the cells, they would not divide in great numbers and would not be suitable for chromosome analysis that requires visible genetic material. Although not limited to a specific condition, analysts typically perform tissue cultures using amniotic fluid or chorionic villus cells to increase the number of cells available for testing for chromosomal abnormalities. A clinician performs amniocentesis, inserting a needle through the abdomen or vaginally, to collect amniotic fluid at about 15 to 20 weeks gestation. Chorionic villus collection, using a catheter or needle placed into the placenta, can occur at 10 to 12 weeks gestation, providing an earlier sample and diagnosis than amniocentesis. Read Less

short_description: Cryopreservation, freezing and storage of cells, each cell line Notes: (For therapeutic cryopreservation and storage, use 38207)
lay_term: The analyst freezes and stores a cell line using cryopreservation, a method of stabilizing a cell line by freezing and storing it at very low temperatures. Freezing preserves samples of cells for future use or testing. Explanation The analyst prepares a cell line, such as stem cells or blood cells, for freezing by examining for contaminants and mixing the cells with a cryoprotective agent appropriate to the particular cell line. These agents may include sugars, glycerol, or dimethyl sulfoxide, DMSO, which all prevent damage to the cells during the freezing process. The analyst places the cells into special vials, inserts the vials into the cryogenic freezer, and slowly lowers the temperature using liquid nitrogen. The lower the temperature, reaching to minus 130 degrees Celsius, the longer the cell line’s viability, which means the ability to live. Storage organization in the freezer minimizes exposure of samples to warmer air when adding and removing vials. An analyst typically freezes cell lines to maintain cellular integrity. short_description: Chromosome analysis, in situ for amniotic fluid cells, count cells from 6-12 colonies, 1 karyotype, with banding
lay_term: The analyst performs chromosome analysis of cultured amniotic fluid cells in situ, counts cells from six to 12 colonies, and prepares one karyotype, with banding. In situ analysis means examining the cells directly on the surface they grow on. Explanation The analyst performs all steps of the chromosome analysis using amniotic fluid cells, which are cells collected from the fluid surrounding a fetus, previously cultured in situ. In situ cultures allow the cells to grow directly on a surface, typically small glass squares called coverslips, and to form groups of cells called colonies. He then counts the chromosomes in cells from each of six to 12 colonies to detect cells having more or less than the normal 46 chromosomes. By examining six to 12 colonies, the analyst observes a wide range of cells that may reveal genetic defects, called true mosaicism. He prepares one karyotype, an arrangement of the chromosomes in chronological order from one to 23, microscopically examines the chromosomes, and makes a photograph of the display. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, a clinician typically orders chromosome analysis, in situ for amniotic fluid cells, to check for fetal genetic defects, such as Down syndrome. In situ examinations commonly provide faster results because analysis occurs on primary cultures that do not require subculturing, which is regrowing one culture from another. short_description: Level I - Surgical pathology, gross examination only
lay_term: The physician, typically a pathologist, performs a level I examination of a surgical pathology specimen. The examination includes accessioning the specimen into the lab, which involves formally receiving the specimen, and then examining gross features of the specimen and reporting findings. Explanation The physician receives a surgical pathology specimen and assigns each specimen vial or specimen an accession number, which is a unique identifier. He performs a gross exam, which is a review of features observed without a microscope, such as the color and shape. He prepares a detailed report for each specimen that may include a diagnosis. Use this code for a level I examination. Tips The codes from 88300 to 88309 represent ascending levels of physician work. If the physician examines a specimen that none of the codes list, you should assign the code that best represents the work required using the listed specimens for comparison. But take note that you should never upcode a listed specimen because it was more work than usual. The service that the pathologist provides for each specimen is accession, examination, and reporting. Except for 88300, Level I, Surgical pathology, gross examination only, the work involves gross and microscopic examination of the tissue, including routine staining with the use of such substances as hematoxylin and eosin. To ensure accurate surgical pathology coding, the pathologist must provide information related to the diagnosis and a specimen description, and the coder must understand what factors will impact code assignment. Knowing the organ or anatomic site is not enough to choose the proper surgical pathology code. Many organs appear under multiple codes for surgical pathology; some even appear at every level of service. To choose the proper code, watch code descriptors for whether the specimen requires microscopic evaluation of surgical margins, the extent of the resection, the presence or absence of lymph tissue, or other distinguishing features. For instance, a breast biopsy, such as a needle localization biopsy procedure, doesn't require surgical margin evaluation, so you should report level IV code 88305, which applies to breast, biopsy, not requiring microscopic evaluation of surgical margins. On the other hand, a lumpectomy indicates the provider’s attempt to remove the entire lesion, and the pathologist would normally evaluate surgical margins. When the pathologist documents evaluating margins, you should list a lumpectomy as level V code 88307, which applies to breast, excision of lesion, requiring microscopic evaluation of surgical margins. If the provider removes breast tissue with contiguous lymph nodes, report level VI code 88309, which applies to breast, mastectomy with regional lymph nodes. The pathology report might describe this type of specimen using different names, such as simple mastectomy with axillary dissection, modified radical mastectomy, or total mastectomy. Read Less

lay_term: The physician, typically a pathologist, performs a level II examination of a surgical pathology specimen. The examination includes accessioning the specimen into the lab, which involves formally receiving the specimen, and then examining the gross and microscopic features of the specimen and reporting findings. Explanation The physician receives a surgical pathology specimen, such as an appendix, a traumatically amputated toe, or a hernia sac, and assigns each specimen vial or specimen an accession number, which is a unique identifier. He performs a gross exam, which is a review of features observed without a microscope, such as the color and shape, and a microscopic exam to determine the presence of disease or abnormalities. He prepares a detailed report for each specimen that may include a diagnosis. Use this code for a level II examination. Tips The codes from 88300 to 88309 represent ascending levels of physician work. If the physician examines a specimen that none of the codes lists, you should assign the code that best represents the work required using the listed specimens for comparison. But take note that you should never upcode a listed specimen because it was more work than usual. The service that the pathologist provides for each specimen is accession, examination, and reporting. Except for 88300, Level I, Surgical pathology, gross examination only, the work involves gross and microscopic examination of the tissue, including routine staining with the use of such substances as hematoxylin and eosin. To ensure accurate surgical pathology coding, the pathologist must provide information related to the diagnosis and a specimen description, and the coder must understand what factors will impact code assignment. Knowing the organ or anatomic site is not enough to choose the proper surgical pathology code. Many organs appear under multiple codes for surgical pathology; some even appear at every level of service. To choose the proper code, watch code descriptors for whether the specimen requires microscopic evaluation of surgical margins, the extent of the resection, the presence or absence of lymph tissue, or other distinguishing features. For instance, a breast biopsy, such as a needle localization biopsy procedure, doesn't require surgical margin evaluation, so you should report level IV code 88305, which applies to breast, biopsy, not requiring microscopic evaluation of surgical margins. On the other hand, a lumpectomy indicates the provider’s attempt to remove the entire lesion, and the pathologist would normally evaluate surgical margins. When the pathologist documents evaluating margins, you should list a lumpectomy as level V code 88307, which applies to breast, excision of a lesion, requiring microscopic evaluation of surgical margins. If the provider removes breast tissue with contiguous lymph nodes, report level VI code 88309, which applies to breast, mastectomy with regional lymph nodes. The pathology report might describe this type of specimen using different names, such as simple mastectomy with axillary dissection, modified radical mastectomy, or total mastectomy. Read Less

short_description: Special stain including interpretation and report; Group I for microorganisms (eg, acid fast, methenamine silver) Notes: (Use 0756T in conjunction with 88312 when the digitization of glass microscope slides is performed) (Report one unit of 88312 for each special stain, on each surgical pathology block, cytologic specimen, or hematologic smear)
lay_term: The lab analyst performs the technical lab steps to stain a specimen with a special stain. This code applies to Group I for microorganisms. A qualified provider, typically a pathologist, interprets the slide and issues a report. Explanation The lab analyst performs all technical steps to stain a specimen slide with a special Group I stain for microorganisms. A qualified provider then interprets and reports the results. In a separate service, the clinician obtains a specimen. The specimen can be from any source. Note that this code describes a special stain of the specimen, not a routine stain performed for bacterial identification in the laboratory such as the Gram stain. There are a number of bacteria that are unable to be stained using the routine process; Mycobacterium is an example. The cell walls of Mycobacteria will not take the usual stain, and so the analyst must treat them first with a process called acid fast staining that includes staining with a carbol fuchsin stain and heating over a water bath, then flooding the slide with an acid alcohol and another stain such as crystal violet. The bacteria will take the first stain and not be decolorized by the acid alcohol, which is the reason the bacteria are called acid fast. The methenamine silver staining procedure follows another series of steps that allows many fungi to stain in different colors allowing for better identification. Although not limited to a specific condition, providers may perform this test when they are trying to identify an organism that does not stain with routine stains. Terminology Mycobacterium: Acid fast bacterium that causes conditions such as tuberculosis and leprosy. Tips Review 88312 to 88319 to be sure you’ve chosen the most appropriate special stain code for your case. Pathologists often use special stains to enhance the microscopic evaluation of tissue, cytology, and other specimens. You won't report every stain your lab uses with one of these codes. Standard stains that are part of routine slide preparation, such as hematoxylin and eosin, H and E, don't require a separate code because they are part of the surgical pathology or cytology service. If the pathologist uses multiple special stains on a single pathology block, cytologic specimen, or hematologic smear, report each stain with a separate code. That may mean multiple units of the same stain code, if the stains are for the same purpose, or different stain codes, if the stains are for two different purposes such as microorganism and morphology. lay_term: The lab analyst performs the technical lab steps to stain a specimen for Group II identification, for example an iron stain or trichrome stain. A qualified provider, typically a pathologist, interprets the slide and issues a report. This code does not include staining for microorganisms, enzyme constituents, or for the antigen–antibody tests of immunochemistry or immunohistochemistry. Explanation The lab analyst performs all technical steps to stain a specimen slide with a special stain for Group II identification. A qualified provider then interprets and reports the results. In a separate service, the clinician obtains a specimen. The specimen may be a surgical pathology specimen, cytology specimen, or hematology smear. The analyst bases the choice of special stains on what the clinician may be looking for. An analyst generally performs an iron stain with Prussian blue. A trichrome stain includes any three special stains in one staining procedure; names vary based on the three stains included. Use this code for each special stain performed on each surgical pathology block, cytologic specimen, or hematologic smear. Antigen: Foreign bodies, such as bacteria, that enter the human body, or substances that form within the body, that cause an immune response, such as antibody production, and possibly infection; lab tests may utilize reactions between antibodies and antigens to identify a substance in a patient specimen. Code +88350 describes the procedure for a single antibody stain following an initial stain with a different antibody. Explanation The analyst performs an indirect immunofluorescent study, or a direct immunofluorescent (DIF) study on a tissue of cellular sample. The procedure involves applying and evaluating slides for one specific antibody stain. The procedure may include steps such as staining the specimen with a solution containing fluorescently labeled antibodies. During an incubation period, the antibodies, typically IgA, IgM, or IgG, bind to specific antigens that indicate autoimmune disorders, such as Lupus. short_description: Morphometric analysis, in situ hybridization (quantitative or semi-quantitative), using computer-assisted technology, per specimen; initial single probe stain procedure
lay_term: The lab analyst applies an initial in situ hybridization single probe stain on a slide or slides prepared from a single patient specimen, such as tumor tissue. The lab analyst processes the slides using computer assisted technology that counts or estimates the number of probes. Then a qualified provider, typically a pathologist, evaluates the stained slides and the results of the computer enumeration, and interprets the results to provide a pathologic diagnosis. Explanation The lab analyst performs the technical steps to prepare stained slides from the patient specimen, such as tumor tissue, using a specialized stain process called in situ hybridization, or ISH. The ISH stain includes a DNA or RNA probe, which selectively attaches to a target segment of DNA or RNA in the patient tissue in a process called hybridization. The probe includes some kind of marker, often a fluorescent molecule, which the lab analyst can visualize using a fluorescence microscope to localize the target in the tissue. The specific process that uses a fluorescent marker is called fluorescence ISH, or FISH. Using a typical specimen such as formalin fixed paraffin embedded tumor tissue, the lab analyst cuts and mounts the tissue onto slides, adds reagents to prepare slides to receive the stain, then applies the initial single probe stain. The procedure also includes computer assisted technology to locate and enumerate the probes on the slides. The pathologist looks at the probe stained slides under the microscope and uses her observation plus the computer enumeration results to report the findings, either as a quantitative value, such as a percentage of probe stained cells, or as a semiquantitative value, such as a numerical score that represents a clinically significant range of probes in tumor cells. This sort of enumeration is called morphometric analysis. The pathologist interprets the findings to reach a pathologic diagnosis and prepares a report for the ordering clinician. If the procedure does not include a quantitative or semiquantitative evaluation, don’t use this code; instead look at codes in the range +88364 to 88366. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, providers commonly perform this test to aid in the diagnosis of certain cancers. Morphometric ISH testing allows the provider to detect, localize, and enumerate in the specimen a gene of interest that may characterize tumor processes in cases such as some breast or cervical cancers. Information from ISH stains can aid the clinician in diagnosing and planning treatment for certain cancers. Terminology Hybridization: Forming a double stranded DNA or RNA molecule by combining two complementary single strands, usually to identify a genetic mutation. Reagent: A substance used in a lab test to bring about a desired change or reaction, often to reveal the presence or quantity of another substance that is the focus of the test. Tips Report this code once per specimen, no matter how many blocks, such as paraffin blocks, or stained slides the lab analyst prepares. CPT® defines surgical a pathology specimen as follows: tissue or tissues that are submitted for individual and separate attention, requiring individual examination and pathologic diagnosis. Use this code only for quantitative or semiquantitative ISH stains. See codes in the range +88364 to 88366 for qualitative ISH. Code 88367 is in a family with +88373, each additional single probe stain procedure to 88374, each multiplex probe stain procedure. The common part of the descriptor specifies that the codes are for computer assisted morphometric analysis of an ISH stain per specimen. This code describes the initial single probe stain. If the lab analyst stains other slides from the same specimen with additional single probe stains, report each additional stain using +88373, Morphometric analysis, in situ hybridization, quantitative or semiquantitative, using computer assisted technology, per specimen; each additional single probe stain procedure, List separately in addition to code for primary procedure. This code describes a stain that uses just one DNA or RNA probe. A multiplex stain uses multiple probes, and you should not use 88367 for a multiplex stain. Instead use 88374, Morphometric analysis, in situ hybridization, quantitative or semiquantitative, using computer assisted technology, per specimen; each multiplex probe stain procedure. Code 88367 represents the global service, meaning that reporting the code without a modifier describes both the technical work that the lab analyst performs to prepare the slides, and the professional work that that pathologist performs to interpret and report on the slides. If you’re billing only for the technical work, append modifier TC, Technical component, to the code. If you’re billing only for the professional work, append modifier 26, Professional component, to the code. For tumor ISH for bladder cancer that uses a cytology specimen, which is cellular material, don’t use codes in the range +88364 to 88377, but instead look to codes in the range 88120 to 88121. If the lab analyst performs an ISH test to assess conditions other than cancer, such as heritable diseases associated with deletions or chromosome abnormalities, don’t use these codes, but look to cytogenetics codes in the range 88271 to 88275 instead. Also, use codes from the range 88271 to 88275 if a provider not approved by payers to interpret an ISH test, such as a PhD laboratory scientist, interprets any ISH test, even a test for tumor analysis. short_description: Caffeine halothane contracture test (CHCT) for malignant hyperthermia susceptibility, including interpretation and report
lay_term: An analyst performs a caffeine halothane contracture test, CHCT, to evaluate a patient’s muscle biopsy for susceptibility to malignant hyperthermia, MH, a life threatening reaction to certain drugs used for anesthesia. Explanation An analyst, typically a pathologist, performs the technical steps to evaluate a patient’s muscle biopsy for susceptibility to MH. Collection of the biopsy, a section of thigh muscle about three inches long, occurs with the patient under general anesthesia. The pathologist receives the muscle sample, places it in a contraction chamber, and applies an electrical stimulation. He repeats the contraction measurements with the muscles exposed to the anesthetic halothane, which increases contractions in susceptible people, and caffeine, which does not increase contractions. Malignant hyperthermia occurs in patients undergoing general anesthesia who experience reactions, such as a high temperature, rapid breathing and heart rate, and muscular rigidity, when exposed to anesthesia drugs such as halothane and succinylcholine. The pathologist provides an interpretation of his observations and testing, and issues a report. Although not limited to a specific condition, a clinician typically orders a CHCT for patients undergoing anesthesia with a personal or family history of MH. If a patient tests positive for CHCT, a clinician may consider alternative anesthesia drugs to avoid MH. Terminology Biopsy: To remove a portion or the entirety of suspicious tissue for pathologic examination; types of biopsies include excisional, incisional, punch, needle, open. Tips The provider who harvests the muscle tissue should use a separate code such as 27324, Biopsy, soft tissue of thigh or knee area; deep, subfascial or intramuscular. Read Less

short_description: Cell count, miscellaneous body fluids (eg, cerebrospinal fluid, joint fluid), except blood
lay_term: A lab analyst performs a cell count of miscellaneous body fluids, such as cerebrospinal fluid, called CSF, or joint fluid. This code is not appropriate for a test on blood. Explanation The lab analyst performs the technical steps to evaluate and enumerate the cell count in a body fluid using manual or automated methods. He receives a body fluid such as CSF, pleural fluid from the chest, or urine but for this service he does not analyze blood. He observes the physical features such as color and counts cells in the specimen. He may count cells manually using a hemocytometer, a specialized glass slide with a grid of etched lines to facilitate counting, or automated cell counters that use flow cytometry methods to count and categorize cells. A flow cytometer counts and identifies cells by surrounding them in a narrow stream of fluid, passing the cells in a single line past a focused light or laser beam that measure the fluorescence and light scatter with a photodetector. Although not limited to testing for specific conditions, a clinician may order a body fluid cell count to determine the cause of meningitis, infection, or inflammation, and to evaluate conditions such as congestive heart failure and gout. Terminology Antibody: Also called immunoglobulin; a protein that the body produces in the blood as part of the immune response to neutralize specific invaders such as bacteria or viruses, but occasionally reacts to the patient’s own body; lab tests may utilize reactions between antibodies and antigens to identify a substance in a patient specimen. Congestive heart failure: Excessive fluid collects in the tissues of the lungs, trunk, or extremities due to heart disease; it results in difficulty breathing and increased blood pressure; too much salt intake contributes to this condition. Eosinophils: A form of white blood cells characterized by large, round granules that stain orange with the dye eosin and increase with allergy and parasitic conditions. Lymphocyte: A mononuclear white blood cell with two types, B cells and T cells, that produce antibodies to fight infection. Meningitis: An inflammation of the meninges, the covering of the brain and spinal cord. Neutrophils: The most abundant form of white blood cells, neutrophils originate from stem cells in the bone marrow, are short lived, and are essential to functioning of the immune system. Tips If the analyst also performs a differential, see 89051, Cell count, miscellaneous body fluids (e.g., cerebrospinal fluid, joint fluid), except blood; with differential count. Read Less

short_description: Cell count, miscellaneous body fluids (eg, cerebrospinal fluid, joint fluid), except blood; with differential count
lay_term: The lab analyst performs the technical lab steps to analyze a body fluid, excluding blood, with a cell count and a differential count to measure the amounts of white blood cells present. Explanation The lab analyst performs all technical steps to complete a cell count for any body fluid except blood, including a differential count. The specimen for this test is a body fluid; examples are cerebrospinal fluid, joint fluid, pleural fluid from the chest, or peritoneal fluid from the abdomen. He evaluates and enumerates cells in the body fluid using manual or automated methods. He counts cells including red blood cells and white blood cells. He may count cells manually using a hemocytometer, a specialized glass slide with a grid of etched lines to facilitate counting, or automated cell counters that use flow cytometry methods to count and categorize cells. Flow cytometry surrounds the sample with a narrow stream of fluid. The cells travel in a single line past a focused light or laser beam that causes the stained cells to fluoresce and scatter light according to their structure. The lab analyst then performs a differential count on the fluid, either manually or by machine. A differential count differentiates the types of white blood cells present in the fluid, indicating what percent of the cells are lymphocytes, monocytes, neutrophils, etc. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians may order this test if a patient has a fluid collection suspected to be from an infection or cancer. Terminology Bronchioalveolar lavage, or BAL: In this service, a bronchoscope is introduced into the patient’s lungs; fluid is then washed through the lungs and collected for analysis. Cerebrospinal fluid, or CSF: Liquid that circulates in and around the brain and spinal cord. Lymphocytes: The second most abundant form of white blood cells, they originate from stem cells in the bone marrow, some then travel to the thymus for differentiation, and are responsible for aiding the immune system. Monocytes: The largest of the white blood cells, monocytes originate from stem cells in the bone marrow and are responsible for helping to get rid of dead cells and foreign materials in the blood. Neutrophils: The most abundant form of white blood cells, neutrophils originate from stem cells in the bone marrow, are short lived, and are essential to functioning of the immune system. Peritoneal fluid: Fluid that can accumulate in the peritoneum; often as the results of liver failure, also called ascites. Peritoneum: The membrane lining the abdominal cavity that attaches various organs to the abdominal wall. Pleural fluid: Fluid that collects in the pleura; the lining around the lungs. Tips If a clinician orders a bronchioalveolar lavage, BAL, you would report 88108 for cytopathology, concentration technique, smears and interpretation; and if the clinician orders a white count and differential on the same fluid, it would also be appropriate to report 89051. For example, if the BAL appears to indicate an infectious pathology rather than a tumor, the clinician might want to get an idea of the presence and types of white cells. Note that the differential count would not be quantitative because of the dilution of the washing. Although labs more commonly use 89051 for body fluids such as CSF, a clinician might order it for a BAL in some circumstances. The key is to report both the cytologic evaluation and the differential count if both services are provided. Read Less

lay_term: The analyst cultures oocytes or embryos for fewer than four days with a coculture of oocytes or embryos as part of an assisted reproductive technology, ART, procedure. Explanation The analyst performs technical steps to prepare an environment, including substances to grow and nourish one or more embryos or developing oocytes, which are immature eggs collected from an ovary. The environment includes feeder cells called a co culture, that supplement the developing cells. Types of feeder cells include fallopian tube cells, uterine cells, and cumulus cells that surround the maturing egg. Other environmental factors may include artificial media such as glucose and amino acids, controlled temperature, and oxygen concentration. After collection, the analyst incubates the oocytes or embryos for fewer than four days. Embryos are oocytes previously inseminated with sperm and allowed to divide until they reach a four cell stage. These cells incubate until implanted into a uterus before the fourth day after collection. The clinician typically performs a culture of oocytes and embryos with coculture to increase the chances of producing a viable embryo for implantation in an ART procedure. Terminology Culture: To cultivate the growth of bacteria or other organisms or tissue cells in an artificial medium prepared with specific nutrients and incubated under specific conditions to encourage reproduction and growth of specific types of cells. lay_term: The lab analyst performs the technical lab steps to isolate sperm to prepare it for insemination or diagnosis. This code is specific to complex prep and includes semen analysis. Explanation The lab analyst performs all technical steps to isolate sperm during a semen analysis using a complex prep, such as Percoll gradient or albumin gradient, for insemination during an in vitro fertilization cycle or for diagnostic purposes to identify sperm abnormalities. Collected semen contains materials other than just sperm, and the analyst needs to separate out these other materials to isolate the sperm. The patient may collect the specimen himself or a clinician may perform the collection by inserting a fine needle into the testicle to obtain the sample in a separately reported service. The analyst analyzes the sperm, usually under a microscope, to ensure there are enough sperm present and to note the shape, size, and motility. Using complex services such as one of the gradient tests mentioned above, the analyst mixes the semen with a medium and then places the mixture in a centrifuge. After the material runs through the centrifuge, which spins the material at high speed, all the sperm will be at the bottom of the tube. Discarding the liquid at the top leaves a purer sperm sample. Sometimes is the analyst may repeat the centrifuge step for better purification. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, providers may order this service for a patient involved in vitro fertilization or for a male patient suspected of having a spermatic disorder requiring a diagnosis. Terminology Gradient: Not the same all the way through, increasing or decreasing levels. Insemination: The introduction of sperm to eggs to fertilize them for pregnancy. In vitro fertilization, or IVF: A laboratory procedure to enhance the likelihood of pregnancy that involves stimulation of the ovaries, retrieval of eggs, insemination of eggs, and transfer of fertilized eggs to the uterus. Motility: The ability to move voluntarily. Semen: Fluid from the male reproductive system that contains sperm. Tips This service includes the work of semen analysis, such as count and motility, so you should not report semen analysis codes such as 89300 and 89310 with 89261. See 89260 for simple prep. Because infertility treatment often involves both a man and a woman, coders aren't always sure whose insurance they should bill. In the absence of specific payer guidance, you should bill whichever patient is most directly connected with a given service. The exception with artificial insemination is when a sperm donor is involved. In this case, you would bill the sperm wash and the insemination code to the female because the female accepts financial responsibility. Generally, physician offices use 58323, Sperm washing for artificial insemination. A high complexity lab is most likely to use the complex prep represented by 89261. Percoll gradient and albumin gradient and other gradient preparations use a specific medium that is less dense at the top of the tube and denser at the bottom so that as the specimen is centrifuged the more dense items in the sample will be able to reach the bottom of the tube. The analyst then places the sample under a microscope and performs a sperm count along with assessing motility, or free movement, and morphology using strict morphologic criteria. Computer–assisted software is also available that can analyze the specimen. This code can be for manual or computer–assisted assessment. Morphology is how the sperm appears, such as whether the size is normal, the shape of the head, the length of the tail, etc. This code is for those specimens undergoing specific strict criteria such as those used by the Kruger test or the World Health Organization (WHO). These criteria use thousands of samples from all over the world to define normal statistics; the lab analyst or computer software will compare the results from this specimen with those using the strict criteria to give a result. Along with the result, the analyst should give a normal value. For instance, the report may state the patient has motility of 35 percent, the normal range is 40 percent to 60 percent. The analyst also performs a differential count on this specimen; this is a differentiation of any white blood cells that are present in the sample. White blood cells in the semen can indicate inflammation or infection and increase infertility. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians may order this test for a male with suspected infertility. Tips Code 89322 includes a more detailed semen analysis procedure using strict morphologic criteria than 89331, Sperm evaluation, for retrograde ejaculation, urine, sperm concentration, motility, and morphology, as indicated. You may report 89331 in addition to 89322. For you to bill 89322, the analyst must inspect each sperm for the head, neck, and tail. Read Less

short_description: Sperm evaluation; cervical mucus penetration test, with or without spinnbarkeit test
lay_term: The lab analyst performs the technical lab test to analyze sperm using a cervical mucus penetration test. This test may or may not include a spinnbarkeit test to test the elasticity of the cervical mucus. Explanation The lab analyst performs all technical steps to analyze a sample of sperm to see how far it can move through cervical mucus. To perform this test, the analyst uses a sample of a woman’s cervical mucus, preferably from the time of ovulation when the mucus is the thickest. The man must then give a semen specimen around the same time. In the lab, the analyst mixes the semen with the cervical mucus and, after waiting a period of time, measures the distance the sperm has moved through the mucus. The analyst may or may not use a spinnbarkeit test to measure cervical mucus elasticity. The analyst measures a string of the mucus to see how elastic it is, which is how far it can stretch before breaking. The mucus is most elastic at the time of ovulation. Although not limited to testing for a specific condition, clinicians may order this test if they suspect male infertility is due to low sperm motility, which is free movement. Tips Code 89330 is not a gender specific code; therefore, payers may allow you to report this code for either male or female patients. Read Less

short_description: Cryopreservation, mature oocyte(s)
lay_term: The lab analyst performs the technical lab test to preserve and store one or more mature living oocytes at low temperatures for future use. This service preserves the egg cells for patients at high risk of infertility due to treatments such as chemotherapy or radiation therapy. Explanation The lab analyst performs all technical steps to preserve and store living mature oocytes at low temperatures for future use. Cryopreservation is a technique to preserve living cells, whole tissues, organs, or other substances in a living condition by cooling them to subzero temperatures and storing them at low temperatures for future use. In a separate procedure, the provider obtains mature oocytes, by superovulation, an infertility treatment using drugs to induce the production of multiple eggs at one time to cryopreserve them. For 89337, there are two typical methods of cryopreservation: slow freezing and vitrification, or ultrarapid freezing. Slow freezing exposes the oocytes to a cryoprotectant solution and cools them slowly to about minus 140 degrees Celsius then places the oocytes in liquid nitrogen to cool them to minus 196 degrees Celsius for storage. Vitrification rapidly cools the oocytes using a high concentration of a cryoprotectant and cooling within minutes to stop ice crystals from forming. Once the provider prepares the mature oocytes, the oocytes will be ready for the separate services of storing them for an artificial form of assisted insemination such as an intracytoplasmic sperm injection, or ICSI, where the provider places a single sperm into an egg to fertilize it and then places the fertilized embryo into the uterus. Although not limited to a specific condition, providers may perform this procedure when a woman requires mature oocytes to be harvested and cryopreserved for future use. Terminology Chemotherapy: Drugs used for cancer treatment; also known as cytotoxic agents. Oocyte: An ovum, or egg, produced in the ovaries. In vitro fertilization, or IVF: Infertility procedure to remove eggs from the ovaries, fertilize them by sperm in a laboratory, and place the fertilized embryo into the uterus. Radiation oncology: Radiation oncology, also called radiotherapy, applies high frequency radiation to target and destroy cancerous tumors. Read Less

Explanation The lab analyst performs a procedure related to the reproductive system that is not represented by any of the standard and active CPT® codes available. You should report the service using only the appropriate unlisted procedure code if no such specific procedure or service code exists. You must report a Category III code when available in place of an unlisted procedure code. When reporting a procedure with an unlisted code, submit a cover letter explaining the reason for choosing the unlisted code instead of a defined, active code. Include one or more similar codes, and compare your service to those codes to justify the claim amount you are billing. Also include the notes from the medical record or other relevant documentation to strengthen the claim and to avoid a possible denial.
